# TO THE READER, SALUTATIONS FROM A. DU VERDIER.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'L' set against a background of intricate floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

*The great Scipio, surnamed Africanus after the nation he subdued, when looking upon the images of the ancient heroes <term>Heroes: in this context, the term refers to both semi-divine figures of myth and the exceptionally virtuous men of antiquity</term>, was accustomed to say that he was greatly spurred toward magnanimous deeds by the reading of their achievements. By this, he meant to show that the principal goal of writing history is to place before one's eyes, as if in a high and eminent place, the examples of the acts of men.*

*Emperor GAIUS <note>likely referring to Gaius Caesar, or Julius Caesar, as the following story is traditionally attributed to him</note>, having seen a statue of Alexander the Great in Spain, began to weep, as if suddenly seized by a shame of himself for having not yet performed any deed worthy of memory at the age in which the other had already subdued and conquered a great part of the world. However, Plutarch says that this happened to Julius Caesar while contemplating some history of the same Alexander painted on a wall of the temple of Hercules. For the ancients had the custom of painting the walls of frequently visited temples with the illustrious deeds of great personages, with a summary of them written below, in order to incite readers to acquire glory by imitating such examples. We read that this happened to the aforementioned Caesar, whose deeds—so numerous and memorable—shall not be erased by any age, but remaining in full force shall be recited for all time. Seeing then that history has such efficacy that it can move the spirits of men to do good, and can better incite them when that which is written is presented and expressed in painting, engraving, high-relief sculpture <note>original: "taille esleuee en bosse"</note>, or otherwise: I have made a collection of several figures of distinguished persons, other than those which have been made heretofore and which are seen in the books of medals <term>books of medals: a popular 16th-century genre of books containing portraits of famous people based on ancient coins and medallions</term>: at the foot of which*

*only, and civil in effect, came to Florence. And because you are a friend of the Muses and their inventions, and hold learning <term>Science: in the 16th century, this term referred broadly to knowledge, wisdom, or the liberal arts rather than exclusively to the modern natural sciences</term> in high esteem—with which your mind is abundantly provided, as testified not only by that learned poet Scévole de Sainte-Marthe <note>A distinguished French poet and orator (1536–1623) who was a contemporary of Du Verdier</note>, but by all those who have the good fortune of knowing you—I wished to give and dedicate this work of mine to you, which I publish bearing your name on its front to serve as a passport recognized by all, and to protect it from the danger of over-severe censors. And if I find that it is pleasing to you, I shall dedicate to you something more worthy of your gaze. From Montbrison <note>A town in the Forez region of France where Antoine du Verdier was born and held office</note>, this first of October, 1572.*

which, having briefly described the lives of those whom the
said figures represent, I have entitled this work *Prosopography*,
that is to say, Description of Persons <term>Prosopographie: from the Greek 'prosopon' (face/person) and 'graphia' (writing/description)</term>. I had proposed to have
portrayed and afterwards engraved a much greater number

age, the printer having kept it six years in his hands, because
of the troubles <note>a common euphemism for the French Wars of Religion (1562–1598)</note>, for which reason it could not be as well polished as would be
fitting for such a subject. It is true that I have always avoided an affec-
tation of language called by the Greeks, *kakozelia* <note>original: κακοζηλίαν—a stylistic vice involving affected, pretentious, or inappropriate language</note>: and have mixed
some Greek and Latin throughout, so as not to lose the grace of the
texts diligently researched by me: though many
would find it better if they were translated into French, seeing
(as one might say) that such a mixture makes the work schol-
astic and obscure to him who does not understand the languages. But I have taken
pleasure in writing in this fashion following the example of Heraclitus, who
knowingly wrote as obscurely as possible in his
book, so that only the learned might read it, and so that if it
were read by the common people, it would not be held in contempt.
Aristotle did the same in his books of physics, just as he himself
gave reason for it and replied to Alexander the Great. And the learned
Muret <note>Marc-Antoine Muret, a renowned French humanist scholar</note> in his various lessons did not wish to translate his Greek. For I
have always esteemed with these great personages that the voice of one
learned man has more power to recommend us to immortality
than that of a thousand ignorant ones. This is one of the reasons by
which I have been induced to write in this way, striving to
content the learned, and taking no account of the censure of the ignorant,
who often speak ill of that which they cannot reach: as

The second reason is to exercise myself in the reading of histories, and to better imprint in my memory the texts and citations even to the very words: my greatest pleasure being in letters. For this reason, some of my neighbors and acquaintances, seeing me so devoted to study and often leaving aside more serious business, advised me that it would be better to occupy myself with visiting my domains, estates, and rents rather than books; I (as a response) cited this tale: A father of a family had two sons, to whom at his death he left many fine goods and furnishings, and among others a great quantity of oil to keep the lamp burning at night <note>Oil was a significant expense for scholars; the phrase "to smell of the lamp" traditionally referred to the hard work of nighttime study.</note>: one of them consumed his oil in banquets and delicious nights, for which reason he was briefly reduced to great poverty: the other took pains with letters, and using his oil in nightly readings to watch and study, he became greatly rich. # F. DE BELLEFOREST OF
## COMMINGES, TO THE AUTHOR,
### on his Prosopography, <note>Comminges is a region in the Pyrenees of southwestern France. François de Belleforest (1530–1583) was a prolific writer and historian famous for his "Universal History."</note>

->Sonnet.<-

No painter, no engraver, whether on wood or
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;copper,
Knows how to paint or engrave so skillfully
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the burin’s line
That which is good in man, or that which he can design,
As you do (my Du Verdier) through the strokes of your book.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The chisel or colors will not make him live,
The engraver's tool cannot eternalize him for a moment:
For color perishes, and the artist,
However excellent he may be, can barely rescue him from oblivion.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But Du Verdier, tracing with an immortal pen <note>original: "burin immortel." Belleforest uses the metaphor of the "immortal burin" (an engraving tool) to suggest that writing is a more permanent form of "engraving" than physical art.</note>
These excellent men, and raising (forever)
To the good and the learned his Prosopography: <term>Prosopography (Prosopographie): from the Greek words for "face" or "person" and "to write." In the Renaissance, this referred to a collection of biographical sketches or descriptions of a person's appearance and character.</term>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as his art surpasses both painter and engraver,
So his hand bestows both soul and great vitality
Upon the learned, granting them name, meaning, and life.

->F. DE BELLEFOREST.<-

<summary>A commendatory sonnet by the historian François de Belleforest praising Antoine du Verdier. Belleforest argues that Du Verdier's biographical writing is superior to visual art because it captures the soul and grants its subjects immortality, whereas paintings and engravings eventually fade.</summary>
<keywords>François de Belleforest, Antoine du Verdier, sonnet, Renaissance humanism, immortality of art, prosopography, commendatory verse</keywords>

# S O N N E T.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'C' depicting a classical seated figure, possibly a philosopher or the god Atlas, holding a large sphere or globe.</image-desc> HOW MUCH (*learned Verdier*) so many
*learned spirits*
*Owe to the greatness of your divine muse,*
*Whose winged renown, reaching to the stars,*
*Grants you a place among the ranks of the most learned men?*

*And not only those who, reading your writings,*
*Savor the sweetness born of your heart,* <note>original: "poitrine" (literally: chest/breast), used here metaphorically as the source of thought and emotion.</note>
*But those others as well whom cruel Fate* <note>original: "parque maline." The Parcae or Fates were the three goddesses in classical mythology who spun, measured, and cut the thread of human life.</note>
*Has deprived of the beautiful day that gilds this world.* <note>original: "pourpris," an archaic term meaning an enclosure, territory, or the world at large.</note>

*For the sacred pencil of your lively writing* <note>original: "creon," an early spelling of "crayon" (pencil), used here as a metaphor for the author's descriptive skill.</note>
*Proves itself such a friend to the works of nature*
*In these strokes enriched with new artistry:*

*That it ensures the living no longer have any*
*fear*
*That their glory shall fall extinguished beneath the coffin,*
*And that even the dead shall live again beneath the tomb.*

->P. Delariuey.<- <note>Pierre de Larivey (1541–1619) was a French author of Italian descent, best known for adapting Italian comedies into French prose, which significantly influenced the development of French theater.</note>

# ON THE PROSOPOGRAPHY
<note>The term <term>Prosopography</term> refers to a work describing the appearance, character, and lives of historical individuals.</note>
## BY NOBLE ANTOINE DU VERDIER,
## ODE.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' depicting two cherubic figures (putti) intertwined with foliage.</image-desc>
JUST as the diligent Pilot,
Writing <note>original: "escriuant." This is a poetic metaphor suggesting the ship’s wake marks the water like a pen on paper, or perhaps a play on the author's own labor.</note> upon the sea,
Bringing his Galley to rest
Upon the shores of the Levant, <note>The "Levant" refers to the lands of the eastern Mediterranean.</note>
With a curious effort <note>original: "pene," likely an archaic spelling of "peine" (effort/labor), though it could also pun on "penne" (quill).</note>
Among the shifting sands,
Seeks the most precious jewels
In which that land abounds,
The world’s rare wealth,
Royal gifts and treasures.

Thus, my Du Verdier, now
Dwelling upon Mount Parnassus, <note>In Greek mythology, Mount Parnassus was the home of the Muses and the symbolic center of poetry and learning.</note>
The Muses whom you diligently
Adorn, go on inciting you
To search through their shops,
Which are full of ancient histories,
For the diverse characters
Whose great renown,
Celebrated through so many ages,
Decorates this universe.

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<summary>A laudatory ode comparing Antoine du Verdier to a seafaring explorer gathering treasures, though his "treasures" are the historical figures he catalogues under the guidance of the Muses.</summary>
<keywords>Antoine du Verdier, Prosopography, Parnassus, Muses, maritime metaphor, biography, Renaissance poetry</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the laudatory ode to Antoine du Verdier. The previous page compared Du Verdier's scholarly pursuits to a pilot searching for treasures in the Levant; this page transitions to comparing his biographical compilation to the epic work of Homer.</meta>

To adorn your portraits <note>original: "pourtraitures." Du Verdier’s *Prosopographie* was famous for including woodcut illustrations alongside biographical sketches.</note>
With a well-composed summary,
In performing many readings
You do not cease day and night,
Within the chamber <note>original: "parquet," referring here to a court or a dedicated space for the arts.</note> of the Muses
Full of their infused graces:
And if you see some features <note>original: "traiz," meaning both the lines of a drawing and the characteristics of a person's life.</note>
Worthy of being remarkable,
You make notable collections of them
Beneath your portraits.

Thus the famous poet, <note>A reference to Homer, the legendary author of the *Iliad*.</note>
Seeing the host of the Greeks
Upon the Trojan height
Hurl the iron of the long wood, <note>A poetic description of spears or javelins.</note>
In the spirited battle
Of the boldest of the army,
Collected the valiant deeds,
And the warlike bravado,
Then made an *Iliad* from them
Of the victors and the defeated.

By such an excellent work
He received such honor,
That despite painful death
His name remains immortal.
Your work shall be the same,
Although it may not be a poem,
But for the collected places <note>original: "lieux amassez." This refers to "commonplaces" (*loci communes*), the Renaissance practice of gathering and categorizing important knowledge and rhetorical themes.</note>

<summary>This page continues a poem praising Antoine du Verdier’s scholarly diligence, comparing his biographical work to Homer’s creation of the Iliad. It emphasizes that Du Verdier’s collection of "commonplaces" and portraits will grant him the same immortality as the ancient poets.</summary>

<keywords>Antoine du Verdier, Homer, Iliad, Muses, commonplaces, portraiture, Renaissance biography, immortality</keywords>

In the Pegasean spring, <note>original: "source Pegasine." A reference to Hippocrene, the fountain on Mount Helicon struck by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus; it was sacred to the Muses and believed to provide poetic inspiration.</note>
Which serves as a workshop <note>original: "officine." In this context, it refers to a place where the records of history are prepared and preserved.</note>
Of all the centuries past.

That is why I see the band
Of the Aganippid sisters, <note>Another name for the Muses, taken from the Aganippe fountain, which was also a source of inspiration on Mount Helicon.</note>
Who all make an offering to you
Of their honeyed sweetnesses:
Who hold your pen ready
To be their interpreter,
Keeping for you as payment
And as a due reward
For your great diligence,
The laurel crown. <note>The traditional Greco-Roman symbol of victory, honor, and poetic achievement.</note>

# TO THE MAN DISTINGUISHED BY VIRTUE,
## LEARNING, AND NOBILITY,
### Antoine du Verdier, <note>original: "Anto. Verderium." Antoine du Verdier (1544–1600) was a French politician and celebrated bibliographer known for cataloging the works of French authors.</note> an Epigram
->by Antoine Valet, physician.<- <note>original: "Anto. Valetij medici." Antoine Valet (1524–1607) was a prominent French physician and humanist scholar.</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'S' decorated with curling vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

*If prophetic Apollo is not playing with me and hates falsehood,* <note>Apollo was the Greco-Roman god of prophecy, music, and poetry.</note>
*If any faith is to be placed in a seer, or in a God,*
*I myself, not ignorant of your destiny, prophesy the omen*
*That your name holds the renown of your distinguished name.* <note>The author is making a pun on the name "du Verdier," which sounds like the Latin "virens" or "viriditas," meaning greenness, vigor, or flourishing.</note>
*For just as a flourishing tree promises fruit,*
*While it prepares to luxuriate in green foliage:*
*So you, **DU VERDIER**, born to flourish in whatever*
*Season, bring back all things more abundantly as you turn green.*
*Such fruits as a fertile tree from its green trunk*
*Pours forth, to the delight of its cultivator.*
*Slippery things, which are scarcely preserved through passing years,*
*And hardly retain their own unviolated beauty:*
*But those things over which the nourishing presence of green spring presides,*
*Which causes all things to flourish in your name.*
*Indeed, you are the sole foster-child of the greening Aonian grove,* <note>original: "Aonij nemoris." The Aonian grove refers to the home of the Muses on Mount Helicon in Boeotia, Greece.</note>
*From which you take the omen of your name.*
*This little book of yours, written with noble effort,* <note>original: "ingenuo... marte." Literally "with noble Mars," a common humanist metaphor for strenuous intellectual or literary labor.</note>
*Will be a witness, flourishing for me in the manner of spring.*
*It discusses Sages, Heroes, and Popes:*
*And it causes ancient virtue to flourish even now.*
*But would that uncultivated virtue might flourish as much*
*As the cultivated Muse of your genius.*

->A. VALET OF JUVIGNAC.<- <note>original: "A. VALETIVS IVNIANENSIS." Referring to Antoine Valet's place of origin or association.</note>

<summary>This page features a Latin epigram by physician Antoine Valet honoring Antoine du Verdier. The poem uses extensive wordplay on Du Verdier's name—linking it to "greenness" and "spring"—to argue that his biographical work preserves the "flowering" of history and human virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Antoine du Verdier, Antoine Valet, Latin epigram, Renaissance humanism, wordplay, Muses, bibliography, Apollo</keywords>

Moses calls him the Serpent by reason of his cunning and transformation: for besides his shrewdness, he transforms into diverse shapes whenever he pleases, sometimes into an Angel of light. The Hebrews say that, just as in the Gospel the prince of devils is called Beelzebub, so Resheph <note>Resheph: A Hebrew term appearing in the Bible usually meaning "flame" or "plague," but here the author links it to the serpent's curse in Genesis.</note> is the name of the devil who holds principality over the others, having taken this name from the curse by which he was condemned by God; for Resheph is interpreted as "crawling on the belly." Our Lord has imposed upon him the name of SATAN, meaning that this unclean spirit possesses a name suitable to the perverse actions of which he is full, and to the sin he committed from the beginning: for Satan in the Judaic and Syriac <note>Syriac refers to Aramaic, the language spoken in the region during the biblical era.</note> tongues means apostate, adversary, and rebel. In Holy Scripture he is called the exterminator, angel of wrath, and mountain of pride <note>original: "superbie," from the Latin "superbia."</note>: for by "mountains," one can allegorically understand the devils who raise themselves up against the knowledge of God and cannot reach it. Wishing to equal the Most High, he fell down low, overconfident as he was in his presumption to undertake a struggle 
<margin>Isaiah 14.</margin> against his creator. Isaiah testifies to this through these words:

### BOOK ONE.
<sig>a 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: for</meta>

Ho**mer** <note>The text continues from the previous page: "Ho-mer."</note> made mention of this enemy of the human race in the *Iliad*, book 18 or 19: not that he calls him by his proper name of "devil," but by another suited to the effects and evil works of which he is full, calling him Até, which is to say "nuisance" and "damage"; and as if he remembered very well what Isaiah the Prophet had said of him, he relates that he was banished and cast out of heaven by their great God. Because of his great lightness and speed, he is named "bird." In this way, then, the devil is called prince of the world, that is to say, of all the wickednesses that are in the world.

Here, Cain killing his brother Abel is seen as a parallel to Christ being killed by his own people.</note>. <margin>Augustine, *Book of Heresies* <note>original: "August. li. de hærefi." refers to Saint Augustine’s work *De Haeresibus* (On Heresies).</note></margin> Saint Augustine gives an account of a strange opinion and sect of certain people in his time living in a small town near Hippo <note>Hippo Regius was an ancient city in what is now Annaba, Algeria, where Augustine served as Bishop.</note>. They called themselves Abelites, after the name of Abel, the son of Adam. They did not live together carnally with women <note>Meaning they abstained from sexual relations.</note>, although it was not permitted by the statutes of their sect to live without women or without being married. Therefore, the man and woman, living together under a vow of continence <term>continence</term> <note>The practice of self-restraint, specifically abstaining from sexual activity.</note>, adopted a son and a daughter to succeed them and inherit their goods. If these two children were taken by death before their parents, other children were chosen and put in their place, provided that two children of different sexes succeeded to the fellowship of that household. When the adoptive father and mother died, the adopted children took two other children fathered by the inhabitants of the surrounding areas, their neighbors, who, because of their poverty, willingly gave up their children in the hope of their future succession and inheritance. This heresy diminished greatly in the time of Saint Augustine, who converted its followers and led them to become Catholics.

# JUBAL.

**Jubal**, son of Lamech, is called in Genesis the father of musicians, because he discovered the art through the sound of hammers with which iron was being beaten, and through the inequality of strings and their unequal tension <note>A common medieval legend suggests that Jubal (or Pythagoras) discovered musical ratios by listening to the different pitches produced by blacksmiths' hammers of varying weights.</note>. > "The builder of Troy <note>Referring to Apollo, who helped build the walls of Troy</note>, notable for his lyre, loved me." <note>original Latin: "Me fide conspicuus Troiæ munitor amauit." From Ovid's *Heroides*.</note>

And Valerius Flaccus:
> "The choir of the Muses and Apollo, the player of the lyre." <note>original Latin: "Musarum chorus & citharæ pulsator Apollo." From the *Argonautica*.</note>

The Greeks maintain that Pythagoras invented the art of music; according to the poets, it was Orpheus and Linus <note>original: "Line"</note>, and according to Pliny, it was Amphion the Theban, whom Horace mentions in *The Art of Poetry*:
> "And Amphion was said to be the founder of the city of Thebes" <note>original Latin: "Dictus & Amphion Thebanæ conditor vrbis." Referring to the myth that Amphion moved stones to build the city walls by the power of his music.</note>

# JABAL.

<image-desc>An oval medallion engraving of the biblical figure Iabel (Jabal). He is depicted as a young shepherd standing in a landscape, leaning on a staff and surrounded by sheep and goats. A primitive tent or hut is visible in the background to the right. The border of the medallion is inscribed with the text "IABEL. F. LAMECH." **LAMECH**, son of **Methuselah**, in the lineage of **Cain**, was the first who, against the law of nature and custom, gave himself over to illicit and damnable unions, being bigamous—that is to say, burdening himself with two wives, even though a man is occupied enough with just one <note>The author offers a moralizing aside here, suggesting that managing a single household is difficult enough for any man.</note>; in doing so, he committed adultery. The first wife was named **Adah**, and the other **Zillah** <note>original: "Ade" and "Selle"</note>. He had seventy-seven children by these two wives, among whom was this **Jabal** <note>original: "Iabel"</note>, whom he had by his wife Adah. It was he who invented the tents and rustic pavilions that are carried into the fields for the guarding of livestock; these are the shepherds' huts, made nowadays of straw, where they sleep at night near the fold to guard their flocks.

...gods. Music is a great treasure to the men who have learned it and who are instructed in it. It establishes morals and appeases anger. Clinas <note>original: "Clynie"</note>, the Pythagorean, although he was rough and difficult in his way of life and in his manners, whenever he felt annoyed and enraged, would take up his lyre and play it. To those who asked him why he did this, he replied, "I am calming myself." <note>original: "Ie me mitigue"</note>.

Achilles in Homer was softened in his heart by the lyre that Homer allows him to take alone from the spoils of Eetion <note>Eetion was the King of Thebe and father of Andromache; Achilles killed him and took his lyre as a prize.</note>, so that he might be able to restrain his wrath. It also heals diseases, as Theophrastus <term>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</term> testifies in the book *On Divine Inspiration* <note>original Latin: "De afflatione numinis"</note>, where he says that those who suffer from sciatica are healed if, according to the custom of Phrygia <note>The Phrygian mode was one of the musical scales in ancient Greek music theory, often associated with religious fervor or healing power.</note>, someone native to that land sings with them in harmony and accord.

The robust Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> were accustomed to carrying flutes to war. Those of Crete used the lyre, and the Lydians used flutes and syrinxes <note>original: "syringues," commonly known as panpipes or sets of reeds.</note>, as Herodotus relates. Several barbarians also, when sent as ambassadors for peace, softened the hearts of their enemies with the sound of flutes and lyres. The Getae <note>An ancient Thracian tribe from the lower Danube region.</note> (says Theopompus), playing their harps, undertake legations and embassies to treat for peace.

Homer introduces the gods using music at the beginning of the *Iliad* after the debate of Achilles, for they listened to:

> *Apollo held the beautiful lyre in his hands,* <note>original Latin: "Formosam citharam, hanc manibus tenebat Apollo,"</note>
> *And the Muses sang, alternating their voices.* <note>original Latin: "Musarum vocem variantes haeq, canebant."</note>

For it was necessary to appease the debates and seditions. It was commonly played at banquets. Homer [wrote]:

> *The lyre of the banquet, which the gods made a companion.* <note>original Latin: "Convivij citharam quam dij fecere sodalem."</note>

And Justin the historian <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd-century Roman historian who summarized the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note>, in his last book, asserts that they are located next to this river.

PROSOPOGRAPHY

# NAAMAH <note>The source uses the French "Noeme." In the Book of Genesis, Naamah is the daughter of Lamech and Zillah, and sister to Tubal-cain.</note>

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration depicting the biblical figure Naamah seated at a horizontal weaving loom inside a room. In the background, a window looks out onto a landscape featuring a hilltop castle. At the bottom of the image, the Latin text reads: "NAAMAH, SISTER OF TUBAL-CAIN, DAUGHTER OF LAMECH" <note>original Latin: "NOEMA TVBALC. SOR. F. LAMEHC."</note></image-desc>

ALTHOUGH some attribute the invention of weaving to Pallas or Minerva <note>Pallas Athena (Minerva to the Romans) was the goddess of wisdom and crafts, including spinning and weaving</note>, as Tibullus does in these verses:
> And some weaver, constantly busy, sings of Minerva... <note>original Latin: "Atque aliqua assidue textrix operata Mineruam / Cantat &c." (Tibullus, *Elegies* 1.3). The poet describes women singing to the goddess while they work at the loom.</note>

And others attribute it to the Egyptian men, or to Arachne <note>A mortal weaver in Greek mythology who challenged Minerva to a contest and was transformed into a spider</note>, who surpassed Pallas in this art: nevertheless, according to the text of Genesis—a true history—it is to Naamah, sister of Tubal-cain and daughter of Lamech, that the art of weaving cloth for clothing was truly first known and practiced by her. This included both sewing and stitching on woolen cloths, as well as linens and tapestries, which was the beginning of worldly vanities <note>Early modern commentators often associated the descendants of Cain with the invention of physical comforts and luxuries that led to worldly pride</note>. Returning to Noah: the poets, who under the veil of their fictions hold some hidden truth—though they do not understand the creation of the world—call Noah "Heaven," "Chaos," "Seed of the World," "Father of the Gods," and "Janus." They depict him with a double face, one old and the other young and beardless, because this king was so prudent that he foresaw the future and looked and thought upon the past. This is the true duty of a wise man, these two times represented by the two faces: the old for the past and the young for the present, which teaches us that we must look at the past and, through it, conduct our coming and present affairs.

Or perhaps he is painted with a double face because the sun (for which they take him) rises every day in the morning and sets in the evening. He is thus called Janus, from *Janua* <note>Latin for "door" or "gateway."</note>. Ovid writes in the first book of the *Fasti*:

> I preside over the gates of heaven with the mild hours;
> And Jupiter himself returns by my duty.
> Thence am I called Janus.
> <note>Original Latin: "Præfideo foribus cæli cum mitibus horis: / Et redit officio Iuppiter ipfe meo. / Inde vocor Ianus."</note>

This is also why painters give him two keys in his hand along with a sword, signifying by the keys that the month which bore his name—namely January—opens and closes the year which ends and begins within it. From this it came that some, when depicting him, placed in his right hand τ <note>The Greek letter Tau, representing 300</note>, and in the other ξ, ε <note>The Greek letters Xi and Epsilon, representing 60 and 5 respectively</note>, to demonstrate that Janus is nothing other than the year which contains and holds within itself 365 days: for τ denotes 300, ξ sixty, and ε five.

Also, Janus (or Noah) divided the year, month, week, day, and hour in this manner: for the year, he ordained twelve months; for the month, four weeks; for the week, seven days; for the day, four <term>quadrants<note>A division of the day into four six-hour periods.</note></term>; for the quadrant, six hours; for the hour, four <term>points<note>A traditional division of the hour into four parts, each lasting 15 minutes.</note></term>; for the point, twelve moments; the moment he divided into seven <term>ounces<note>Derived from the Latin *uncia* (a twelfth), used here as a technical term for a fractional division of time.</note></term>; the ounce into forty-seven <term>atoms<note>In ancient and medieval science, an "atom" was the smallest possible unit of time or matter that could not be further divided.</note></term>, which is so small that it cannot be divided: giving to all of this a name, which has since changed several times, as it is at present.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a man in classical or biblical dress, seated and holding a staff, surrounded by foliate patterns.</image-desc>
NOAH the Patriarch, considering the dissension and war that might arise among his children—both those born before the deluge and those after—wished to settle his monarchy and divide it among them, reserving for himself the <term>usufruct<note>The legal right to use and derive profit from property while the ownership remains elsewhere; here, Noah retains the "income" or authority of the world while giving the "land" to his sons.</note></term>: and knowing that the right of primogeniture <note>The right of the firstborn child to inherit the family estate.</note> should be kept and maintained, valued and obeyed by the inferiors and those younger in age, he wished (by divine inspiration) to grant to Shem, his firstborn, the first part of the world, which is Asia, containing half of the earth; to Ham—although he had received his father's curse—Noah did not wish to defraud him of his <term>legal portion<note>original: "legitime"; in civil law, this is the portion of an estate that must by law go to a deceased person's children.</note></term>, giving him the part of the earth called Africa; and to Japheth, his third son, Europe, the third part of the earth. All of these contain several kingdoms and great provinces, which are described in detail hereafter.

### PROSOPOGRAPHY

Far more detestable was the intention of Protagoras <note>Protagoras (c. 490–420 BC) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher and one of the most famous Sophists.</note>, a native of a town in Thrace, who in a work of his begins thus: "I do not know what to write concerning the gods, whether they exist or whether they do not: for there are many things that prevent one from knowing, as the uncertainty of such a matter is great, and human life is short." This sentiment so displeased the republic of Athens that immediately the wicked Protagoras (as Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> and Cicero <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> testify) was driven out and sent into exile, and his books were burned in the square of Athens to his great ignominy. For there is no people nor nation, however barbarian they may be, that does not have a sense of a God. There is no Diagoras <note>Diagoras of Melos (5th century BC), a poet and philosopher nicknamed "the Atheist" for his perceived impiety.</note> (who was surnamed the atheist), no Theodoros of Cyrene <note>Theodoros "the Atheist" (c. 340–250 BC), a philosopher of the Cyrenaic school.</note>, nor any Euhemerus <note>Euhemerus (4th century BC), who argued that the gods were originally great kings deified after death.</note> who—seeing this beautiful structure of the world, the seasons so well ordered, and hearing the thunders in the air—is not terrified and does not fear him who made such things. It is true that although the ancients knew that an eternal God existed, they nevertheless did not know who he was. Those demonstrated it well enough who debated the unknown God <note>original: "Dieu incogneu"; a reference to the altar "To the Unknown God" found in Athens.</note>, to whom Saint Paul made him known—namely Jesus Christ, the Son of God—to whom we must all have recourse as to the living fountain and pure truth. His excellence is such that our mind cannot conceive such greatness, because he is incomprehensible; the power of the eyes cannot perceive him, because he is invisible; the tongue cannot express him in any way, for he is ineffable; time does not measure him, for he cannot be measured. In short, he is insuperable and incomparable, and every creature in comparison to him is wanting and lacking, insofar as one cannot compare the finite to the infinite.

PLUTO, son of Saturn and Ops, is represented by the poets as the god of the underworld because he invented funeral rites and mourning ceremonies. The Latins call him *Dispater* <note>From the Latin "Dives Pater," meaning "Wealthy Father."</note>, which is to say, father of riches. The beginning of the tithe <note>original: "disme"</note> offered to Melchizedek the priest, whom the Hebrews say is Shem, the eldest son of Noah, and who lived until the time of Abraham.

Sodom, Gomorrah, and other surrounding cities were burned by fire from heaven and swallowed up for the execrable sins of their inhabitants; Lot, his wife, and his daughters, warned by the Angels, were saved by flight. Lot’s wife, for transgressing the commandment of God, was converted into a pillar of salt, not without great significance. The two daughters of Lot made their father drunk, who knew them carnally: by one he fathered Moab, and by the other Ammon, from whom came the Moabites and Ammonites who inhabited the valley of Syria.

Damascus, a city six days' journey from Jerusalem, began to be built.

fittingly: which art is called Music, that is to say, the science dealing with singing. To understand this subject, it is necessary to know that this name *Muse* <note>original Greek: Μοῦσα</note> came from the heart of Greece, and is interpreted in English as Muse, or song. From this, it follows that the Poets have imagined the Muses to be fictional characters and daughters of Jupiter and Mnemosyne, who is memory; they preside over Poets and music because it is necessary for a learned man to be capable of intelligence and memory. The Florentine Dante demonstrates this in the second chapter of the *Canticle of Hell*:

> *O Muses, O high genius, now help me,*
> *O memory, that wrote down what I saw,*
> *Here shall your nobility appear.*
> <note>original Italian: "O muse ô alto ingenio, hor m' aiute, / O mente, che scriuesti cio chi' vidi, / Qui si parra la tua nobilitate." From Dante Alighieri’s *Inferno*, Canto II.</note>

And in the first chapter of *Purgatory*:

> *But here let dead poetry rise again,*
> *O holy Muses, since I am yours,*
> *And here let Calliope rise up a little.*
> <note>original Italian: "Ma qui la morta poesia risurga / O sante muse, poi che vostro sono, / Et qui Calliope al quanto surga." From Dante’s *Purgatorio*, Canto I. Calliope was the Muse of epic poetry.</note>

The most ancient poets established only two Muses. Phurnutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD, often called "Phurnutus" in older texts.</note>, naming them, says that one represents speculation and the other action; because the entire state of human life consists of the contemplative and the active. The number was later increased to three. Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> names the first *Practice* <note>original Greek: μελετή (Meletē), meaning practice or meditation.</note>, the second *Memory* <note>original Greek: μνήμη (Mnēmē).</note>, and the third *Song* <note>original Greek: ἀοιδή (Aoidē).</note>. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar and writer.</note> also places them at three, and considers one to be born from the movement of water, another to give sound from the striking of the air, and the last to consist of the pure voice alone. Of this same number, Censorinus <note>A Roman grammarian and author of *De Die Natali*.</note> names them otherwise, namely: *Hypate*, *Mese*, and *Nete* <note>original Greek: ὑπάτη, Μέση, Νήτη. These terms refer to the lowest, middle, and highest strings/notes on a three-stringed lyre.</note>, by reason of the three sounds—low, middle, and high—which one discerns most easily in the tension or...

...of the planet named Venus: because it was believed that the celestial Venus influenced this terrestrial one not only with great beauty, but also with burning lust, just as it is her nature to cause a delightful life and concupiscible <note>Meaning driven by strong desire or carnal lust, particularly in a biological or generative sense.</note> generation in the lower world. She was an immodest woman, abandoned to the will of all men, and she was the first to discover the art of prostitution and of placing girls in brothels, commanding the ladies on the Island of Cyprus (where she was Queen) to abandon and prostitute themselves, making it lawful for them, so that she should not be considered lewd alone, wanting women to earn money by this means. From the adultery she committed with Mars, she gave birth to Harmony <note>original: "Hermonie."</note>. She had several bastards by others, and indeed more adulteries are numbered of her than births. The Poets pretend that Saturn, with his scythe, cut off the genitals of his father Caelus <note>original: "Celie," referring to the sky god Uranus/Caelus.</note>, and others say it was Jupiter who cut them from his father Saturn, with his own scythe, and that he threw them into the sea; from whose blood, along with the foam of the sea, Venus was engendered and produced.

<margin>Fulgentius, *Mythologies* <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius was a Latin writer of late antiquity whose work focused on the allegorical interpretation of myths.</note></margin> From this it comes that she is called Aphrodite: for *Aphrodite* <note>original Greek: ἀφροδίτη</note> means "foam." A mystical sense lies hidden—sometimes physical, sometimes ethical, sometimes theological—which can only appear to the initiated, that is, those imbued with true and solid philosophy. <note>original Latin: "Neque diuina illa veterum poetarum ingenia eo stupiditatis & dementiæ perueniffe exiſtimandum eſt, quaſi ea quae fabuloſè propoſuerunt ſimpliciter talia eſſe affirmare voluerint. Now, the harvests of the seasons having been cut—namely, the fruits or sustenance <note>original: "viandes." In this period, the word referred to food or nourishment in general, not strictly animal meat.</note> as if with a scythe—and cast into the humors of the entrails, as if into the sea, they engender pleasure and lewdness; for from being overfull, lust is bred; on the contrary, *Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus freezes* <note>original: "Sine Cerere & Baccho friget Venus." Here is the allegory of such a strange birth of Venus, depicted naked in a shell in the sea, the meaning of which represents the effects, nature, and temperament of the celestial sign named after her. The testicles of Caelus <note>original: "Celie." Referring to Uranus or Caelus, the personification of the Sky, whose castration by Saturn is a central creation myth.</note> represent the generative power which descends from the heavens to the lower world; of this power, Venus is the proper instrument, as she grants generative power to animals. Saturn cut them from him with his scythe, which signifies Time—the occasion for generation in this lower world—because it is necessary that the temporal things of this world, which are not eternal, have a beginning and be engendered. Furthermore, Time corrupts the things that are subject to it, from which it follows that all corruptible things must be born. Thus, Time, signified by Saturn, brought generation from the heavens to the lower world by means of Venus. This world is called the "sea" by reason of its continual mutation <term>mutation: the constant changing of one physical form into another</term> from one form into another, along with constant generation and corruption.

This is brought about by the incision of the genitals <note>original: "genitoires."</note> cut with the scythe, insofar as through corruption, generation occurs in this world. Additionally, it is the property of Saturn to corrupt, just as it is the nature of Venus to engender; she is the cause of the beginning, and he of the end; for if things were not corrupted, nothing new would be engendered. A type of gold coin used in France.</note> that lovers spend in pursuit of love; which must be understood through the proverb that says *Cupid's purse is tied with leek tails.* <note>A phrase suggesting that the purse is easily opened or that the contents are quickly spent, as leek stalks are fragile or easily stripped.</note> Which proverb demonstrates the liberality of love: for love is in no way prevented from putting his hand into the purse, which he unties easily; and gold can do much in love,

as Ovid says,

> *Truly now are the golden ages: much honor comes by gold, by gold is love procured.* <note>original: "Aurea nunc verè sunt secula, plurimus auro / Venit honos, auro conciliatur amor." She is called Aphrodite <note>original: "ἀφροδίτη"</note> as if from *aphrosyne* <note>original: "ἀφροσύνης"</note>, which is to say, the goddess of folly, seeing that from her proceed madness and fury. This is how Euripides interprets it. The ancients consecrated the oyster to her, a fish which provokes lewdness. The same antiquity attributed doves to her, because they are very much given to carnal copulation. The myrtle was dedicated to her, the fruit of which is black, demonstrating that the state which proceeds from love is melancholy. The rose was also dedicated to her because of its sweet scent and beauty, and because it is surrounded by thorns just as love is by sorrows and stinging passions. Let us leave poetry aside and return to history. In ancient times, the earthly Venus was worshiped as a goddess on the Island of Paphos, in Rome, and in several other places, where temples, statues, and altars were raised and constructed in her honor. And not only did the whores worship her, but also the modest virgins and chaste matrons, who were dressed in clothing different from the foolish women: for they wore on their heads certain veils and headcoverings that it was not lawful for others to wear, along with a long robe trailing on the ground, so that one could not see their feet. The clothing of the lewd women was short, a garment considered shameful by the Romans. All the women together celebrated her feast every year on the calends of April <note>April 1st, known as the *Veneralia*.</note>, and stripping the statue of its ornaments, they would wash it, then adorn it anew with roses and flowers, wearing garlands of myrtle, washing themselves afterward and going into another temple of Virile Fortune <note>Fortune Virilis was a Roman deity worshiped by women to ensure they remained attractive to their husbands or to hide physical flaws from men.</note>, where they

This poem references the "Judgment of Paris," a mythological contest where Venus won the prize of beauty while unclothed; she mocks Athena by suggesting that if she won while naked, she is even more formidable when armed.</note>

*But after, etc.* The fable of his fall from heaven denotes nothing other than that the first spark of fire which men began to use was first found and taken from the brilliant and burning lightning seen falling from above. Many attribute the invention of various arts to Vulcan and Minerva: to Minerva, as she is prudence itself; and to Vulcan, because through fire many mechanical arts, crafts, and masterpieces reach their perfection. For the fire of the air which we use is called *Hephaestus* <note>original: $\tilde{\alpha}\phi\alpha\iota\varsigma$ (aphesis). And by Vulcan, nothing else was understood but fire. > That the African <note>likely referring to the Carthaginian general Hannibal, who famously used fire and vinegar to break through the rocks of the Alps.</note> subdued

## MERCURY

# PROSOPOGRAPHY

Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> credits him with the honor of the invention of vocal harmony and music, as we have said. He is the holy God of eloquence, because he spoke very well and eloquently, the messenger of the gods and their interpreter, insofar as he taught the interpretation of words and expressions to the Greeks. Virgil <note>The Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro; this line is from the *Aeneid*.</note>:

> Now even the messenger of the gods, sent by Jove himself.
<note>original: "Nunc etiam interpres diuum Ioue missus ab ipso."</note>

And he is the god of traders and merchants: for *Mercurius* <note>Mercury</note> comes from *merchandise*, because he presides over profit and trade. <note>original: "Mercurius vient à Mercibus, quod lucro & mercaturæ præsit."</note> He himself testifies to this, speaking in Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus, a Roman playwright; these lines are from the prologue of his play *Amphitryon*.</note> in this manner:

> As you wish me to bless your commercial dealings, in buying and selling, with joyful profits, and to assist you in all matters.
<note>original: "Ut vos in vestris voltis mercimonijs / Emundis, vendundisque me laetum lucris / Afficere, atque adiuuare in rebus omnibus."</note>

And for this reason he was called by the Greeks <term>kleptēs</term> <note>κλέπτης: a thief</note>, meaning thief; for this cause he was also named <term>strophaios</term> <note>στροφαῖος: of the hinge or door-turning</note>, because he presided over the guarding of doors <note>original: "quod ianuarum custodiæ præesset"</note>: for which reason he was placed at the doors of houses, so that he, being a thief, might keep watch for other thieves, and being hidden behind the door, might drive them out. Thus in Aristophanes' <note>The ancient Greek comic playwright.</note> comedy *Plutus*, he reports this of himself. He was also called *Cyllenius*, on account of Mount Cyllene, the highest mountain in Arcadia, where Maia gave birth to him. Virgil:

> Mercury is your father, whom fair Maia conceived and brought forth on the icy peak of Cyllene.
<note>original: "Vobis Mercurius pater est, quem candida Maia / Cyllenus gelido conceptum vertice fudit."</note>

He is also the God of wrestling: for wrestlers did him honor along with Hercules; signifying that physical strength is not only necessary for wrestling, but also reason combined with judgment. Therefore one must use strength with reason and prudence: for to those who trust only in their strength, despising reason—by the benefit of which the arts are brought forth—one might rightly say, <term>Wretched man, your own strength will destroy you</term> <note>original Greek: "Δαιμόνιε, φθίσει σε τὸ σὸν μένος", a line from Homer's *Iliad*.</note>, which means,

He is also called *Mercurius*, as if to say *running in the middle*, because speech runs in the middle among men. <note>original: "Mercurius, quasi medius currens, quòd sermo currat inter homines medius." This is a traditional medieval etymology linking the name Mercury to the social function of language.</note> Wings are placed on his heels and his hat to demonstrate that speech is carried lightly through the air, or because the star called <term>Stilbon</term> <note>From the Greek στίλβων (*stilbōn*), meaning "the gleaming one."</note>—which the pagans attributed to him and from which they took the name of the day <note>Wednesday, or *Mercredi* in French, named for Mercury.</note>—moves faster than the other planets, with such speed that in seven days it completes all its circles; a feat the planet Saturn only accomplishes in twenty-four years, and Jupiter in twelve. Lucan <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, a Roman poet; this line describes the planet's movement in the sky.</note>:

->*And Cyllenian Mercury, swift in motion, pauses.*<-
<note>original: "Motúque celer Cyllenius, hæret." *Cyllenian* refers to Mount Cyllene, Mercury's birthplace.</note>

In Crete, festivals called Mercuriales were celebrated in his honor, where the custom was that for the duration of the feast, the servants sat at the table and were magnificently treated and served by their masters. Xenodorus <note>A famous bronze sculptor of the 1st century AD.</note> had a statue of Mercury made in Auvergne <note>Likely referring to the colossal statue at the sanctuary of Mercury on the Puy de Dôme in France.</note> that was 400 feet high. By his sister Venus, he fathered Hermaphroditus; he also killed Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant.</note> and bound Prometheus to Mount Caucasus. Here is an emblem by Sambucus <note>Johannes Sambucus, a Hungarian humanist and emblem writer.</note> dedicated to Adrien Turnèbe <note>A renowned French classical scholar.</note> which explains the symbols of Mercury:

> *The wings and the traveler's staff,*
> *And the goat with the long beard,*
> *To show what he can be:*
> *A quick wit and well-spoken,*
> *A good thief and vigilant,*
> *Apt for knowing all things well.*

# PITUMNUS.

<image-desc>An oval-framed engraving depicting the deity Pitumnus as a muscular, nearly nude man standing in a rural landscape. He holds a long-handled tool, likely a pitchfork or spade, used for tilling or fertilizing the earth. The border of the oval is inscribed with the Latin text: "PITVMNVS D. D. STERQVILINVS E." <note>This translates roughly to "Pitumnus, God of Manure."</note> In the background, a small village with thatched houses is visible, along with another figure working in the fields.</image-desc>

Servius <note>A famous 4th-century grammarian best known for his influential commentary on the works of Virgil.</note>, writing on the 9th book of Virgil's *Aeneid*, records that Pilumnus and Pitumnus were brothers. The former, Pilumnus, who was in ancient times the god of bakers, discovered the use of grinding wheat; for before the invention of millstones, the ancients dried all types of grain over a fire, and then, having placed them in large mortars, they would pound them <note>The name Pilumnus is traditionally derived from the Latin *pilum*, meaning "pestle," the tool used for pounding in a mortar.</note>. And Pitumnus was the first to use manure to fertilize the earth in order to make it more fertile, which is why he is called Sterquilinius <note>original: "Sterquilinius," a title derived from *stercus*, the Latin word for dung or manure.</note>. He took as his wife Danaë, the daughter of Acrisius, by whom he had his son Daunus; after his son's name, he called the region where he reigned Daunia, in the land of Apulia. He also built a beautiful city called Ardea, named for the great heat <note>From the Latin *ardere*, meaning to burn or glow.</note> found in the region where it is situated, or (as Servius is pleased to say) as if it were *Ardua*, which is to say, great and noble.

### TAGES.

<image-desc>A circular emblem depicting the mythological figure Tages. Tages is shown as a young man with wild, flowing hair and a muscular build, emerging from the earth. **TAGES**, son of Genius (according to the author Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus was a Roman grammarian whose work is a major source for early Roman and Etruscan traditions.</note>) and grandson <note>The original French uses *nepveu*, which today means nephew, but in the 16th century—following the Latin *nepos*—it commonly meant grandson, as confirmed by the image caption.</note> of Jupiter, being a young child, taught the people of Etruria (which is now Tuscany) the science of divination. Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD) known for his epic on the Roman Civil War.</note> says:
> But Tages, the founder of the art,
> May have fashioned these things, etc. <note>original: "Sed conditor artis / Finxerit ista Tages &c."</note>

And Ovid:
> The natives called him Tages, who first
> Taught the Etruscan nation to reveal future events. <note>original: "Indigena dixere Tagem, qui primus Hetruscam / Edocuit gentem casus aperire futuros." From *Metamorphoses*, Book XV.</note>

Cicero, in his book *On Divination*, recounts a marvelous case, more poetic and fabulous than true. A plowman (he says), while plowing in the Tarquinian <note>Tarquinii was one of the most ancient and important cities of the Etruscan League.</note> field, and with the plowshare sinking deeper into the earth, Tages emerged and suddenly rose up, appearing young of face and old in wisdom, and spoke to the man who was plowing. Astonished by this, the laborer cried out in wonder; at this cry, nearly all [those] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword.</note>

# NARRATION ON FALSE
## *Astrology called divination.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'L' featuring a seated figure in classical robes, possibly a philosopher or astrologer, holding an open book.</image-desc>
True Astrology consists, before any other work, in the knowledge of the sphere—an instrument by which the figure of the world, both the earth and the heavens, is represented. <note>In the 16th century, "Astrology" often encompassed what we now call Astronomy; the author is defending the study of the physical cosmos while attacking fortune-telling.</note>
The false kind, called judicial and divinatory, lies in the observation of the birth of persons, when one pays heed to the hours and parts of the sky which, along with the stars residing in them, reveal themselves at every instant as they rise toward the East. And this part of the sky is called by the followers of this astrology the Horoscope, <term>Horoscope: From the Greek "horoskopos," meaning "observer of the hour." In this period, it specifically referred to the Ascendant, the sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</term> wishing by this means and by the subsequent revolution of the heavens to divine the natural inclinations of men toward good or evil, good or bad morals, health or sickness, luck or misfortune, poverty or wealth, and the length or brevity of life, as if this observation could always infallibly yield a certainty. Yet there is nothing more uncertain, doubtful, frivolous, or damnable than such a science (if science it should be called). For following it, if you have committed some great crime worthy of punishment, you will say: "Destiny or necessity made me do it." But I ask you, what is destiny? You will say further, "The stars were the

cause. But tell me, what are the stars? Certainly (you will reply) they are the celestial bodies that we see and contemplate in the sky. Who made them? It was God. Who arranged them and placed them so well in order? God. Take heed then to what you intended to say and conclude: By this, God caused me to sin. Thus, by your own words, He is then unjust, and you as well: for if He had not created them, you would not have sinned at all. Cast out, cast out these arguments from your understanding, which only serve to excuse your faults and sins, remembering what the Psalmist says: *Incline not my heart to evil words, to make excuses for sins with men who work iniquity.* <note>original Latin: "Ne declines cor meum in verba maligna ad excuſandas excuſationes in peccatis cum hominibus operantibus iniquitatem." This is a citation from Psalm 141:4.</note> Be also mindful of the voice of the Lord saying: *Behold, you are healed, watch yourself from now on against sinning, so that something worse does not happen to you.* <note>A reference to John 5:14, where Jesus heals a man at the pool of Bethesda and warns him to live a moral life afterward.</note> Certain heretical astrologers strive to extinguish this spiritual health, saying: The inevitable cause of sinning comes from the sky, and Venus does it, or Saturn, or Mars. Oh, what a great blasphemy against God! As if the Creator of the stars, having arranged them, should be accused of it. 

But how does it happen that sometimes, from this judicial astrology, one sees many things come to pass afterwards that are found to be true and in conformity with the judgment of these diviners? Saint Augustine asked a learned physician the reason for this, who replied to him: *The power of chance does this, which is spread everywhere in the nature of things. For if, from the Pagan Poets, someone singing and intending something quite different, when by chance someone consulted them, a verse often came out marvelously in harmony with the matter, it is not to be wondered at if, from the human soul by some higher instinct—without knowing what was happening within itself—something sounded not by art but by chance that harmonized with the affairs and deeds of the questioner.* <note>original Latin: "Vim ſortis hoc facere in rerum natura uſquequaq; diffuſam... [to] ...concineret." This passage from Augustine's *Confessions* (Book IV) explains "sortes"—the practice of seeking guidance by randomly picking a passage from a book—arguing that any accuracy is pure coincidence.</note> So it is that if prognostications founded on judicial astrology happen to encounter in some place...

This judicial astrology, a fountain of superstitions, has produced a great number of follies of its kind, such as: **Physiognomy** <note>judging character from facial features</note>, **Geomancy** <note>divination by patterns in the earth</note>, **Chiromancy** <note>palm reading</note>, **Onomancy** <note>divination based on a person's name</note>, **Hydromancy** <note>divination using water</note>, and others belonging to false magic. These are all so uncertain, abusive, and ill-fated that Nebuchadnezzar, Caesar, Crassus, Pompey, Deiotarus, Nero, and Julian the Apostate—promising themselves long and happy lives through these means—died miserably, with everything happening to them the opposite of what they trusted and of which they felt assured.

What shall we say of the folly and superstition of those who take judgment and advice from <term>auguries</term> <note>divination based on natural signs, such as the flight of birds or animal behavior</note>, whether in moving things or in inanimate ones, such as a stone, a dog, a cat, and other things? Regarding this, that foolish Agostino Nifo <note>Italian philosopher Agostino Nifo (c. 1473–1538), who wrote on the influence of stars and divination</note> has left writings as testimony to his superstitious reveries. He also showed clear signs of folly when, being seventy years old and suffering from the gout, he fell so deeply in love that he became senseless, as Giovio <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian</note> recounts. The Emperor Heraclius, amusing himself with these arts without piety, fell at last into heresy. Is all of this not a true idolatry? 

Is it a presage of future evil if it happens that mice have spoiled a robe with their sharp teeth? Cato the Elder <note>A Roman statesman known for his traditionalism and wit</note> teaches this joyfully by the answer he gave to one who consulted him because rats had eaten his breeches. "That," he said, "is not strange; but it would indeed be a strange and monstrous thing if your breeches had eaten the rats." The poet Accius says:

> *I place no trust in augurs, who enrich the ears with words, only to enrich their own homes with the gold of others.* <note>original Latin: "Nihil credo auguribus, qui aures verbis diuitant, Alienas ſuas vt auro locupletent domos."</note>

Favorinus <note>Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–160 AD), a skeptical philosopher</note>, wanting to divert young men from putting faith in these imposters and the kind of people who, through a prodigious art, promise to predict the future, concluded with these arguments: They say either that adverse and bad things will happen, or prosperous and good things. If they predict good things and they do not happen, you are made miserable by waiting in vain; if they predict bad things and they lie, there you are still miserable, fearing in vain. If the bad things do occur, you will become miserable in your spirit long before you are made so by destiny. If good fortune [is promised] by them...

I do not say that one cannot know the natural effects which may occur through the dispositions of the stars—such as eclipses of the Sun and the Moon, rains or droughts—but that is predicted by true <term>astrology</term> <note>here meaning "natural astrology," what we now call astronomy and meteorology, as opposed to "judicial astrology" which predicts human fate</note> (as we have said). Otherwise, the proposition that inferior bodies are ruled by superior and celestial ones would be false, even though the wise man will dominate and be above the stars. And this science is of great use: for Pericles defeated Nicias by nothing other than his knowledge of the course of the stars when, having foreseen an upcoming eclipse of the Sun, he alerted his men. Whereas Nicias, who understood nothing of astrology, was so troubled—as was his entire army—that the victory of that day remained with Pericles by this means. I also do not wish to deny that some individuals may be able to predict high things of great consequence that are yet to come; but those who do so are incited by God to announce His great deeds, just as the Prophets of old were, to whom the Holy Spirit gave the understanding of future mysteries. -><image-desc>An oval engraving depicting the personification of Fortune. She is blindfolded and wears a cap with points similar to a jester's hood. ALTHOUGH Fortune is nothing in herself, insofar as the ancients made her a goddess and counted her among the deities, it will not be out of place to set down her description here.

Cebes the Philosopher <note>Cebes of Thebes (c. 430–350 BCE), a disciple of Socrates; he was traditionally credited with the "Tablet of Cebes," an allegorical work describing the path to virtue and the dangers of life.</note>, in the depiction he made of human life, portrays Fortune as blind, has her standing upon a round ball, and gives her as ladies-in-waiting who follow her closely: Pleasure, Flattery, and Thoughtlessness <term>Inconsideration: In this context, a lack of reflection or a state of heedless imprudence.</term>. Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator and statesman.</note> in his work on rhetoric recounts some verses by the ancient poet Pacuvius <note>Marcus Pacuvius (c. 220–130 BCE), an early Roman tragic poet whose works often survived only as fragments cited by later authors.</note> which give the reason why she was depicted in this way:

> *Philosophers maintain that Fortune is insane and senseless,* <note>original: "Fortunam insanam esse & brutam perhibent philosophi"</note>
> *And they declare her to be rolling like a spherical rock:*
> *Because wherever chance pushes the rock, there they say Fortune falls.*
> *For this reason they call her blind, because she sees nothing to which she attaches herself.*
> *Moreover, they say she is insane, because she is cruel, uncertain, and unstable.*

## FORTUNE.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut depicting the personification of Fortune. She is shown as a blindfolded woman standing precariously on a small sphere. She holds a large, crescent-shaped sail or banner that billows around her head and body, which bears the inscription "FORTVNE". ALTHOUGH Fortune is nothing in herself, since the ancients made her a goddess and placed her among the number of the gods, it will not be out of place to provide her description here.

The philosopher Cebes <note>Cebes of Thebes (c. 430–350 BCE), to whom a famous philosophical allegory called the *Pinax* or "Tablet of Cebes" is attributed, describing the dangers of human life.</note>, in the depiction he made of human life, portrays Fortune as blind, has her stand upon a round ball, and gives her as handmaidens who follow her closely: Pleasure, Flattery, and Thoughtlessness. Cicero, in his work on rhetoric, records some verses by the ancient poet Pacuvius <note>Marcus Pacuvius (c. 220–130 BCE), an early Roman tragic poet and nephew of Ennius.</note> which explain the reason why she has been depicted in this way:

> *Philosophers maintain that Fortune is insane and senseless,* <note>original: "Fortunam insanam esse & brutam perhibent philosophi"</note>
> *And declare her to be as rolling as a spherical stone:*
> *For they say that wherever chance has pushed the stone, there Fortune falls.*
> *They call her blind for this reason: because she discerns nothing to which she attaches herself.*
> *But they say she is insane because she is harsh, uncertain, and unstable.*

*Blind, because she cannot distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy.* <note>original: "Brutam, quia dignum aut indignum nequeat internoscere." This completes the quote from the Roman poet Pacuvius begun on the previous page, explaining why Fortune is considered "brutish" or "senseless."</note>

The pagans made her a goddess, to whom—according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 CE), Roman author of "Natural History."</note>—they attribute so much that, by the consensus of all ages, in all places and at all hours, she is granted full power over both happy and adverse things, as well as command and dominion. In short, she alone is invoked, and she alone manages the income and the expenses <note>The author uses a ledger metaphor here: "elle seule fait la mise & la recepte."</note>. If something happens as desired, she alone is praised; if otherwise, she is accused with tears and frustration, and she alone fills both pages of the book <note>Referring to the "ledger" of life or fate, where she is responsible for both the good and the bad entries.</note>. For this reason, temples were publicly dedicated to her, and statues were raised within them; some were called "Feminine Fortune" and others "Virile Fortune." Some called her Nemesis <note>The Greek goddess of retribution.</note>, others Tyche <note>The Greek word for "luck" or "fortune."</note>, and others Nortia <note>An Etruscan goddess of fate.</note>. Spartianus <note>Aelius Spartianus, one of the historians of the "Historia Augusta."</note>, in his *Life of Severus* <note>The Roman Emperor Septimius Severus.</note>, gives her the title "Royal." The most superstitious believe there are two: a good one and a bad one. Apelles <note>The most renowned painter of ancient Greece.</note> depicts her sitting because (as he replied to those who asked the reason) she never stands upright or straight—which is to say, she is never firm or constant. Modern painters seat her upon a wheel that turns incessantly; for fortune rarely remains in one state, sometimes lifting men up, and sometimes casting them down. Juvenal says:

> *If Fortune wills it, you shall become a consul from a rhetorician;*
> *If she wills the same, you shall become a rhetorician from a consul.* <note>original: "Si fortuna volet fies de rhetore consul: / Si volet hac eadem fies de consule rhetor." From Juvenal's Satire VII.</note>

And Ariosto in his *Orlando Furioso*:

> *The higher you see a wretched man rise*
> *Upon the unstable wheel of Fortune,*
> *The sooner you must expect to see his feet*
> *Where his head is now, as he falls headlong.* <note>original: "Quanto piu su l'instabil ruota vedi / Di fortuna ire in alto il miser' huomo, / Tanto piu tosto hay da vedergli piedi, / Oue hora ha il capo, & far cadendo il tomo." From Canto 45 of Ariosto's epic poem.</note>

The poor idolaters have troubled their heads much over Fortune, being ignorant of the providence of God.

<note>This page continues the sentence from the previous page: "...he also..."</note> so obscured and diminished the glory of all the other kings who had preceded him: for which reason he deserved, with good and just cause, to be named specifically as thrice-excellent and sovereign. It was he who, first among all philosophers, after having carefully immersed himself in physics and the mathematical arts and having perfectly understood them, raised his spirit to contemplate things from on high and divine matters. It was he who, first before all other humans, debated the majesty of God, the order of the Angels, and the change and mutation of souls. For this cause, he was in former times called the author of theology, being reputed as the God of eloquence, of wit, and of fine invention. Orpheus was his imitator, who obtained the second place of honor in this ancient Theology; he was succeeded by Aglaophemus, after whom came Pythagoras, who was followed by Philolaus, the master of the divine Plato. This school of ancient theology (which was as concordant and unified in its faith as any that has existed since) was thus confirmed by six learned and expert theologians: taking its source from Mercury <note>The author uses "Mercury," the Roman name for Hermes, interchangeably with the Greek name to emphasize his role as the source of wisdom.</note>, and receiving its entire perfection and accomplishment from the divine Plato.

This later moved the minds of men so strongly, and especially those of the Egyptian nation, toward every virtue, art, and science, that in ancient times no one was reputed learned among the Greeks and Athenians, nor received as a virtuous man, who had not traveled as far as Egypt to be instructed in the laws, sciences, and arts by the prophets, philosophers, priests, and Gymnosophists <term>Gymnosophists: literally 'naked philosophers,' a term used by the Greeks to describe ancient ascetic sages who practiced self-discipline and meditation</term> of that country. They sought instruction as much in theology, arithmetic, music, geometry, cosmography, and architecture as in other subjects. # AESCULAPIUS.

<image-desc>An oval medallion containing a woodcut illustration of Aesculapius. He is depicted as a man in classical drapery, standing in a hilly landscape with fortified buildings in the background. He holds a staff entwined with a serpent in his right hand and a bundle of medicinal herbs in his left hand. The name "AESCVLAPIVS" is inscribed along the top inside of the oval frame.</image-desc>

AESCULAPIUS, son of Apollo, and taught by Chiron <note>In Greek mythology, Chiron was a wise centaur who tutored many heroes in the arts of medicine, music, and archery.</note>—from whom the herb <term>*Centaurea*<note>Commonly known as Centaury; the name refers to Chiron the Centaur's discovery of its medicinal properties.</note></term> took its name—first brought the art of medicine to men. From him, his successors called the Asclepiads <note>The Asclepiads were a guild of physicians who claimed descent from Aesculapius.</note> received this art in a state of perfection, and "complete in all its parts" <note>original: "absolue de tous ses nombres," a classical idiom meaning a work is finished to the highest degree of detail.</note> (as the saying goes). After having practiced it, they passed it on to their descendants until the time of Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) is traditionally regarded as the "Father of Medicine."</note>, who restored it to its greatest perfection. Excellent in both mind and nature, Aesculapius took such great pains in the study of medicine that he discovered many things beneficial to human health. He was so highly skilled in this art that many who were in extremis, expecting nothing but death, were by him delivered from their illness and cured. What is more, the ancients believed that he even restored life to certain dead men, specifically to Hippolytus and to Androgeus, the son of Minos, whom the Athe-

...[A]thenians had killed. For this reason, Virgil in the 7th book of the *Aeneid* says that Jupiter, jealous of him, struck him with a thunderbolt:

> *He himself [Jupiter] cast down the son of Phoebus, the discoverer of such medicine and art, with a lightning bolt to the Stygian waves.* <note>original: "Ipfe repertorem medicinæ talis, & artis / Fulmine Phœbigenam ftygias detrufit ad undas." — Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.772–773. "Son of Phoebus" refers to Aesculapius, son of Apollo (Phoebus).</note>

An infinite number of people flocked to him from all parts of Greece, as if to an oracle. He invented surgery, the composition of medicines, the power of herbs, and the extraction of teeth. Nor was he ashamed to taste the superfluities of nature—the filth and excrement of the sick—to better understand the nature of the disease, so meticulous was he in his desire to drive it from human bodies. His surname was Triccaean, on account of the city of his birth, as he himself said when speaking of himself:

> *I was born in sacred Tricca, to whom the whole art of healing is indebted, as well as all wisdom.* <note>original: "Natus ego ex facra Tricca, cui tota medendi / Ars debet, fimul atque omnis fapientia debet." Tricca (modern Trikala) in Thessaly was a major center for the cult of Aesculapius.</note>

He was worshipped in Epidaurus in the form of a serpent.

### Quintus Serenus, poet and physician,

> *And you, master of the art, who know how to grant lives anew, and to recall buried souls back to the sky; you who dwell in the Aegean, in Pergamon, and in Epidaurus; you who once, hidden beneath the skin of a peaceful serpent, sought the Tarpeian heights and the renowned temples, driving away foul diseases with your divine presence; come here, and whatever you have often promised me in answer to my prayers, set it all forth upon the tender papyrus.* <note>original Latin: "Tuq; potens artis, reduces qui tradere vitas / Nofti, atque in cælum manes reuocare fepultos..." This poem by Quintus Serenus Sammonicus (3rd century CE) invokes Aesculapius and references the legend of the god being brought to Rome's Capitoline Hill (the Tarpeian rock) in serpent form to end a plague in 293 BCE.</note>

Antiquity dedicated the serpent to him because many remedies are found in this animal. In a city in Italy, a statue of Aesculapius was found dressed in a tunic <note>original: "chemise"</note> made in the Greek fashion, and a cloak, in the fold of which he holds with his left hand

letters, along with the invention of vermilion <note>Original: "vermillon." A bright red pigment (cinnabar) traditionally used for rubrication or highlighting important text in manuscripts.</note> for writing, as well as methods for hunting fish and birds. Lucan writes:
> *The Phoenicians were the first (if fame is to be believed) who dared / To mark the enduring voice with crude figures.* <note>Original Latin: "Phœnices primi (famæ si creditur) ausi / Mansuram rudibus voce signare figuris." From Lucan’s *Pharsalia*.</note> And Pannonius says:
> *The Phoenicians hold this region, they who were the first to watch the stars, / And the first to paint the shapes of voices.* <note>Original Latin: "Hunc Phœnices habent tractum, qui sidera primi / Spectarunt, primi vocum pinxere figuras." Cadmus, the son of Agenor, King of the Phoenicians, left his country by the command of his father to search for his sister Europa, who had been abducted. Departing with orders not to return without news of her and to bring her back, he came to Greece. Having arrived there, one day while he was sitting near the fountain of Hippocrene <note>A spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses, said to have been formed by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus.</note>, he reflected within himself on how he might create certain marks and characters to express to the eye what one conceives in the mind, so that one might know how to write. And having pondered sufficiently in his spirit, he discovered sixteen of them, which he chose to paint as follows: alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, iota, kappa, lambda, mu, nu, omicron, pi, rho, sigma, tau, upsilon <note>The author lists sixteen early Greek letters: α, β, γ, δ, ε, ι, κ, λ, μ, ν, ο, π, ρ, σ, τ, υ.</note>. These letters he taught to the Greeks. Having arrived in Boeotia, he built Thebes, the most magnificent city under the heavens, where there were pyramids as large as mountains, built by kings in rivalry with one another, and which was enriched with a hundred gates, each of them guarded by two hundred knights. There, also, the statue of Memnon <note>The author is conflating the Greek city of Thebes in Boeotia with the Egyptian city of Thebes, famous for its "hundred gates," pyramids, and the "Singing Statue" of Memnon which supposedly made a sound at sunrise.</note>, struck by the rays of the sun, gave off the sound of a voice. Some hold that Amphion <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology credited with building the walls of Thebes by playing his lyre, the music of which moved the stones into place.</note> had it built before Cadmus. Regardless, both lived at nearly the same time.
