## FAUNUS.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration showing two standing figures in a landscape. On the left, a younger man with a loincloth holds a staff or club. On the right, a bearded, older man wearing a crown and holding a leafy branch. In the background are hills and a classical building or temple. An inscription within the top of the oval border reads: "FAVNVS REG. I LATIO."</image-desc>

Opinions vary regarding Faunus. Some maintain that he was the son of Picus, King of the Latins, and that Latinus, the ancient leader <note>Original French: "duc." In this context, it refers to a sovereign leader or military commander of a tribe.</note> of the Aborigines <note>The "Aborigines" were a legendary group of people said to be the earliest inhabitants of central Italy.</note>, was his son; others hold that he fathered the Fauns, satyrs, and sylvans, who were rustic demigods. Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian who epitomized the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note> writes that he came to reign in Italy after Saturn, at which time Evander arrived there from Arcadia with a rather small number of followers. There, Faunus, having received him honorably, gave him the fields and the hill that was later named the Palatine by Evander, around the year of the world 2724, or 1235 years before Jesus Christ. He ordained cruel sacrifices to Saturn. He foretold the future to men and sang of what was to come in verses called Saturnian <note>The *versus Saturnius*, an ancient Italian meter used by early poets before the adoption of Greek hexameters.</note>, fashioned in the same style as those with which Naevius <note>Gnaeus Naevius (c. 270–201 BC), an early Roman poet and dramatist who wrote an epic poem on the First Punic War.</note> described the Punic War. His sister, called Fatua or Fauna, was his wife, who

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Faunus and his family. The previous page ended while discussing early Roman poets like Naevius; this page shifts focus to Faunus’s wife (often identified as Fatua or the Bona Dea) and the cultural history of wine consumption.</meta>

### BOOK ONE.

n 3

[The wife of Faunus] predicted the future to women just as her husband did to men. These women made sacrifices to her and gave her the name of the **Good Goddess** <note>original: "bonne Deeſée"; in Latin, *Bona Dea*. She was a divinity associated with chastity and fertility, whose rites were strictly for women.</note>. She was whipped with myrtle branches so severely by her husband that she died from it, because, contrary to custom and royal honor, she secretly drank a jar of wine and became intoxicated. For at that time, the use of wine was forbidden to women, as it was later by the **Massiliotic law** <note>The laws of Massilia (modern Marseille), a Greek colony known for its strict social codes, including the prohibition of wine for women to ensure sobriety and modesty.</note>, which was in effect (says **Theophrastus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>) among the Milesians. 

The **Romans** also formerly considered it a criminal offense for any man to drink wine before the age of thirty; and their servants did not drink it at all, except on certain feast days and solemnities. It was forbidden by express command to their wives, as recounted by **Alessandro degli Alessandri** <note>An Italian humanist jurist (1461–1523) known for his work *Genialium Dierum*.</note>, Book 3, Chapter 11; **Macrobius** <note>A Roman author of the early 5th century.</note>, Book 2; **Valerius Maximus** <note>Referred to in the text as "Valere le grand," a 1st-century Roman historian.</note>, Book 2, Chapter 1; **Aulus Gellius** <note>Author of *Attic Nights*.</note>, Book 10, Chapter 25; and **Aelian** in the 2nd book of his *Various History*: and that was the beginning of the kisses given by husbands to their wives, to discover if they smelled of wine. 

**Aeneas Silvius** <note>The secular name of Pope Pius II (1405–1464), a prominent humanist scholar.</note>, in the second book of his commentaries on the deeds of **Alfonso, King of Aragon**, recounts that when it was said to the **Emperor Frederick** <note>Frederick III (1415–1493), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>—a man who was a great lover of sobriety—that **Eleanor** his wife (who had never tasted wine in her father's house) would soon conceive and bear children if she drank wine in Germany, which is such a cold region; he replied: That he would much rather have a sterile wife than one addicted to wine. He intended to convey that he was not ignorant of how many evils accompanied drunkenness, especially when the female sex devotes itself to too great a love of wine taken immoderately. 

Finally, to return to our first subject, Faunus, sorrowful at having caused the death of his wife from... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

# BOOK ONE.

## RULE OF THE JUDGES.

**OTHNIEL**, brother of Caleb, the first Judge, delivers the people of Israel from the oppression of the king of Mesopotamia.

**Aioth** or **Ehud**, Judge, called "ambidextrous" <note>The original French "gaucher destrier" refers to the biblical description of Ehud as being "restricted in his right hand," which was often interpreted in this era as being able to use both hands with equal skill.</note>, because he could use both hands, the left as well as the right, delivers Israel from the tyranny of the king of the Moabites, whom he overcomes and kills.

**Bacchus**, surnamed **Dionysus** and **Father Liber**, invents honey. *Ovid: — and they say that honey was discovered by Bacchus.* <note>original: "Et a Baccho mella reperta ferunt" (Ovid, Fasti, 3.736).</note>

**Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Minos**, king of Crete. <note>In Greek mythology, these three were famous for their wisdom and later became the judges of the underworld.</note>

# NICOSTRATA.

<image-desc>An oval-framed engraving depicting two women in classical dress. One woman is seated and writing on a tablet with a stylus; the tablet contains the letters "ABC" over "EF". <margin>2726.</margin>
NICOSTRATA, mother of Evander, King of Arcadia, brought letters to the Latins and taught them to them. It is worth noting that the ancient letters of the Greeks were, in the beginning, almost the same and similar to the Latin ones, as was seen on an ancient copper tablet dedicated to Pallas <note>The goddess Athena</note>, placed in the library of the palace in Rome; and upon it were engraved these letters: Nausikrates, son of Tisamenus, an Athenian, dedicated this. <note>original Greek: ΝΑΥΣΙΚΡΑΤΗΣ ΤΙΣΑΜΕΝΟΥ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΑΝΕΘΗΚΕ</note>

This woman was first called by her proper Greek name, Nicostrata, and later Carmentis or Carmenta: because she predicted future things in verses called *Carmina* <note>songs or poems; original French: "Carmes"</note> by the Latins, which verses interpreted the oracles of Apollo. Alternatively, she was called Carmenta because it seemed as if she had become mad (which the Latins call "to lack a mind" <note>original Latin: "Carere mente"</note>). <note>The author is referencing the ancient belief that prophetic inspiration resembled a form of divine madness or frenzy.</note>

# THESEUS.

<image-desc>An oval-framed woodcut portrait of Theseus. He is depicted as a bearded man in ornate classical armor and a flowing cloak, wearing a crown. He holds a wreath or crown aloft in his right hand and a club in his left—the club being a trophy from his first victory. The background shows a classical building on the left and a hilly landscape. A Latin inscription "THESEVS · ATHEN · REX" borders the upper half of the oval, which translates to: "Theseus, King of Athens."</image-desc>

**Theseus**, son of Aegeus, king of Athens, and Aethra, daughter of Pittheus, performed great exploits in war, being very valiant and an imitator of Hercules. First, he killed Periphetes at Ragouze <note>original: "Ragouze." While the text names this location, classical sources typically place this encounter at Epidaurus, where Theseus took the bronze club from the brigand Periphetes.</note>, who, armed with a club, tried to block his passage. He also killed Sinis the *Pine-bender* <term>Pityocamptes: a Greek epithet meaning "the one who bends pine trees." Sinis would tie his victims to bent trees and then release them, tearing the victims apart.</term> in the same manner that the said Sinis used to put others to death. Similarly, he defeated Sciron in Megara, and afterwards in Eleusis he conquered and defeated Cercyon of Arcadia in a wrestling match. Shortly thereafter, he put to death the thief Damastes <note>Better known in Greek mythology as Procrustes, the "stretcher," who forced guests to fit his bed by stretching them or cutting off their limbs.</note> at Hermione, giving him the same death he was accustomed to give his guests. Theseus did this in imitation of Hercules: for to bring justice to the wicked, he punished them with the same penalty they used to make others end their lives. He also put to the sword all the traitors who had set an ambush for him at Gargettus, on behalf of the Pallanti[des]... <note>The Pallantides were the fifty sons of Pallas, the brother of Aegeus, who sought to seize the throne from Theseus.</note>

## PALAMEDES.

<image-desc>An oval-framed woodcut depicting Palamedes as a bearded man in classical robes, seated in a rocky, mountainous landscape. He holds a stylus and a tablet inscribed with the Greek letters Θ (Theta), Ξ (Xi), Φ (Phi), and Χ (Chi). He is surrounded by three cranes; one stands tall to his right, and two others are at his feet. A scroll-like banner at the bottom of the illustration identifies him as "PALAMEDES".</image-desc>

PALAMEDES was named *pansophos* <note>original: "πανσοφος"; meaning "all-wise" or "all-knowing"</note>, which is to say, all-knowing, because of the knowledge he possessed of all things. He was the inventor of four Greek letters, which he added to those of Cadmus <note>The legendary founder of Thebes, credited with bringing the first sixteen letters of the alphabet to Greece from Phoenicia.</note>, namely: θ (theta), ξ (xi), φ (phi), and χ (chi). He also invented the organization of a military camp, the watchword, and the use of sentinels, having learned all these things, along with those four letters, from cranes and by their example: For cranes, by their nature, choose a leader from among themselves who flies in front so that they may all follow together; they place others at the tail of their flock, keeping the whole troop in order by their cry; and they have those who keep watch during the night, holding a stone in one foot, which, if it falls when they are overcome by sleep, wakes them by the sound it makes striking the ground. All the others who sleep always have one foot raised in the air and the other resting on the ground.

<meta>catchword: The leader</meta>

<summary>This page describes the legendary Greek hero Palamedes, crediting him with the invention of four Greek letters and various military protocols inspired by his observations of crane behavior. It illustrates the Renaissance belief that human wisdom and technology were often derived from the study of the natural world.</summary>

<keywords>Palamedes, pansophos, Greek alphabet, Cadmus, cranes, military tactics, sentinels, natural history, invention</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Palamedes, specifically describing how he observed the natural behavior of cranes to develop human systems of writing and military organization. <header>BOOK ONE.</header>

The leader and guide merely raises his neck and anticipates needs. Furthermore, in flying and changing their order, they seem to represent the shapes of certain letters. This is why *Ulysses* <note>also known as Odysseus</note> objects to *Palamedes* that he did not invent (as he boasted) letters, the battalion, and the order of a camp: but that the cranes taught him all of this. To which *Palamedes* replies to him in *Philostratus* <note>referring to the Greek writer Flavius Philostratus</note>: "I did not (he says) find the letters, but the letters found me: which, being hidden in the house of the *Muses*, had great need of such a man." The gods also bring such things to light through wise men. The cranes do not know the letters, but they maintain order in flight when they go to *Africa* to fight the *Pygmies*. *Palamedes* also first invented counters <note>tokens used for calculation or games</note>, gaming tables, and chess. He was the son of *Nauplius*, King of *Euboea*, an island commonly called *Negropont* <note>a medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea</note>. *Ulysses*, feigning madness to avoid going to war against the *Trojans*, was plowing the seashore with goats, sometimes with mules, and sometimes with various other animals. *Palamedes*, wishing to uncover this deception, placed *Telemachus*—the child of *Ulysses* and *Penelope*—in front of the plow or tillage-tool. *Ulysses* immediately stopped and ceased plowing, for fear of running over the child and harming him. Another time, *Ulysses* had gone to *Thrace* to buy grain, and returning empty-handed, he claimed he could find none. *Palamedes*, going there himself, had a great quantity brought back: at which, and other things, *Ulysses* was aggrieved; he conceived such envy against *Palamedes* that he sought by all means to have him killed. Finally, *Palamedes* having obtained a command from the *Greeks* against the *Trojans*, either as captain or in some other office,

<meta>catchword: the detra</meta>

Ulysses redoubled his envy, won over some of Palamedes' servants, and had a great sum of gold and silver buried and hidden beneath his tent. This done, he stationed a man who, pretending to be a messenger, came to the Greeks with letters of warning, claiming that Palamedes had promised Priam <note>the King of Troy</note> to betray the army, and for doing so had received a great treasure. Upon hearing this news, at the persuasion of Ulysses, they sent to Palamedes' tent, where the said gold and silver were found in the ground. And by the consent of all, without being heard or allowed to justify himself, he was stoned to death as one guilty in the middle of the camp. Thus we see how slander and envy brought about the death of poor Palamedes.

## ARGUMENTATION
### *concerning detractors, slander, and envy,*
### *causes of the death of Palamedes.*

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'C' containing a figure, possibly a philosopher or saint, seated within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>
Although Palamedes was esteemed the wisest of all the Greeks, and a man capable of handling great affairs, it is nevertheless held that through an extreme fire of envy, he plotted the death of one of his kinsmen, a friend and companion in war; and you have seen how he was repaid in kind <note>original: "rendu de tel pain souppe," a French idiom literally meaning "returned such bread-soup," equivalent to being given a taste of one's own medicine</note>. The very plot he had brewed for another fell upon himself through detraction, false reports, and envy. This gave an opening to the slander that Ulysses was easily able to persuade Menelaus <note>King of Sparta and brother of Agamemnon</note> to believe against him, accusing him of collusion with the Trojans, although there was no truth to any of it. All detractors possess two qualities: namely, envy and hypocrisy; and these two conditions were found among the Jews <note>a reflection of the common anti-Semitic tropes used in 16th-century moralizing literature</note>. Saint Bernard describes this very well...

Horace shows clearly <note>original: "à l'œil," literally "to the eye"</note> who the slanderer is through these verses, translated from his 4th Satire by Habert, as follows: <note>François Habert (c. 1508–1562) was a popular French translator who turned classical Latin works into French verse.</note>

> He who, with insult and slander,
> Comes to wound his friend in his absence,
> And who does not save or defend his honor
> When seeing him dishonored by another,
> And who seeks the laughter of men,
> Which is not valued by good people,
> And who affects and seeks with all his heart
> To have the reputation of a wit and a mocker,
> He who fakes and affirms a thing
> That he never saw containing any truth,
> And who cannot keep secrets hidden
> That were revealed to him in confidence:
> Roman people, it is he who keeps venom
> Within his heart; therefore, be on your guard.

The slanderer speaks ill of the one he maliciously accuses, and of his friends; but it is in their absence, for fear that he might be confounded if the truth were suddenly known and the lie discovered, knowing well that he could not and would not know how to sustain it. For commonly such people are cowards and of little power. They are of such weak heart that they dare do nothing openly, but are like one who spies on his enemy and shoots at him from some hedge or ditch, so that they do not know from where the arrow comes...

Thus, these people speak ill in secret, which demonstrates clearly enough that their report is in no way true. And just as those who fight in a closed field <note>A "camp clos" refers to a formal dueling arena or tournament ground where judicial duels took place.</note> watch attentively to see if their enemy has some poorly armored part where they might strike, so our detractors cast their eyes upon us and take note of everything we do or say, in order to find an occasion to slander and harm us. However, this path is not always the safest nor the easiest, for the entrance to it is through envy, which keeps them continually fearful in pain and hope; and afterward, the outcome is ordinarily unhappy and full of misery. Additionally, the greatest fear they have is of revealing their own distress; without that, their trickery could not cause damage, if it were easy to recognize it clearly and early on.

Also, detractors are most often frustrated in their expectations and cannot do great harm, seeing that truth always surmounts lies, and virtuous men who love honor do not make a habit of slandering. Rage and fury proceed from envy. *Alecto*, the infernal fury, is as much to say as "without rest"; and the restlessness within the envious person is the beginning of fury. <note>The name Alecto is derived from the Greek *alēktos*, meaning "unceasing" or "never-ending."</note> *Megaera*, another fury, takes her meaning from hatred, through which one reaches extreme madness. <note>Megaera is derived from the Greek *megairō*, meaning "to grudge" or "to envy."</note> Now, is it not madness to wish to lose one eye so that another may lose both? From where does this foolish desire come, if not from envy? 

A master, wishing to reward two servants who had served him for a long time, granted them whatever they might ask for, under the condition that whatever the first asked for, the other would receive double. One of them, being extremely greedy, decided not to be the first to ask, preferring to have nothing at all rather than go first, and waited for the other to make a request so that he might receive the double reward promised by the master. His companion, seeing this, was moved by envy; and while they waited for one another to speak, he chose to ask for something that would be entirely to the detriment of his companion, or at least bring him no profit. He prayed his master to pluck out one of his eyes as his entire reward, so that the other would have both eyes removed.

The Emperor, being very generous, found the fruits beautiful, and taking great pleasure in their diversity, commanded the bearer to ask for whatever he wished. Now the Amazons, warlike women descended from the Scythians, first came to live near the river Tanais <note>The Don River in modern Russia</note>, and later beside the river Thermodon <note>A river in northern Turkey</note>. But the women, seeing themselves widowed, took such great courage that through the use of arms they grew their republic without men, calling marriage "servitude." Then, having secured peace with their neighbors through the victories they obtained over them, they knew them carnally so that their race would not perish. They killed all their male children and trained the girls in arms, searing their right breast so that it would not hinder them from drawing a bow. They were called Amazons, a name composed of "without" <note>original Greek: α</note>, and "breast" <note>original Greek: μαζὸς</note>.

Now the Amazons, warlike women descended from the Scythians, came to live first near the Tanais River <note>The Don River in modern-day Russia</note>, and later next to the Thermodon River <note>A river in northern Turkey, legendary home of the Amazons</note>. They conducted themselves so valiantly in war that they occupied a great part of Asia. Their husbands, raiding the lands of their neighbors, were defeated and killed; because of this, the victors intended to drive out these women. But seeing themselves widowed, the women took such great courage that through arms they grew their republic without men, calling marriage "servitude." Then, having secured peace with their neighbors through the victories they obtained over them, they knew them carnally <note>engaged in sexual relations</note> so that their race would not perish. They killed all their male children and trained the girls in arms, burning their right breast so that it would not hinder them from drawing the bow. They were called Amazons, a name composed of *a*, "without," and *mazos*, "breast." <note>original Greek: α, sans, & μαζός, mammelle</note>.

## A FORMAL DISCOURSE
### on the magnanimity of women.

## PROSOPOGRAPHY <note>From the Greek *prosopon* (person/face) and *graphia* (writing); a description of a person’s appearance, character, or life.</note>

There is often some difficult detractor <note>original: "calomniateur," meaning a slanderer or a person who argues in bad faith.</note> to be found among a company of people; one of the group, being of a different temperament than the others, obstinately insisted on maintaining the opposite view through several sophistical arguments. And seeing, through the certain and true replies of the young ladies, that he could not win his case against so many opponents, he was forced to concede to their opinion and admit his defeat <note>literally "confess the debt" (*confesser le debte*).</note>. Then, suddenly, to provide a veneer for his retraction, he recited an epigram written about Queen Tomyris <note>The legendary Queen of the Massagetae who defeated Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BCE.</note>, which contains within it a ridiculous narrative and covertly offers a mocking jab at women, so that one might not use this queen’s magnanimity as an argument in their favor. Tomyris speaks:

> While combing <note>original: "pignant," an archaic form of *peignant*.</note> my hair, I received the sad news
> That a son of mine was a captive or dead:
> Immediately I had "To horse!" <note>original: "Boute-celle," a military trumpet signal literally meaning "put on the saddle."</note> sounded:
> I took up arms and placed myself in the thick
> Of the battle, where I made such an effort
> That I made my fleeing enemies bleed,
> Then I returned to finish combing my hair.

### DARES THE PHRYGIAN.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut medallion depicting a bearded man in profile facing right, wearing a patterned cap or turban. The inscription "DARES PHRYGIVS." runs along the left and right interior edges of the circle.</image-desc>

Dares the Phrygian utilized, following Cadmus, the letters invented by that son of Agenor and by Palamedes <note>In Greek mythology, Cadmus is credited with introducing the Phoenician alphabet to Greece, while Palamedes is said to have added several letters to it during the Trojan War.</note>, in writing the history of the Trojan War, in which he was a participant. He so carefully observed the truth of the deeds and sayings that occurred in that war that Cornelius Nepos <note>A Roman biographer and historian (c. 110–25 BCE) who was believed to have translated Dares' work from Greek into Latin.</note> rightly offers high praise for his history, for which he deserves the title of historiographer. For history is named by Cicero <note>original: "Tesmoin des tēps, lumiere de verité, vie de la memoire, maistresse de la vie, messagere de l'ancienneté." These famous epithets are from Cicero’s *De Oratore* (II, 36): "Historia vero testis temporum, lux veritatis, vita memoriae, magistra vitae, nuntia vetustatis."</note> the witness of the times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the mistress of life, and the messenger of antiquity; and by Thucydides <note>A Greek historian of the 5th century BCE.</note>, a royal treasure. Thus, he who writes history must take care above all else not to include false things or matters far removed from the truth. He must also follow another rule, which is to neither flatter nor show himself to be more biased toward one side than the other. He truly ought to praise and exalt the good, detest and cast down the wicked, incite readers to virtue, and divert them from vice and condemn it, so that through examples the readers may gather the fruit of instruction. This is what our Dares the Phrygian knew well how to do in his history.

<note>original: "Multoties tali peſte ſubiecta maligne / Mors cita, vita breuis, Patauos in pace volentes / Viuere, non paſſa eſt, genus hoc fatale ferentes / Admonet, & punit nullo diſcrimine ciues." These Latin verses emphasize the recurring tragedies and "plagues" (likely both disease and war) that afflicted Padua.</note>

It is believed that long after the tomb was built, these barbaric verses were engraved on the sword by some prophet and soothsayer, who placed it inside the tomb; and what followed proves the prophecy of these verses true. For since then, the Paduans have always been mistreated by their princes, whose names began with the letter A, such as Attila the Hun, Agilulf the Goth, Ezzelino the Tyrant <note>Ezzelino III da Romano (1194–1259), a notoriously cruel ruler of the March of Treviso.</note>, Anfosidie <note>Anfuso, a lieutenant of Ezzelino.</note>, Alberto Scaliger <note>Alberto I della Scala (d. 1301), Lord of Verona.</note>, and Andrea Nerie.

**HESIOD**, a Greek poet native to Ascra, a village in Boeotia, was the first to write about agriculture in Greek verse, which Virgil later imitated <note>Referring to Virgil's *Georgics*.</note>. He lived for a very long time, which gave rise to the proverb *Hesiodic old age* <note>original: "ἡσιόδειον γῆρας"</note>. There is an epigram in Pindar regarding his long life:
> Hail, you who twice reached youth and twice encountered the grave,
> Hesiod, possessing the measure of wisdom for mankind.

<margin>2838</margin>
**HOMER**, the prince of Greek poets, was so named because he was blind (for the Ionians call blind men "Homers"), whereas previously he was called Melesigenes. He wrote the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey* in Greek verse. There is a diversity of opinions regarding the time in which he lived, for eight other Homers lived before this one, though they were lesser in subtlety of mind and learning.

Following God’s command, Samuel anointed and consecrated Saul as their king.

## DAMASCIUS OF SIGEUM

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of a man in profile facing right, with a thick beard and short curly hair. The portrait is framed by a circular border containing the Latin text: Damascius of Sigeum, Historian <note>original: "DAMASCIVS SIGIAEVS HIST."</note></image-desc>

Although Damascius of Sigeum, the historian, did not live during this exact time, I will not fail to include him here: for he wrote a book concerning the relatives of those who went to the Trojan War. All those who have written about the Trojan War include: Dares the Phrygian <note>A supposed eyewitness to the war, though the text attributed to him is a later forgery.</note>, Dictys <note>Dictys of Crete, another legendary chronicler of the war.</note>, Ephippius, a student of Isocrates, Damascius of Sigeum, Aemilius Macer the poet, Homer, Claudius Sabinus, and Euripides in his tragedy *Hecuba*. There was another Damascius from the time of Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor (r. 527–565 AD); this Damascius was the last head of the School of Athens.</note>, who wrote *excerpts* <note>original Greek: "παρεκβολάς"</note> *on the first book of Aristotle's "On the Heavens"; Doubts and Solutions Concerning First Principles; Commentary on Plato's "Parmenides"; and a History of Philosophers.*

### Epigram in honor of David.

A David has been king, poet, and shepherd,
And even now serves as an example to these three:
For he teaches Kings to render a just honor
To him who is King above all kings.
He teaches the poet not to employ his voice,
Except to sing of the Almighty’s <note>original: tref-haut</note> excellent grandeur:
And teaches shepherds the straightest paths
To guide their flocks in the ways of the Lord.

**DIDO**, daughter of a king of the Phoenicians or Tyrians, after the death of Sychaeus <note>original: Sichee</note>, priest of Hercules, her uncle and husband, comes by sea to Africa with great treasures in the company of Pygmalion <note>The text states she was "in the company of" her brother, though most classical accounts describe her fleeing from him after he murdered her husband for his wealth.</note> her brother. There she builds the city of **Carthage**, which was called **Byrsa** <note>A name meaning "ox-hide," relating to the legend that she claimed as much land as could be encompassed by an ox's skin.</note> before this name was imposed upon it, according to the opinion of some authors. The account that **Virgil** <note>original: Virgile</note> gives of her love for **Aeneas** <note>original: Aenee</note> is entirely false, and nothing less than plausible: for between her time and that of Aeneas there are more than a hundred years. **Boccaccio** <note>original: Boccace</note> highly esteems her chastity: for she preferred to die rather than remarry with **Iarbas**, King of Gaetulia <note>original: Getulie</note>, and to kill herself rather than soil the rights of her first marriage bed <note>original: premier lict</note> through second nuptials. I wished to include here an epigram that the poet **Ausonius** <note>original: Ausone</note> took from the Greek, which is relevant to this subject.

->On the image of Dido.<- <note>original: In Didus imaginem.</note>

> I am that Dido whom you behold in face, traveler, <note>original: Illa ego sum Dido vultu quam conspicis hospes</note>
> Represented in marvelous and beautiful ways.
> Such I was, but the mind Virgil <note>original: Maro</note> fashioned for me was not mine,
> Nor was my life joyful with unchaste desires.
> For neither did Trojan Aeneas ever see me,
> Nor did he reach Libya with the Trojan <note>original: Iliacis</note> fleets.
> But fleeing the furies and the arms of the wanton Iarbas,
> I preserved my modesty, I confess, through death:
> With my breast pierced, which endured the chaste swords,
> Not by madness or raw grief from wounded love.
> Thus it pleases me to have fallen: I lived without a wound to my reputation,
> Having avenged my husband, I met my end with hands laid down.
> Why, envious Muse, did you goad Virgil against me,
> To devise the ruin of my modesty?
> You readers, believe the historians more concerning me,
> Than those who sing of the deceits and couplings of the gods.

**SARDANAPALUS** <note>original: SARDANAPALE</note>, the thirty-first and last king of the Assyrians, was effeminate and lustful. He was not ashamed to keep company with harlots in women’s clothing and to spin wool with them. Because the Assyrians were unwilling to be ruled by one who was more a woman than a man, they revolted against him and waged war under the leadership of **Arbaces** <note>original: Arbax</note>, their chief. Sardanapalus, having been defeated, threw himself into the fire. **Ovid** writes:

**Lycurgus** <note>original: Licurgue</note> establishes laws for the Spartans <note>original: Lacedemoniens</note> that are good and useful for the maintenance of a popular and communal society. He divides the lands and estates equally, so that no one person has more than another. He abolishes gold and silver currency, leaving only iron money in use; he curtails extravagance in food and clothing.

**Aremulus** <note>original: Aremule; a legendary king of Alba Longa</note> reigns over the Latins.

<margin>Year 3120</margin>
**JEROBOAM [II]**, son of Joash, succeeds to the kingdom of Israel, which he rules for 41 years.

**Jonah** the prophet, thrown into the sea, is swallowed by a whale; he remains in its belly for three days and three nights, and then emerges safe and sound. He is a prefiguration of our savior Jesus Christ, who remained just as long in the tomb and, at the end of three days and as many nights, rose again in glory. He preaches repentance to the Ninevites and writes a prophecy contained in three chapters <note>The Book of Jonah in the Bible actually contains four chapters.</note> in the Old Testament.

# SECOND BOOK.

...[na]med <note>The text continues from the previous page's "nom-", forming "nomma" or "named".</note> a hundred senators called τιμιῦχοι <note>original: τιμιῦχοι (*timiouchoi*), a Greek term meaning "holders of honor" or "office-holders."</note>, which signifies powerful and honorable men; they were called **Conscript Fathers** for the sake of honor, and their descendants were called **Patricians**. He also organized three hundred men-at-arms to serve as his bodyguards both in times of war and peace, dividing the Roman youth into military orders, each of which contained three thousand infantry and three hundred knights. **Lucius Piso** <note>Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, a Roman historian and statesman who lived around 120 BCE.</note>, writing on the life and character of **Romulus**, relates that while at a banquet, Romulus drank only a very little because he had business to attend to the following day. One of the company said to him: "If everyone did as you do, wine would be cheaper." To which Romulus replied: "On the contrary, it would be much dearer if everyone drank as much as they wished, and more than they ought." He subjugated many of his hostile neighbors. Authors write differently regarding his death. Some say that as he was haranguing his soldiers, he was surrounded by a thick cloud and his people lost sight of him; however, this is more legendary than likely. Others say that the **Patricians** and **Senators**, being dissatisfied, conspired against him, killed him, and cut his body into pieces, which they buried secretly; this opinion is considered more truthful. He left the city of Rome populated and fortified with 46,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry; whereas in the beginning (as we have said), he had only 2,000 on foot and 300 on horse. Rome was thus built in the first year of the seventh **Olympiad** <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks to measure time; the 7th Olympiad corresponds to approximately 752 BCE.</note>, and in the 17th year of the reign of **Amulius** <note>The King of Alba Longa and great-uncle of Romulus.</note>. From the building of Rome until the birth of our Lord **Jesus Christ**, there were 752 years.

->**The Erythraean Sibyl** <note>A prophetess of classical antiquity; Christian historians often claimed she had predicted the life of Jesus.</note> predicts the coming of the Son of God, his passion, and the final judgment.<-

# NUMA POMPILIUS.

<image-desc>An oval medallion depicting a portrait of Numa Pompilius. He is shown as a bearded man standing in classical robes, holding a long staff or scepter. The background illustrates a detailed cityscape with various buildings and a stone bridge. An inscription circles the border: NVMA POMPILIVS II. ROM. R.</image-desc>

<margin>3250 <note>The date 3250 refers to the year from the creation of the world (*Anno Mundi*), which the author aligns with approximately 712 BCE.</note></margin>
UPON the vacancy of the kingship in Rome by the death of **Romulus**, the senators established ten decurions <term>Interrex: officials who shared power and took turns governing during the transition between kings</term>, who governed the kingdom for one year: and **Numa Pompilius** was afterward created King of Rome in the 3rd year of the 16th Olympiad, 712 years before the coming of Christ. He was a lover of peace and tranquility, and established the Romans in laws and good morals; he was the first to strive to increase the religion of the gods through sacrifices, built temples, and invented many ceremonies, which he compiled into eight books. He made his people worship more than one hundred and seventy thousand gods <note>The original French text "cent septante mille dieux" likely contains an error. Historical sources usually state that Numa forbade images of gods for the first 170 *years* of Rome; the author appears to have mistaken the years for the number of deities.</note>, though without statues or likenesses, *judging it a sacrilege to represent better things by lesser ones* <note>original: "nephas esse iudicans deterioribus meliora assimilare"</note> (as Julien Aurel <note>Julien Haurech, a 16th-century historian and author</note> says). He recommended piety above all to his people, and added two months to the year, which previously consisted of only ten: namely January (called *Gamelion* <note>original: γαμηλιών. The "month of weddings" in the Athenian calendar, roughly corresponding to January/February.</note> by the Athenians, because they sa-

...sacrificed in this month to Juno, goddess of weddings, whom they believed presided over the month: but Numa named it *January*, after King Janus, to whom he consecrated a statue with two faces: or from <term>Ianuárion <note>original: ἰανουάριον. This is a Greek transliteration of the Latin month name; the author connects it to the "head" or beginning of a period.</note></term>, as head or father of the age) and February (called <term>Elaphebolion <note>original: ἐλαφηβολιὼν. A month in the Athenian calendar, typically occurring in spring, dedicated to Artemis (Diana) the huntress.</note></term> by the Athenians, because in this month they hunted stags in memory of Diana; and called *Februarius* by the Latins, from *Februum*, which was the wool, the branches, and all that was needed for the sacrifices of purification, or from the god Februus invoked in this month during the processions ordered by Numa, or from Juno Februella, to whom the Romans solemnized their Lupercalia <note>An ancient Roman festival involving purification and fertility rites.</note> in this month). He built the Capitol from base to summit, and dabbled in hydromancy <term>Hydromancy: a method of divination by which a person attempts to see the future or spirits in water.</term>. Saint Augustine says this in *The City of God*: <note>original: "Numa hydromantiam facere compulsus est, ut in aqua videret imagines dæmonum, & audiret ab eis quid in sacrificiis institueret, & observare deberet."</note> *Numa was compelled to practice hydromancy, so that in the water he might see images of demons, and hear from them what he should institute in the sacrifices, and what he ought to observe.* He died at the age of 80: reigned 43 years: left four sons and one daughter, from whom was born Ancus Marcius, who was king of the Romans.

# MANASSEH, King of Judah, wicked and cruel,
restored the idolatry that his father Hezekiah had abolished: he had the prophet Isaiah cut into two parts: sacrificed his children to idols: shed the blood of righteous people in Jerusalem, for which God became angry, and raised up against him the King of Babylon, who took him captive and led him away with irons on his feet. Recognizing God, he was restored to his kingdom after having remained a prisoner for 8 years: and he had the idols torn down. He reigned 55 years.

->SECOND BOOK<-

## THE NYMPH EGERIA.

<image-desc>An oval medallion depicting the nymph Egeria in a classical landscape with trees, a river, and buildings in the background. She is depicted with long hair and flowing robes, looking toward the left. The border of the oval contains the inscription: "Egeria, Nymph, Wife of Numa" <note>original: "AEGERIA NYMPHA VX. NVM."</note></image-desc>

Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome (reigned c. 715–673 BC), who succeeded Romulus and was known as a peaceful lawmaker.</note> often went all alone into some very thick forest, or else entered into a secret cave, remaining there for a good length of time, feigning to go there to receive the oracles and the will of the gods, in order to make his people believe that the gods came there to speak to him, so that he might be better obeyed, and that his people might place more faith in his laws <note>The original uses "constitutions," referring to established political or religious rules.</note>. And above all, he claimed to be very familiar with a certain Nymph called Egeria, whom some have said was one of the muses who lived in the Arician forest <note>The *Nemus Aricinum* (Arician Grove) near Lake Nemi, a site sacred to Diana and Egeria.</note>. He entered there every night, giving it to be understood upon his return that this Nymph came there to give him advice on everything he had to do, and to teach him the laws and ceremonies that he ought to command his people, and institute for them divine service—to the end that it would be believed his ceremonies were not...

ordained thus by him alone, but by the will of the gods. And he did this following the example of the Greeks, Minos and Lycurgus. One of these, in order to make the people of Crete receive his laws with more honor and observe them with greater reverence, feigned that he had consulted with Jupiter on the mountain where he was raised by the Corybantes <note>The Corybantes were the armed and music-making worshippers of the goddess Cybele; in mythology, they protected the infant Zeus (Jupiter) on Crete.</note>, or priests of Cybele, from where he said he had brought the laws which he had received from Jupiter in a cave. And the other, namely Lycurgus, by going frequently to Delphi to the temple of Apollo, gave it to be understood that he had taken from there the laws that he gave to the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedemoniens"</note>. The poets feign that this nymph Egeria wept so much for the death of Numa that she was transformed into a fountain of tears. Ovid says in the 15th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *Happy with a nymph for his wife, and with the Muses as his guides, he taught the sacrificial rites, and led a race accustomed to fierce war toward the arts of peace.* <note>original: "Coniuge qui fœlix nympha, ducibúſque camœnis / Sacrificos docuit ritus, gentémque feroci / Aſſuetam bello, pacis traduxit ad artes."</note>

<margin>3292.</margin> **AMON**, king of Judah and son of Manasseh—more wicked than his father—reigned for two years. He was killed by his servants, who were in turn killed by the people.

And the very creator of this cruel punishment was the first to experience it: for Phalaris commanded that the wretched Perillus be burned in this manner. Ovid:

> *And violent Phalaris scorched the limbs of Perillus in the bull;*
> *the unhappy creator was the first to use his own work.*

divine frenzy <note>Continuing from the previous page: "through divine frenzy, as a comic poet."</note>. There are some who have never seen a single precept of the poetic art, yet who compose verses on the spot: their words are measured verses, and they do so by nature, without even thinking of it. Ovid, speaking of himself in the fourth book of the *Tristia*, bears witness to this:

> Song came of its own accord to fit the right meters,
> And what I attempted to say was verse.
<note>Original Latin: *Sponte sua carmen numeros veniebat ad aptos: / Et quod tentabam dicere versus erat.*</note>

Pope Leo, tenth of that name, held his own against Camillo Querno, one of his familiars, by responding to him on the spot in verse upon the subject of the verses Querno had uttered just as suddenly. For as Querno—who called himself the "archpoet," that is, prince of poets, and who was gouty—was at Leo's table, where he was accustomed to eat often, he was commanded to recite two brand new verses composed by him in that instant. He began with this hexameter:

> The archpoet makes verses for a thousand poets.
<note>Original Latin: *Archipoëta facit versus pro mille poëtis.*</note>

And stopping as he thought of the pentameter <note>In classical poetry, an elegiac couplet consists of a hexameter line followed by a shorter pentameter line.</note>, Leo suddenly replied subtly and to the point:

> And for a thousand others, the archpoet drinks.
<note>Original Latin: *Et pro mille aliis Archipoëta bibit.*</note>

Then Querno, catching himself, replied:

> Hand me the Falernian wine that may make learned songs for me.
<note>Original Latin: *Porrige quod faciat mihi carmina docta falernum.* Falernian was a prestigious wine from ancient Rome, often associated with poetic inspiration.</note>

Immediately Leo, borrowing from Virgil, added:

> This even unnerves and weakens the feet.
<note>Original Latin: *Hoc etiam eneruat debilitátque pedes.* This is a clever pun: "feet" refers both to the metrical feet of the poem and to Querno’s physical feet, which were afflicted by gout.</note>

And Ennius <note>The text reads "Enne," referring to Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet.</note> rightly calls poets "holy," for they are commended to us as a gift and present from the heavens.

Zaleucus, lawgiver of the Locrians <note>A Greek tribe in Italy.</note>, established a law that whoever should be found in adultery shall have both eyes plucked out as punishment. His own son transgressed this law; Zaleucus had one of his son's eyes put out, and one of his own. By leaving the use of sight to both, he exercised justice and piety together.

TARQUIN the Elder, or the Ancient, previously named Lucumo (according to the author Sabellicus), the fifth king of the Romans, is the first to wear the *praetexta* robe <note>original: "robbe pretexte"; the *toga praetexta* was a white robe with a broad purple border worn by certain magistrates and high-born children.</note> in Rome after he subjugated the Tuscans. It is a sleeveless garment that one threw over the shoulders like a Spanish-style cape. <note>The author uses a contemporary 16th-century fashion reference—the Spanish cape—to explain the ancient Roman toga to his readers.</note> There were several kinds: the *puerile* for children, that of women, the priestly, the military, the triumphal, and that of the magistrates. He defeated the Sabines; conquered the Latins; was the first to enter Rome in a triumph; had the Circus built; and began the building of the Capitol, so called because a man’s head was found there. <note>The word "Capitol" is traditionally derived from *caput*, the Latin word for head.</note>

The Amalthean Sibyl presents three books to Tarquin the Elder, for which she asks three hundred crowns, at which he mocks her. She burns one of them and asks no less for the remaining two. Tarquin laughs even more at the foolish request. The Sibyl burns yet another, and demands as much for the one remaining out of the three as she had for all of them. The king, astonished, gives her the three hundred crowns and has the book carefully kept in the Capitol under the charge of fifteen men, who, in times of eminent danger to the state, would consult it for advice. <note>These were the famous Sibylline Books, consulted by the Roman Senate during crises.</note>

JOACHIM, otherwise known as Jeconiah, aged 18, besieged by the Assyrians, surrenders with his mother, his princes, and a large part of the people to Nebuchadnezzar, who leads him captive to Babylon, where he will beget Salathiel Mesezebel in prison.

# THALES THE PHILOSOPHER.

<image-desc>An oval-framed engraving of Thales of Miletus. He is depicted as an elderly man with a long beard, seated and leaning over a desk while looking back. A plaque on the right is inscribed "THALES MILESIVS." In the background, a window looks out onto a building, and a figure appears within a cloud. In the foreground, a circular instrument or diagram featuring geometric and celestial symbols sits on the desk.</image-desc>

THALES, a native of Phoenicia and a citizen of Miletus, a city in Ionia where he had settled, was the first Physician <note>In this historical context, "Physician" refers to a practitioner of "physics"—the study of the natural world and the laws of nature—rather than a medical doctor.</note> and one of the seven sages of Greece who flourished at the same time. The others are Chilon of Lacedaemonia <note>Ancient Sparta.</note>, Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mytilene, Cleobulus of Lindos, Periander of Corinth, and Solon of Salamis; all were called *sophes*, which is to say, wise men. Saint Augustine says: *The world was very poor and naked of wisdom when only seven were named from the whole universe. But even these wise men of the world were made foolish: for because they did not have wisdom—namely, the true knowledge of God—they perished due to their own folly.* <note>original Latin: "Valde mundus pauper erat & nudus sapientia, quando solum septem nominabantur ex uniuerso. Sed & hi quoque sapientes mundi, stulti facti sunt: quia enim non habuerunt sapientiam, scilicet veram Dei notitiam, perierunt propter insipientiam suam."</note> Pythagoras, coming after them, had himself called a Philosopher, a lover of wisdom: and he thought it right to no longer call science *sophia* [wisdom], but rather *philosophia* [philosophy], inasmuch as there is no one wise among all living beings except God alone: for which reason all those who

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Seven Sages of Greece, transitioning from the general definition of "sophes" to the specific schools of philosophy and the life and maxims of Thales of Miletus.</meta>

<header>PROSOPOGRAPHY</header>

Those who came after him in the profession were called philosophers: some of whom took their name from cities, like the **Megarian**, **Elian**, and **Cyrenaic** philosophers; some from places, like the **Academics** and **Stoics**; from events or the marketplace, the **Peripatetics**; from insults or reproaches, the **Cynics**; from their results, the **Eudemons**; and others from their teachers, like the **Socratics** and **Epicureans**. Those who have written of the nature of things, called *physis* in Greek <note>original Greek: "φύσις"</note>, are named **Physicians** <note>As noted on the previous page, this refers to "natural philosophers" or scientists who studied the physical world, not medical doctors.</note>; those who treat of morals are called **Ethicists**, for *ethe* <note>original Greek: "ἤθη"</note> are morals; those who involve themselves in disputing, debating, and resolving questions are called **dialecticians**, from the term for discussing or debating <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ διαλέγεσθαι"; original Latin: "à differendo."</note>. As for the wise **Thales**, he possessed knowledge of natural things, eclipses and their occurrences, and of the Greater and Lesser Bear—celestial signs that the **Phoenicians** were accustomed to observe in their navigations, as witnessed by **Callimachus**: *And he was said to have measured the stars of the Wagon [the Big Dipper], by which the Phoenicians sail.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τῆς ἁμάξης ἐλέγετο, σταθμήσασθαι τοὺς ἀστερισκούς, ᾗ πλέουσι φοίνικες."</note>

He provided the definition of God, invented the clock <note>In antiquity, this usually refers to a gnomon or sundial.</note> for the **Milesians**, was the first to maintain that souls are immortal, measured the course of the sun, divided the year, and left behind several beautiful maxims, explained by **Ausonius** <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a Roman poet of the 4th century.</note> as follows:

> *Fear to do something shameful, even when you are your own only witness.* <note>original Latin: "Turpe quid ausurus te sine teste time."</note>
> *Life perishes, but the glory of death shall not die.* <note>original Latin: "Vita perit, mortis gloria non morietur."</note>
> *What you are about to do, refrain from speaking of it beforehand.* <note>original Latin: "Quod facturus eris, dicere sustuleris."</note>
> *It is a torment if you fear what you cannot overcome.* <note>original Latin: "Crux est, si metuas, vincere quod nequeas."</note>
> *When you rebuke truthfully, even as an enemy you are helpful.* <note>original Latin: "Cum verè obiurgas, sic inimice iuvas."</note>
> *When you praise falsely, then even as a friend you do harm.* <note>original Latin: "Cum falso laudas, tunc & amice noces."</note>
> *Nothing in excess is enough, lest even this be in excess.* <note>original Latin: "Nil nimium satis est, ne sit & hoc nimium."</note>

He gave thanks to fortune for three things: namely, that he was a human and not a brute beast, a male and not a female, and a Greek and not a barbarian.

**Draco**, the severe and cruel legislator of the **Athenians**,

After the death of **Tarquin the Elder** <note>original: "Tarquin le Prisque"; Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth King of Rome.</note>, **Servius Tullius** was elected king of the Romans by the Senators and by the people. He first established the census <note>original: "le cens"</note>, which requires that everyone provide an inventory <note>original: "denombrement"</note> of their property before the censor, so as to be assessed according to its value and to pay at a proportional rate. He was the first to surround the walls with moats; he enlarged the city of Rome by three hills—the **Quirinal**, **Viminal**, and **Esquiline**—which he had enclosed by high and strong walls, with moats and other ramparts. **Pythagoras of Samos**, son of Mnesarchus, and pupil of **Pherecydes of Syros** and **Hermodamas**, sailed to Egypt to learn theology, their customs, and manners. From there, he went to **Babylon**, where he acquired knowledge of the **Chaldean** <term>Chaldean: Relating to the ancient people of Babylonia, renowned for their advancements in astronomy and astrology.</term> discipline, namely astrology and the movement of the stars. Curious to see and know more, he passed through **Sparta** to sail to **Crete**, in order to understand the laws of **Minos** and **Lycurgus**. Afterward, he returned to his own country, from which he went to that part of Italy called **Magna Graecia** <note>original: "la grand Grece"; a coastal area of Southern Italy extensively populated by Greek settlers.</note>. There, he acquired the title of **Philosopher**. He had a good six hundred students, to whom he first taught arithmetic, which he greatly adorned with numbers and specific characters invented by him. He commanded silence for five years; forbade the eating of meat and beans; devised the **transmigration** <note>original: "transmutation"; the belief that the soul moves into a new body after death.</note> or change of souls from one body to another; and died at **Metapontum**, an island situated between Rhodes and Cnidus <note>The author mistakenly identifies Metapontum, a city in southern Italy, as an island in the Aegean; Pythagoras did indeed die in Metapontum in Italy.</note>. **Polycrates**, tyrant of the **Samians**, was happy in this world throughout his life; but his pitiful end and infamous death show that **no one is happy before death** <note>A common Greek philosophical theme, famously attributed to Solon.</note>. For **Orontes**, the governor of Persia, having captured him, had him hanged and strangled. **Democedes** was the physician of Polycrates.

**Solon**, one of the seven sages of Greece, gave laws to the **Athenians**. He repealed those of **Draco** for being too rigorous, except for those which punished homicide. He refused the position of prince; and seeing that **Pisistratus**, his relative, had usurped it, he went to Egypt to study wisdom for ten years. See **Diogenes Laërtius** in his *Life of Solon*.

**Anacreon**, a lyric poet and a great drunkard, died while drinking, choked by a small grape seed.

# PISISTRATUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait in profile of a bearded man facing right. **Pisistratus**, tyrant of the Athenians, born of a noble family, was so well-spoken that through his eloquence the Athenians stripped themselves of their liberty—the most precious thing they possessed—preferring his beautiful words and promises to the holiness of **Solon**, who had been the "god" <note>Referring to Solon's status as the revered lawgiver and savior of the Athenian state.</note> of the City. Solon assembled the people of Athens one day, saying to them:

> I am wiser than some among you, and stronger than others: wiser than those who do not take heed of the schemes of Pisistratus, and stronger than those who know them well but dare not say a word for fear.

# PROSOPOGRAPHY

<meta>catchword: To Ty-</meta>

*It shall be part of my peace to have touched the tyrant’s right hand.* <note>original Latin: "Pars mihi pacis erit dextram tetigisse tyranni." A line from the Roman poet Lucan’s "Pharsalia," suggesting that even a handshake with a tyrant can be a form of survival or submission.</note>

But since then, the name of "tyrant," taken in a negative sense, has been given to those who through insolence abused the power of their dominion, governing according to their own appetite and whims, contrary to justice and equitable laws. Regarding such men, **Juvenal** says through <term>prosopopoeia</term> <note>A rhetorical device where the speaker provides a voice to an absent person or an imaginary character—in this case, the voice of the tyrant themselves.</note>:

> ->*Thus I will it, thus I command; let my will stand for reason.*<- <note>original Latin: "Sic volo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas." A famous line from Juvenal’s "Satires" (6.223) describing someone who offers no reason for their actions other than their own desire.</note>

**Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most famous medieval jurists, whose work on the law of tyranny remained a standard text for centuries.</note>, in his treatise *On Tyranny*, says: *A tyrant is named from the Greek word* <term>tyros</term> <note>original Greek: τυρὸς. Medieval scholars often used creative, if linguistically inaccurate, etymologies; here he attempts to link the word to "distress" or "strength."</note>*, which in Latin is interpreted as tribulation, distress, or strength.* and since then, it has come to pass that only wicked and iniquitous kings, who practice cruelty toward their subjects, are called tyrants. He is called a tyrant (says **Saint Gregory** in the eleventh book of his *Morals*) who rules over the republic not by right but by force. There is a great difference between a prince and a tyrant. *For the duty of princes is to make those who obey them happier through their care and industry. But the custom of tyrants is to secure their own comforts and pleasures from the misfortunes and disasters of others.* <note>original Latin: "Nam principum officium est..." This passage highlights the Renaissance ideal of "the Mirror for Princes," contrasting the "good shepherd" ruler with the "wolf-like" tyrant.</note> It is true that God rewards them in the end according to their merits. We commonly see all these tyrants come to a bad end. It happens that they are killed by their brothers or sisters, some by their children, others by their wives, or otherwise they die in great misery. This is the vengeance of God, which is slow, but is eventually carried out. For if we are afflicted by tyrants, let us believe that our own enormous sins are the cause, and that God makes these perverse men the ministers of His high justice; as **Ariosto** sings in four or five stanzas of the 17th canto of his *Orlando*:

> *Just God, when our sins* <note>original Italian: "Il giusto dio, quando i peccati nostri..." from Ludovico Ariosto's epic poem "Orlando Furioso."</note>
> *Have passed the mark of forgiveness,*
> *So that He may demonstrate His justice*
> *Equal to His mercy, often from a kingdom...*

Now God allows us to be punished
By peoples who are perhaps worse than ourselves,
Because of our multiplied and infinite,
Nefarious and shameful errors.
A time will come when we shall go to plunder their shores,
If ever we should become better men;
And when their own sins reach such a height
That they move Eternal Goodness to indignation.

## MONARCHY OF THE Persians.

### *Panthea, a lady of exceptional virtue.*

## PANTHEA.

<image-desc>An oval medallion framed woodcut illustration. At the top of the oval's interior is the name "PANTHEA." written in an arch. The scene depicts a woman in classical robes standing over a man who lies on the ground. She holds a dagger in her hand. The background features a large leafy tree on the left and a cityscape with several towers and spires on the right.</image-desc>

AFTER Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great (r. c. 550–530 BC), the founder of the Persian Empire, often portrayed in literature as a model of the ideal ruler.</note>, the first King of the Persians, had defeated the Assyrians, a young lady named Panthea, the wife of Abradates <note>A king of Susa who was initially an ally of the Assyrians but later joined Cyrus.</note>, King of the Susians <note>The people of Susa, an ancient city in what is now Khuzestan, Iran.</note>, was brought in as a prisoner. When the spoils of war were divided and the King’s gifts set aside, Cyrus said to his men: "I receive with a good heart what you have given me; however, whoever has a greater need for it may take it, and I give it to him." Then a Mede <note>A person from Media, an ancient Iranian people who were close allies and subjects of the Persians.</note> who was very devoted to music said to him: "Sire, yesterday I was greatly delighted to hear the two female singers <note>original: "chanteresses"</note> who were given to you; and if it please you to give me one of them, I would rather follow you than stay at home." "And I give her to you," said Cyrus, "and I assure you that by asking her of me, you have done me more [pleasure]..."

And having summoned **Araspes the Mede** <note>A childhood friend and confidant of Cyrus, who figures prominently in Xenophon's account of this story.</note>, his childhood companion, he entrusted to him the beautiful tent and the beautiful prisoner, the wife of **Abradates**. Now, Abradates had gone, at the time of the Assyrians' defeat, on an embassy to the King of the **Bactrians** <note>An ancient Iranian people living in the region of modern-day Afghanistan and Uzbekistan.</note>, on behalf of the King of Assyria, to negotiate peace.

After Cyrus had commanded Araspes to guard **Panthea** for him until he should ask for her, Araspes asked him if he had not yet seen the woman he had been charged with. Cyrus said he had not. "But I certainly have," said Araspes, "both when I chose her for you and another time when we entered her tent. At first, we did not recognize her, for she was seated on the ground with her ladies all around her. Furthermore, her robe was just like that of a chambermaid. But to identify the mistress, we looked at them all, and having seen her, we knew well by her beauty how much she surpassed the others, even though she was seated, muffled in a veil, with her eyes cast toward the ground. 

When we made her stand up, her servants stood up with her; then we saw how she surpassed them not only in beauty, but in her fine bearing and a countenance of good grace and virtue—even though she was not dressed according to her status, and, on the other hand, tears were flowing down her clothes even to her feet. When the eldest among us said to her: 'Madam, take heart, for although your husband is a handsome man and the best in the world, we shall nevertheless give you to one who is in no way inferior to yours, whether in wisdom, beauty, and goodness, or in wealth and authority. It is Cyrus, King of the Persians, to whom you shall be given from this hour, who deserves'

Then her lovely face, her beautiful mouth, her white neck, and her delicate, white hands were revealed to our eyes. And know that, in my judgment and that of everyone, nature never made such a beautiful creature among men; for she is the most beautiful woman in **Asia**. To know this, you must see her. "I do not wish it," said **Cyrus**, "if she is as beautiful as you tell me." "And why?" asked **Araspes**. "Because," he replied, "if I look at her as you advise based on the report of her beauty, I fear (even now when I have no leisure) that I might be induced by the sight of her to see her even more, and that, having forgotten our affairs of importance, I would consume my time sitting beside her and gazing at her." Araspes, laughing, replied to him, "Do you believe it is possible that a woman's beauty could compel a man to do such things against his will? If you mean to say that this is the nature of man, I will clearly show you the contrary. For just as it is the nature of fire to burn one substance as well as another, so the beauty of women would compel all men equally to do wrong if it were its nature; and yet, among beautiful people, we love some and hate others. One man will love one woman, another will love another; seeing that love is a passion and a <term>voluntary accident</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to the subject; Araspes argues that love is a choice one makes, rather than an inescapable biological drive like hunger or the heat of a fire.</note>, and each person loves what they choose. Do you not often see that a brother will not feel good affection for his sister, whom a stranger might love dearly? Or that a father does not love his daughter, who nevertheless pleases someone else? ...great power: for fear and the laws have enough power to prevent love when one wishes to forbid it. This does not happen in natural things. For if one made a law to forbid those who do not eat from being hungry, and those who do not drink from being thirsty; or that during winter one should not be cold, and during summer not hot: there is no penalty nor reason, whatever it may be, that could make men obey such a law, insofar as nature pushes them directly to the contrary and subjects them to its passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to things the body "suffers" or experiences involuntarily, like hunger or temperature.</note>. But love proceeds from a **free will**, which is the reason why everyone loves the things they consider their own, such as their garments and their robes. 

"Why is it then," said **Cyrus**, "if love is voluntary, that one cannot leave it when one wants? For I have sometimes seen men weep from the passions of love, and serve their mistresses, even though they considered the servitude miserable, and gave away the largest part of their goods; and who nonetheless desired to be delivered from this love, as if from a grievous disease, and yet could not rid themselves of it, finding themselves bound and constrained no more nor less than if they had been attached with **thick chains of iron**. They are so enslaved that they long and foolishly obey their lovers; and even though they are oppressed by so many evils, they do not strive to escape, but rather take care that their lovers do not flee from them." 

"It is certain," replied **Araspes**, "that such lovers, living in the manner you describe, are miserable; and it is from this that they desire and persevere in dying in perpetual calamity. Moreover, although the means to escape this folly are diverse, the truth is that they cannot escape it in their lives; and falling from one vice into [another]..." <note original: "autre">The text ends here with the catchword "another," which would begin the first sentence of the following page.</note>

<summary>Araspes argues that love is a choice rather than a biological reflex like hunger, while Cyrus counters by describing the obsessive, "chained" state of those who cannot escape their romantic devotion.</summary>

others, give themselves over to larceny, and do not abstain from the goods of others. It appears then by this that love is voluntary: for when, to serve their amorous desire, they have stolen and robbed something, you are the first to accuse the thief; and not only do you not forgive him, but you have him punished according to the laws, signifying that this theft is a voluntary thing, and that one is not at all constrained to do it. Similarly, beautiful people do not constrain anyone to love them, nor to desire anything that is not honorable; but the vicious, given over to their foolish lusts, allow themselves to be carried away by their disordered passions <note>In the 16th century, "passions" referred to emotions or physical urges that "act upon" a person, potentially overriding their reason.</note>, and then afterwards accuse and blame Love. But if good and honorable men do not cease to desire good horses and love beautiful women, they nonetheless abstain from these things when they please, and do not make themselves subject to them more than is lawful. For this reason, having seen the grace of this woman <note>Araspes is referring to Panthea, the beautiful queen of Susa who was captured in battle.</note>, although she seemed beautiful to me, I nonetheless do not fail to stay near your person, to mount my horse, and to perform all acts required by my duty.

"It is possible," said ***Cyrus***, "that this is because you left her sooner than the time Love requires to enslave a person to itself. For even fire does not immediately burn everyone who touches it, and logs also do not catch flame at the first stroke. But for my part, it is my safest course not to touch fire of my own will, nor to look knowingly upon beautiful women. And I advise you also, ***Araspes***, not to let your eyes wander like vagabonds at the sight of beautiful things. For just as fire burns in the long run those who touch it, so also beautiful creatures light, little by little, an amorous flame in the heart of those who look upon them. Do not fear..."

# PROSOPOGRAPHY

"Not so for me," said Araspes, "for even if I never ceased looking at her, I am so certain of myself that I will never be forced to do anything other than what is honorable." "You speak very well," said Cyrus. "For this reason, guard this woman carefully for me, and treat her as I have commanded you: for I hope that she will be of great use to us one day." 

Having said this, they departed; but Araspes, full of youth and vigor, by frequently contemplating the excellent grace of Panthea, treated her humanely and strove to please her in many things. He especially noted that she was not ungrateful, but rather gave orders through her servants that Araspes, upon his return home, should find everything necessary. Finally, he was overcome by love for her, to such an extent that he was compelled to reveal his affection to her and request her dishonor <note>A 16th-century euphemism for requesting sexual favors or an illicit affair.</note>, which she refused him. 

At last, when Araspes, inflamed with desire, judged that he would fall into great servitude <note>In this context, "servitude" refers to being a slave to one's own passions or desires.</note> if he did not enjoy the thing he desired, and when he had threatened Panthea to take her by force if she did not yield to his intentions, the virtuous lady, fearing she would be forced, sent word through her eunuch to recount the entire matter to the king. 

The king, hearing these news, first mocked Araspes because he had boasted of mastering his affections; afterward, he sent Artabazus to tell him that he should be very careful not to force such a lady in any way. But if he could persuade her by words to his will, and she were willing of her own accord, the king would place no obstacle in the way. When Artabazus arrived, he began to rebuke him harshly, seeing that the woman was in his hands only as a trust <term>depositum</term> <note>original: "depost"; a legal and moral concept where an item or person is left in someone's care but remains the property of another.</note>; and he reproached him greatly for his wickedness. Consequently, Araspes, overcome by sharp grief, began to weep and shed tears in abundance.

Then Cyrus was moved even more by grief, and the beautiful woman <note>Panthea, often cited in Renaissance literature as a paragon of marital devotion.</note> became further distressed. She took back her husband's right hand <note>In Xenophon's original account, Abradates' hand had been severed in battle; when Cyrus took it, it came away from the body, leading to this poignant moment of grief.</note> from Cyrus's hands, and having kissed it several times, she put it back in its place, saying, "Alas, all the rest of him is just like this. Cyrus, moved by pity, said to her, "Do not grieve any longer, noble lady, for the death of your husband; for he died in honor, a victor over his adversaries, which is the greatest glory a man can desire. Furthermore, I promise you that my people will build him a very magnificent tomb, and you will not remain a widow or abandoned; for I will honor you in every way possible, as much for your great chastity as for your other virtues." And after he had made a great lamentation, he departed from there to return to the city.

Soon after, Panthea sent her eunuchs <note>eunuchs: high-ranking attendants in the Persian court.</note> away from her and commanded her nurse to stay, charging her to wrap her together with her husband in the same cloak as soon as she had passed away. And at that instant, with a sword she had already prepared, she cut her throat, and laying her head upon her husband’s chest, she died immediately. The nurse, at this pitiful spectacle, made a great lamentation and covered her as she had been commanded. Cyrus, who was not yet very far away, suspecting what this woman might do, ran back to her in a state of shock to see if he could provide any remedy. And at that same instant, the three eunuchs, seeing their mistress dead, killed themselves with their swords. **TARQUIN the Proud**, son of Tarquin the Elder <note>Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome.</note> and son-in-law of Servius Tullius, is the sixth and last king of the Romans; a cruel man, nicknamed *hyperēphanos* <note>original: "ὑπερήφανος" — meaning arrogant or proud.</note>, for his tyranny and contempt for laws and justice. He reigned twenty-five years. During the 61st Olympiad, he was driven from the kingdom by the Romans, who hated him, and also because of the assault and rape committed by Sextus Tarquin, his son, upon Lucretia, a chaste lady and wife of Tarquin Collatinus.

**Papirius**, a jurisconsult <term>jurisconsult: a legal expert or jurist whose opinions helped shape the law</term> living at this beginning of Roman liberty, reduced to public use all the laws, both sacred and profane, made by the Roman kings, and wrote a Code called since then, *The Papirian Civil Law*.

The year that Tarquin the Proud was driven from the kingdom, a dog and a serpent (if it is permissible to believe this omen) spoke.

After Tarquin, the Roman people used another kind of republic called a Timocracy <note>While usually referring to rule by property owners, the author defines it here as a "principality of the multitude" or a representative government.</note>, which is a rule of the multitude; and instead of a king, the Romans created Consuls for the government of the public state, of which the first were L. Junius Brutus and L. Tarquin Collatinus, in the 244th year from the founding of Rome <note>509 BCE.</note>.

...nevertheless held in such high esteem by the Athenians that he governed their republic peacefully alongside **Themistocles**, to whom he was totally opposed; for having both been raised together from youth, they always had a bone to pick <note>original: "maille à partir" — a French idiom referring to a small coin that is difficult to divide, used here to describe a persistent disagreement or rivalry.</note>. It was here that the difference in their natures was first revealed: Themistocles being lively, audacious, cunning, and sharp; Aristides, on the contrary, was steady, upright, and constant, neither a liar nor a deceiver. Through his leadership and valor, the Athenians defeated and routed the barbarians <note>The "barbarians" here refers to the Persian forces during the Greco-Persian Wars.</note>; out of envy, Themistocles plotted by every means to have him banished, which was achieved through **ostracism**.

This was a custom that cities governed by a popular state <term>a democracy or government by the people</term> used in ancient times to exile or banish for a certain period (which was commonly ten years) one of those who began to possess the influence and favor of the people, and who was preferred for his wealth, friends, favor, or support more than any other power. This was not intended as a punishment for any crime committed, but to moderate such authority, so that the individual might not achieve a tyranny and sole rule.

And this process took place in a full assembly in a space enclosed by barriers, where each citizen took a tile or slate and, writing upon it the name of the citizen they believed should be banished, brought it to the governors and magistrates. They would first count the total number of ballots in a pile. If the number did not reach six thousand, the ostracism was void. Then, setting aside the names of those written down, they would banish the person who received the most votes; however, the right to enjoy all his property was reserved for him. Now, as they were writing on the tiles in Athens following this custom, a certain dull-witted and coarse fellow...

In short, even though he had acquired the right to command so many people, he persisted until death in poverty, being always poorly dressed and walking through the city clothed in a shabby cloak. His uncle Callias was very wealthy; Aristides gave such a beautiful account of Callias's riches and his own poverty that there was not one among the listeners who did not prefer the indigence of Aristides over the goods of Callias. When asked, "What is justice?" <note>original Greek: τί ἐστὶ τὸ δίκαιον;</note>, he replied: "Not to covet that which belongs to others" <note>original Greek: τὸ μὴ ἐπιθυμεῖν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων</note>. He died so destitute that his entire estate could not have furnished the expenses for his funeral; and it is said that after his death, nothing was found in his house but an iron roasting spit. The Athenians married off his daughters using the city's funds, and made a gift to his son of one hundred silver minas <note>An ancient unit of currency; the text estimates this at 1,750 livres.</note>, and as much...
