<image-desc>Circular woodcut portrait of Sophocles, showing a bearded man in profile wearing a turban-like head covering. The inscription around the border of the circle reads: "SOPHOCLES ATHE. TRAG. ET POET." <note>Latin: "Sophocles, Athenian Tragedian and Poet."</note></image-desc>

**SOPHOCLES**, an Athenian captain and poet, was born in the 73rd Olympiad. <note>An Olympiad was a four-year period used by the Greeks to track time; the 73rd Olympiad began around 488 BCE.</note> He greatly adorned tragedy after Aeschylus; he wrote 33 tragedies, which Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian from the 2nd century AD.</note> cites by name, and of which we have only seven published, which are *Ajax*, *Electra*, *Oedipus the King* <note>original: "Oedipe tyran"</note>, *Antigone*, *Oedipus at Colonus*, *The Women of Trachis* <note>original: "les Trachinies"</note>, and *Philoctetes*. Cicero, in his book *On Divination*, calls him a "divine poet"; and in his book *On Old Age* <note>Latin: "De Senectute"</note> he speaks of him thus: Sophocles the poet wrote several tragedies in verse, in which were shown the wicked and foul deeds of kings and great lords. It seemed to his children, because he was so intent upon his studies, that he was negligent in managing his estate; and for this reason, one of them named Iophon (Cicero says, all of them) had him summoned to judgment, so that, just as it is customary according to the laws of Rome to forbid and take away the administration of assets from those who manage their affairs poorly, the judges of Greece might do the same to Sophocles, as one insane or careless in the governing of his own property. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of ancient drama, transitioning from the life of Sophocles to a formal distinction between the genres of tragedy and comedy. It builds upon the previous page's mention of tragedy as a "divine poem" by providing specific definitions and etymological origins.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>
## SECOND BOOK

The difference between comedy and tragedy consists in this: that the calamities of kings, princes, and courtiers are represented in tragedy, with a sad and lamentable end, murders, plunderings <note>original: "saccagemẽs," referring to the violent sacking or looting of cities.</note>, and other impieties. In tragedy, the gods and Heroes are also sometimes introduced; its nature, however, is to be sad, and the entire plot full of mourning. For this reason, Euripides <note>One of the three great Greek tragedians, known for his realism and interest in the inner lives of his characters.</note> replied to King Archelaus <note>Archelaus I, King of Macedon, who invited many artists and poets to his court.</note> (who was asking him to write a tragedy about him): "I pray to the gods that nothing proper or suitable for a tragedy should ever happen to you."

And in comedy, only private persons are brought forward, of low and common condition, with a beginning of affairs troubled by love or marriages, and an ending that is entirely joyful, full of gladness and contentment. Some have wished to say that tragedy was so named because, in ancient times, the first prize for this poem was a goat, called by the Greeks *tragos* <note>original: "τραγος"</note>, or perhaps a goatskin full of wine. Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> wrote: *He who competed in tragic song for a worthless goat.* <note>original: "Carmine qui tragico vilem certauit ob hircum" — a line from Horace's *Ars Poetica* describing the humble origins of the theater.</note>

See the other definitions of tragedy in our epistle <note>A formal letter or preface.</note> of the tragedy of *Polyxena* <note>Polyxena was the youngest daughter of King Priam of Troy; the author likely refers here to a specific edition or commentary they authored.</note>.

<sig>A 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: HER</meta>

<summary>This page defines the structural and thematic differences between tragedy and comedy, highlighting tragedy's focus on royal misfortune and comedy's focus on common life. It also explores the etymological roots of "tragedy" as being linked to the Greek word for "goat."</summary>

## HERODOTUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut medallion portrait of the historian Herodotus, shown in profile facing right. He has a beard and is wearing a draped garment. The Latin inscription "HERODOTVS HALICARNAS." <note>original: "Herodotus of Halicarnassus"</note> is set within the border of the medallion.</image-desc>

Herodotus of Halicarnassus, whom Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the influential Roman orator and statesman who famously dubbed Herodotus the "Father of History."</note> calls the father of history, wrote nine books of histories in Greek, each of them titled with the name of one of the Muses <note>The nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>. Quintilian <note>A celebrated Roman rhetorician and teacher of oratory.</note> gives this judgment of him:
> Many have written histories very elegantly: but there are two who have greatly surpassed the others. And although their virtue and excellence consist in different qualities, the praise is nonetheless equal for both. One is Thucydides <note>The historian of the Peloponnesian War, known for his analytical and clinical approach.</note> who is brief and concise: the other is Herodotus, elegant and copious. One is more forceful for moving hearts: the other more relaxed and gentle. One is more exceptional in his orations and harangues: and the other in his manner of speaking. One is more vivid: the other more pleasant.

Seeing that his country was held by the tyrant Lygdamis <note>The ruler of Halicarnassus in the mid-5th century BCE.</note>, he went to the island of Samos: and after the death of the tyrant, he returned there. He died in a city of Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia, the Greek-settled coastal areas of Southern Italy.</note>, which was a colony of the Athenians, called <term>Thurii</term> <note>original: "ϑούριοι"</note>.

<image-desc>A circular medallion portrait of Hippocrates in profile, showing him with a beard and wearing a hood or cap. Around the portrait, the Latin text reads: HIPPOCRATES OF COS, PHYSICIAN.</image-desc>

**HIPPOCRATES**, son of **Heraclides** and **Phaenarete**, was born on a small island called **Cos**, where **Lycurgus**, a captain of the Athenians, and **Bria**, a prince, had also been born...

<page-num>192</page-num>
->PROSOPOGRAPHIE<-

prince of the Lacedaemonians. He claimed to be descended from Hercules on his mother’s side, and from **Asclepius** <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing; the French text uses "Aesculape."</note> on his father’s side, the twentieth of the line of the one, and the nineteenth of the other. He was a student of **Gorgias of Leontini** <note>A famous Greek sophist and rhetorician.</note> and of **Democritus**, whom he cured, along with **Perdiccas**, King of Macedonia. All of Greece admired him because of his knowledge, so well-versed was he in medicine. Even **Artaxerxes** <note>King of the Persian Empire.</note> sent for him and held him in great honor, writing to **Hyscan**, governor and lieutenant in the **Hellespont**, as follows:

   The fame of **Hippocrates**, descended from the race of **Asclepius**, has reached me. Take care to give him as much gold as he wants, and all other things he may need, then send him to me: for I shall make him equal in honor to the greatest of Persia. And if there is any other illustrious man in Europe, make him a friend of our house, and do not spare any money.

He was of short stature, a little squint-eyed; he had a large head, spoke little, was hardworking in the study of letters, and possessed a great and subtle spirit. From the age of fourteen until thirty-five, he remained in the Academies of **Athens**, studying, reading, and philosophizing; upon leaving Athens, he traveled through various kingdoms and provinces for a period of twelve years, asking everyone and learning the properties and virtues of plants, as well as the practical experiences that had been observed with them. Afterward, he retired to **Ephesus** and the Temple of **Diana**, where he took a copy of the medical tables and clinical accounts <note>Likely referring to the "votive tablets" left by patients in temples of healing, which recorded their symptoms and cures.</note> that had long been recorded and hung there; he set in order what was confused and added many good things discovered and tested by himself. He was the first who wrote the art of medicine in an orderly manner.

### BOOK TWO.

Galen gives judgment of Hippocrates in this way: "that he was a good and noble man, a lover not of ambition or glory, but of truth" <note>original Greek: καλὸν καὶ ἀγαθὸν ἀνέρᾳ ἀυτὸν γεγονέναι, μὴ φιλοτιμίας ἢ φιλοδοξίας, ἀλλ' ἀληθείας ἐραστήν</note>. This is to say: That he was a man of integrity and a man of good, neither greedy nor a lover of honor or glory, but rather of truth. And of his writings: "that he wrote nothing badly" <note>original Greek: ὅτι κακῶς οὐδὲν ἔγραφεν</note>: that is to say, that he wrote nothing but what was good. He required his disciples to take an oath, by which they swore by **Apollo** the physician, **Asclepius**, **Hygieia**, and **Panacea** (goddesses whom the ancients believed presided over health), taking as witnesses all the gods and goddesses for the full observation of the oath, which they promised to keep inviolably: First, to honor the Teacher who taught them this science, to hold him as a father, and to help him in his times of need; to consider his children as brothers, and to teach them (if they wished to learn) the art of medicine without receiving any payment or being bound by any contract, along with those disciples who had taken this medical oath—but not to others. They swore to prescribe a suitable and beneficial diet for the sick; never to give anyone any venom or poison to drink, regardless of any urgent plea, request, or gift offered for it; even less to offer advice on how to do so; to preserve their life and their art in holiness; to give no suppository <note>In this context, an abortifacient pessary.</note> to a pregnant woman to cause an abortion; not to cut <note>The surgical procedure of lithotomy.</note> those suffering from the stone <note>Bladder stones.</note>, but rather to leave the incision to the traveling specialists <note>original French: "coureurs," referring to itinerant lithotomists who specialized in this dangerous surgery.</note> and practitioners of surgery; never to enter a house with the intent of doing injury or harm, but only for the benefit and health of the sick; to abstain there from any sexual act or work of lust; and not to reveal, but rather to keep secret, everything they might see or hear during the treatment of a patient, if the matter was worthy of confidence. ### CURTIUS.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the Roman hero Marcus Curtius (Curce) in full armor on a horse, leaping into a dark, smoke-filled chasm in the middle of a city square. In the background, classical buildings and arches are visible, with a group of onlookers standing to the left and right witnessing the sacrifice.</image-desc>

**CURTIUS**, a Roman knight fully armored and mounted on a fine horse, throws himself into an abyss that a sudden earthquake had opened in the middle of the city, in a large square. This pit could not be filled regardless of what was thrown into it, and from it issued a great stench. Thus **Curtius**, sealing the entrance to the chasm, makes a voluntary sacrifice of his body and soul to the devil <note>The author applies a 16th-century Christian perspective to this Roman legend, suggesting that Curtius’s pagan sacrifice was actually an offering to a demonic power.</note>, believing he did so for the gods, in the hope of delivering the people from such a calamity and for the benefit of his country. <note>This refers to the legend of the *Lacus Curtius* in the Roman Forum, dated traditionally to 362 BC.</note>

**Titus Manlius Torquatus** and **Valerius Corvinus**, military tribunes and brave Roman men. <note>Both were iconic heroes of the Republic; Torquatus was named for the neck-ring (*torque*) he took from a Gaul, and Corvinus for the raven (*corvus*) that helped him in combat.</note>

The three Roman **Decii**—father, son, and grandson—perform magnificent deeds of war. <note>The Decius Mus family was famous for the ritual of *devotio*, in which a commander sacrificed his own life to the gods of the underworld to ensure the destruction of the enemy army.</note>

In **Rome**, one hundred and seventy matron sorceresses, convicted of the potions and enchantments they practiced, are punished with death. <note>This event in 331 BC was one of the first recorded large-scale trials for poisoning in Rome, which the populace interpreted as witchcraft.</note>

**Jaddua**, High Priest of the **Jews**. <note>original: "Iade". Jaddua is the high priest mentioned in the Book of Nehemiah and by the historian Josephus; he is famously said to have met Alexander the Great.</note>

<image-desc>A circular engraved portrait of Callisthenes of Olynthus. He is depicted with a dense curly beard and hair, with an expression of intense emotion or speech. ALEXANDER the Great, made arrogant by his victories and the Persian war, wished to be worshipped; and to achieve his aims, he began to ponder how he might deify himself and seize the honors of heaven. He did not only wish to be called the son of Jupiter, but desired that people believe it firmly—as if he could master hearts just as easily as tongues. He wanted the Macedonians, when greeting him in honor according to the Persian fashion, to prostrate themselves to the ground <term>proskynesis</term> <note>The traditional Persian act of bowing or prostrating oneself before a person of higher social rank. To the Greeks and Macedonians, this was seen as a religious act reserved only for the gods, making Alexander's demand highly controversial.</note>. Agis of Argos <note>The text reads "Hages Largien," referring to Agis, a poet from Argos and a notorious flatterer of Alexander.</note> and Cleon of Sicily, flatterers by nature, being in King Alexander’s circle, opened the gates of heaven to him. They boastfully told him that he would surpass Hercules, Bacchus <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and theater.</note>, Castor, and Pollux, all of whom would yield their places to his new divinity. On this occasion, Alexander held a magnificent banquet, to which he summoned not only the Macedonians and those...

> Friends and well-known acquaintances will weep at my death:
> For all the people cried while I was alive.
> <note>original Latin: "Flebunt amici, & bene noti morte mea: / Nam populus omnis me viuo lachrimatus est."</note>

## MENANDER.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of the Greek dramatist Menander. He is depicted as an older man with a voluminous, curly beard and hair, wearing a classical robe. The inscription "MENANDER ATHEN." runs along the upper inner edge of the circular frame.</image-desc>

Comic poets were once biting, and criticized the vices, faults, and defects of men very harshly, as Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> testifies:

> Eupolis and Cratinus, and the poet Aristophanes,
> And others who belong to the Old Comedy,
> If there was anyone worthy of being singled out because he was evil, or a thief,
> Or an adulterer, or a murderer, or otherwise
> Infamous, they marked him out with great freedom.
> <note>original Latin: "Eupolis atque Cratinus, Aristophanésque poëta, / Atque alij, quorum comædia prisca virorum est, / Si quis erat dignus describi, quòd malus, aut fur, / Quòd mœchus foret, aut sicarius, aut alioqui / Famosus, multa cum libertate notabant." From Horace's Satires, 1.4.</note>

But Menander, the comic poet, began to soften the bitterness of comedy. It is defined as follows: Comedy is the understanding of private and civil fortune. Or otherwise: Comedy is the mirror of human life. This name comes from *kōmos* <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ κώμου"</note>, meaning feasting or revelry, because in the past, banquets, drinking bouts, and dissolu-

...the [emotions] of young men in love were recited in such stories. Those who have taken the side of Terence <note>A Roman playwright (c. 195–158 BCE) celebrated for his refined style and psychological depth.</note> have distributed the prize in the matter of comedy thus: they made Caecilius <note>Caecilius Statius, a Roman comic poet who preceded Terence.</note> the leader in invention, Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus, famous for his boisterous and energetic Roman comedies.</note> the leader in speech, and Terence in the treatment of manners. But Menander carries the victory over the other three in this: they all imitated him and Diphilus, and stole many good things from them, by their own admission.

*Thus Menander expressed every image of life (says Quintilian) <note>A celebrated Roman rhetorician of the 1st century CE.</note>; so great in him was the abundance of invention and the faculty of expression; thus he was suited to all subjects, characters, and emotions.* <note>original Latin: "Ita omnem vitæ imaginem expreßit Menander... tanta in eo inueniendi copia, eloquendi facultas, ita eft omnibus rebus, personis, affectibus accommodatus."</note>

He wrote a letter to King Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>The King of Ptolemaic Egypt (309–246 BCE) known for his patronage of the Library of Alexandria.</note> and one hundred and eight comedies, in one of which he defends the adoration of statues <note>The original French "defend l'adoration" could imply either a defense of the practice or a prohibition; given the context of the monotheistic poem that follows, the author likely interprets Menander as a "virtuous pagan" leaning toward monotheism.</note>. and although he was among the pagans in the time of ignorance of the true truth—the light of life and the sun of justice having not yet appeared on this earth—see a little of the opinion he held touching the essence and nature of God, and of the honor one owes Him, just as Maumont <note>Jean de Maumont, a 16th-century French cleric and translator.</note> has translated it:

> Therefore you must honor, and believe me,
> A single God, sole father and sole king:
> And give him glory without end.
> He alone led us into the world,
> He alone invented, made, and ordained
> The outcome of all good things.

While swimming in a small river, he drowned by great misfortune. Ovid <note>The famous Roman poet of the Augustan age.</note> says:

*As the comic poet perished while he swam in the clear waters.* <note>original Latin: "Comicus vt liquidis perijt dum natabat in undis." From Ovid's Ibis.</note>

Diphilus <note>A poet of the Athenian New Comedy and a contemporary of Menander.</note>, the comic poet, wrote 100 stories. Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian of the late 2nd century.</note> in the 5th book of the *Stromata* <note>The "Miscellanies," a work by Clement of Alexandria.</note> recites his verses concerning the judgment to come. He died in Smyrna, a city of Ionia.

Hannibal makes a new path through the rocks using fire and vinegar. <note>A legendary engineering feat where Hannibal supposedly cracked Alpine boulders by heating them with fire and pouring vinegar into the cracks to make them brittle.</note>

**Wonders** in Rome. A child of six months cries out loud, "Triumph!": in the district of Ancona it rained stones.

Upon which news, two mothers in Rome die of unexpected joy at having recovered their sons, whom they thought had died there: but he is well repulsed by **Fabius Maximus** <note>Known as "The Delayer" for his strategy of exhaustion rather than direct battle.</note>. Being trapped, Hannibal attaches bundles of vine branches to the horns of oxen, and having set them on fire, makes the Roman guards take flight; thus he escapes the pass. By this means he burns everything in the surroundings, except for the lands of Fabius, to make him appear suspect of treason. Afterward he regains his strength, and battle is given against him at **Cannae**, where forty thousand Romans are slain, along with the consul Paulus <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus</note>, 80 consular Senators, and thirty of those of praetorian or aedilician rank <note>These were former high-ranking magistrates of the Roman Republic.</note>. He sends to Carthage three pecks <term>muys; an ancient French measure of capacity, here used to translate the Latin 'modii'</term> full of gold rings, which had been pulled from the fingers of the Romans killed in the battle. He is afterward defeated by **Scipio Africanus the Elder** in the Libyan war.

Hannibal pitches his camp three miles near Rome, where a storm arises which breaks off the combat. Scipio Nasica <note>The author likely conflates Publius Cornelius Scipio, later "Africanus," with his cousin Nasica.</note> (who will be called Africanus the Great once he has subjugated Africa), son of one of those who had been killed in Spain, presents himself to go to Spain and takes New Carthage <note>Modern-day Cartagena, Spain.</note> by force in one day, being then 24 years old; and fighting near Baecula, he defeats Hasdrubal.

Marcellus <note>Marcus Claudius Marcellus, a famed Roman general</note> is killed by a lance thrust, having been surprised with Titus Quinctius Crispinus by an ambush that Hannibal had set for them; Crispinus escapes by swiftness.

The censors hold a general muster in Rome: in the census, they count one hundred thirty-seven thousand, one hundred and eight citizen men, to know how many men had been lost in so many routs and defeats.

Hasdrubal, having crossed the Alps with a new army to join Hannibal, is entirely defeated, himself and fifty-six thousand of his men, by Marcus Livius and Claudius Nero, the consuls <note>This refers to the Battle of the Metaurus in 207 BC, which prevented Hannibal from receiving reinforcements.</note>.

Scipio is repelled from the siege of Utica by the arrival of Hasdrubal, Syphax, and one hundred thousand fighting men with them.

Scipio, with the help of Masinissa, is victorious over the Carthaginians in several battles. He takes two forts by force, in which forty thousand of the enemy’s men are burned or killed <note>This refers to the "Battle of the Great Plains" and the earlier surprise attack where Scipio set fire to the Carthaginian and Numidian camps</note>. And Syphax is made prisoner by means of Laelius <note>Gaius Laelius, Scipio’s close friend and general</note> and Masinissa. Masinissa, overcome with love for Sophonisbe—the wife of Syphax and daughter of Hasdrubal <note>Hasdrubal Gisco</note>, now his prisoner—marries her under the promise he makes to her that she will not fall into the power of the Romans.

The wedding having been performed, Scipio strongly rebukes Masinissa, telling him that he intends to have her so that she may be brought to Rome with Syphax, her first husband, to receive such sentence as the Senate and the people might please; this was because she had led away a king who was previously their friend <note>Syphax had originally been an ally of Rome before Sophonisbe persuaded him to side with Carthage</note> and incited him to come against them with the force of arms. Therefore, Masinissa sends poison to Sophonisbe to fulfill his promise to her. Taking it, she chose death rather than the preservation of her life, so as not to become a captive or remain in the servitude of the Romans.

The kingdom is restored to Masinissa after Hannibal is defeated in battle by Scipio in Africa <note>The Battle of Zama, 202 BCE</note>, where the desperate Carthaginians had recalled him from Italy, and the peace they requested is granted to them under such conditions as the Romans desired.

Scipio, upon his return to Rome, celebrates a triumph. He is the first to be surnamed after the nation he subjugated: namely, Africanus, from Africa.

Ptolemy Epiphanes reigns in Egypt under the guardianship of the Romans for 24 years.

Mattathias, a priest and governor of the Jews, kills a Jew who was publicly sacrificing to idols; he bravely resists the commissioners of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who attempted to suppress Jewish customs</note> and upholds the law in all things.

## SECT OF THE PHARISEES.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration depicting a man in long, layered robes and a tall, conical headpiece, representing a Pharisee, standing amidst crumbling stone architecture and ruins. An inscription following the upper curve of the oval frame reads "SECT OF THE PHARISEES" <note>original Latin: "PHARISEORUM SECTA"</note>.</image-desc>

While the priesthood and leadership of the Jews began to decline due to the tyranny and war of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, whose attempts to Hellenize Judea sparked the Maccabean Revolt.</note>, several dissensions arose; three sects and heresies took root in the Jewish religion. The first was that of the Pharisees <note>Greek: *diairetàs*, meaning "the dividers" or "separatists"</note>, a term which comes from the Hebrew *Pharas*, which is to say "to divide": for the most noble and learned, separating themselves from the company of the common people and the masses, were called Pharisees. *For this word is said (says Saint Augustine) to be interpreted as a segregation, just as in the Latin language, "egregious" means as if separated from the flock.* <note>original Latin: "Nam dicitur hoc verbum... quasi à grege separatus." Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) frequently used etymology to explain theological divisions; here he links the word "egregious" (from *e*—out of, and *grege*—flock) to the Pharisaic separation.</note> These people, misinterpreting the commandment of the law to bind the commandments of God to their hands and to never remove them from before their eyes <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 6:8, the basis for the use of tefillin.</note>, wore upon their foreheads, like a crown, scrolls and labels where the said commandments were written. The frin-

Attalus, King of Pergamum, who by the help and favor of the Romans had obtained a kingdom in Asia, dying in his bed, makes the Roman people heir to his treasure and his kingdom. His testament is carried to Rome by the people of Pergamum.

The laws regarding the management of the fields <note>The Agrarian Laws, intended to redistribute public land to the poor</note> by the Gracchi, one of whom—namely Tiberius, tribune of the people—supporting the cause of the poor and the common folk, was hated by the wealthy because of this land law. By this law, it was decreed that the citizens of Rome could no longer possess more than five hundred acres <term>the original French uses "journaux," a measurement of land a man could plow in one day</term> of land; for the Romans used to partly sell, partly reserve for the public, and lease to the poor inhabitants the conquered lands for a small fee. However, the rich, by setting the fees very high, bought up far too much of it and left none for the poor. Because of this, Tiberius Gracchus, while supporting the poor, was massacred with thirty others in a riot plotted by the wealthy, and their bodies were thrown into the river. Flaccus was also killed, and Scipio <note>Scipio Aemilianus, who opposed the reforms; his sudden death led to rumors of murder</note> was found dead because of this law, which remained unexecuted through his influence.

<margin>Year 3857.</margin> Aristobulus, son of Hyrcanus, cruelly puts his brothers in prison and causes his mother to die of starvation. He is the first who, since the Babylonian captivity, placed a crown upon his head, reducing the government to royal power. He dies miserably and suddenly in the same place where he had caused his brother Antigonus to be killed.

PTOLEMY Alexander, having driven out his brother Lathyrus, reigns in Egypt for 17 years. Later, he is himself driven out by his own people for the death of Cleopatra, his mother—an otherwise wicked woman.

Micipsa <note>While the text names Micipsa, the actions described—bribing Rome, the war with Metellus and Marius, and the betrayal by Bocchus—attribute the biography of Jugurtha, Micipsa's nephew and successor, to him</note> King of the Numidians, corrupts and wins over the city of Rome three times through money, throwing it into turmoil: thus he buys peace. And he lent them because he never wanted to trade or sell them. A very small house of his was sold for one hundred thousand crowns because of its ponds.

# ROSCIUS GALLUS.

<image-desc>A circular medallion portrait of a man in profile, facing right. He wears a headband or laurel. The inscription around the inner border reads: ROSCIVS GALLVS COMOEDVS.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'T' <note>The original French used 'L' for 'Le'</note> featuring an illustration of a seated figure, likely a scholar or author, engaged in reading or writing.</image-desc>

THE Theater, which was constructed in the shape of a semi-circle, was so named from the Greek <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ θεάσθαι (*apo tou theasthai*)</note>, which means "I see": this is why it can be called a "spectacle," a word derived from the Latin. On the front and at the forepart of the Theater, between the two horns <note>The "horns" (*cornua*) refer to the curved ends of the semicircular seating area</note>, was the Stage <note>original: *la Scene*</note>, so called from the Greek <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς σκηνῆς (*apo tēs skēnēs*)</note>, meaning "tent" or "tabernacle," because it provided shade. The Stage was either revolving or sliding <note>referring to ancient stage machinery: *scena versatilis* or *scena ductilis*</note>, and there were three types: tragic, comic, and satyric, as you may see at length in the works of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BCE), a Roman architect and engineer whose work *De architectura* is the primary source for ancient building techniques</note>, to whom I refer you. You might also consult him if you wish to know what the <term>Orchestra</term> <note>the circular space for the chorus</note> and <term>Proscenium</term> <note>the area in front of the stage building</note> were; and likewise look in the works of Alessandro Alessandri <note>a 15th-century Italian jurist who wrote about Roman antiquities in *Geniales dies*</note> to understand the places called the <term>Bouleuterion</term> <note>a council house</note>, <term>Ephebeum</term> <note>a place for youth training</note>, <term>Podium</term>, and <term>Choragium</term> <note>a room for preparing the chorus</note>, along with the various games: <term>Circensian</term>, <term>Apollinarian</term>, <term>Popular</term>, <term>Natalician</term> <note>birthday games</note>, <term>Nuptial</term>, <term>Quinquennial</term> <note>held every five years</note>, <term>Decennial</term> <note>held every ten years</note>, <term>Gladiatorial</term>, <term>Actian</term>, <term>Scenic</term>, and <term>Augural</term>. Once such games, dances <note>original: *saltations*</note>, and spectacles were introduced, players were brought from Etruria <note>modern-day Tuscany</note>, who, leaping and dancing without any verse, style, or poetic meter, performed to the sound of flutes, making gestures with their bodies that were pleasant and entertaining to see. ### PROSOPOGRAPHY

...the new amusement was found so agreeable by the people that the youth, after joking amongst one another with taunts, witty banter <note>original: *mots de gueule*, literally "mouth-words," referring to sharp-tongued or ribald humor</note>, and verses without art or reason, began to imitate what they had seen performed by the Etruscan **Histriones** <note>actors</note>, named from the Tuscan word *Hister*, which is to say, "player." These ridiculous terms, uttered thus without rhythm or music, were called **Exordia** <note>original: *Exordes*; introductory or preliminary remarks</note>, just as what they sang were called **Epodes**.

Later, Livius Andronicus <note>c. 284–204 BCE, an enslaved Greek who became the first Roman dramatist</note>, following this first invention, provided a play written in measured verse to be recited. This occurred (according to Polydore Vergil <note>c. 1470–1555, a Renaissance historian</note>) in the year 513 from the founding of Rome <note>roughly 240 BCE</note>. Thus, little by little and successively, such pastimes were reduced to an art. Later, comic and tragic actors and players recited their verses there, among whom **Roscius**—the teacher of Marcus Tullius Cicero—was the first to mount the stage <note>original: *efchafaut*, literally "scaffold"</note> for this purpose, and who, using gesture and pronunciation, played his character very well upon the Scene.

He, despite having crossed eyes and a very ugly countenance, practiced this art so well and with such great passion for the sake of profit that he never performed anything before the people without having first rehearsed it in his house. He achieved such great authority that Cicero writes it was an act of great temerity and impudence for any who dared to perform in the presence of Roscius, because there was no man, however expert he might be in this craft, in whom Roscius would not find something to criticize or some fault, whether in gesture or pronunciation.

Macrobius <note>a Roman writer of the early 5th century CE</note> in the *Saturnalia* writes that Cicero was accustomed to debating with Roscius to see which of the two could do better: whether Cicero could express a single fact or sentence through eloquence and varied language, or whether Roscius could represent the same thing through a variety of gestures and countenances. Nevertheless, returning afterwards to his studies <note>original: *lettres*; referring to liberal arts and rhetorical training</note>, far from it appearing that he had forgotten or lost anything, he seemed instead to have gained much from his idleness and pleasure; for he returned all the more vividly to study and comprehension. He possessed a memory that was good and blessed by nature, which he greatly improved by art: so much so that he never wished to reread things he had read even once to remember them, because he had learned, retained, and imprinted them in his brain for his entire life simply by writing or reading them; and he said that he never failed to recall a single word for lack of memory. Having knowledge of all histories, he would have someone name some great personage, captain, or army leader—whomever one wished—and he would promptly recount at length the life, the fine deeds, and the exploits of the one named to him. One finds in the chronicles that Porcius Latro, being afflicted by a double quartan fever <note>a recurring fever, often associated with malaria, where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day</note>, killed himself by his own hand, and thus passed away.

Now, the **dictatorship** was an extraordinary office and magistracy that the Romans were accustomed to give to one they recognized as grave, authoritative, and of good mind—but only when the **Republic** saw itself in imminent danger due to the private dissensions of the citizens or because of foreign wars; at any other time, it was not used. And as soon as he was created by the voice of the people for six months (for at the end of this time his authority was abolished), he governed all the affairs of the Republic, and like a king, he had all power over both the greatest men of the city and over the common people; for this reason, he was called **Master of the People**, having the power to name and elect all other magistrates.

Now **Julius Caesar**, being consul with **Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus**, was given the charge of conquering **Gaul** and **Illyria** with ten legions: in which he bore himself so valiantly and skillfully that in nine years he brought under the power of Rome and conquered all of **Gaul** which lies between the **Pyrenees** mountains, the **Alps**, the **Rhine**, and the **Ocean sea**. # PROSOPOGRAPHY <note>From the Greek *prosopon* (person) and *graphein* (to write); a study or collection of biographies.</note>

...[daughter of] **Calpurnius Piso**, <note>Referring to Calpurnia, Caesar's last wife</note> who brought all of Caesar’s money to **Mark Antony** after he was killed. The books and commentaries he wrote show clearly how excellent he was in eloquence. He is a true mirror for all princes, to inspire in them the desire to learn literature, through the study of which they can better lead their armies; and by the example of past acts, recorded in histories—the ruses of war and the mistakes made in various military campaigns—they may beware of surprises and avoid the misfortunes for which knowledge and history have given them understanding, in place of the experience they have not yet acquired. And these two qualities <note>the ability to act and the ability to write</note> were present in our Caesar, as this distich <note>A pair of poetic lines</note> expresses:

> To have recorded deeds is a great work; to have performed deeds worth recording

# PROSOPOGRAPHY
<note>A "prosopography" is a description of a person’s social and professional life, character, and career.</note>

He is a true mirror for all princes, to give them the desire to learn literature <note>literally "good letters," referring to the classical education and humanities essential for a Renaissance ruler</note>, through the study of which they can better lead their armies; and through the example of past actions recorded in histories, ruses of war, and mistakes committed in various military engagements <note>original: "factions"</note>, they may guard against surprises and avoid the misfortunes of which science and history have given them knowledge in place of the experience they have not yet acquired. > To have recorded great deeds is a massive task:
> To have performed deeds worth recording is a greater task:

BOOK TWO.

# TIMAGENES.

---

-><image-desc>Circular woodcut medallion portrait depicting Timagenes as a bearded man in profile wearing classical robes. The Latin inscription within the circular border reads: "TIMAGENES THE GRAMMARIAN." <note>original: "THIMAGENES GRAMMAT."</note></image-desc><-

---

**Timagenes**, an Alexandrian grammarian and orator, was taken prisoner in Asia by **Gabinius** <note>Aulus Gabinius was a Roman general and statesman who restored Ptolemy XII Auletes to the Egyptian throne.</note> and brought to Rome. **Faustus**, the son of **Sulla**, ransomed him. Having been freed and manumitted <note>To be manumitted was the formal process of a slave being granted their legal freedom by their master.</note>, he first kept an open school in the house of **Pompey**; and after his death, he taught at the palace. He sold one of his books, which dealt with rhetoric, for two **Attic talents**, which were worth, according to the calculations of **Budé** <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540) was a preeminent French humanist scholar who wrote extensively on ancient weights, measures, and coinage.</note>, as much as twelve hundred **crown ecus**, each ecu being worth thirty-five **sols tournois** <note>These are early modern French currency units used by the author to help his 16th-century readers understand the immense value of the sale.</note>. **Pliny the Younger** boasted of having been able to sell (while he was serving in Spain) his commentaries to **Largius Licinius** for forty thousand **sesterces** <note>original: "H-S," a standard Roman abbreviation for sestertii.</note>. "But who is the king," says the learned **Budé**, "who would wish to spend at this time on a beautiful library, well-completed and filled with good books, the sum of ten thousand ecus—as much as a private citizen offered to **Pliny** for some notes and registers made on the fly?" as if he wished to say: People hardly care for literature anymore. And indeed, the study of knowledge is cooling significantly. Oh, how much more reason **Budé** would have to complain of it today!

<summary>This page recounts the life of Timagenes of Alexandria, who rose from a prisoner of war to a prestigious teacher in Rome, using his story to lament the declining financial and social value of scholarship compared to antiquity.</summary>

## MANILIUS.
---

-><image-desc>A circular engraved medallion showing a profile portrait of a bearded man with curly hair, facing right. The border of the medallion contains the inscription "C. MANILIUS, ASTROLOGER AND POET." <note>original: "C. MANLIVS ASTROL. E POET."</note></image-desc><-

**Gaius Marcus Manilius**, born of a noble family from **Antioch**, wrote poetry in Rome during the time when **Augustus** happily governed the Roman Empire, to whom he dedicated five books on astrology <note>In the 16th century, "astrologie" referred to the study of the stars, encompassing both what we now call astronomy and astrology.</note> written in hexameter verse. In these, he mostly imitated **Hipparchus**, **Eudoxus**, **Aratus**, **Dorotheus**, and **Sidonius** <note>These were famous Greek astronomers and poets whose works served as foundations for celestial knowledge.</note>, apologizing that because of the difficulty of the work, he seems to instruct rather than to delight; for:

> *The subject itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught.* <note>original: "Ornari res ipsa negat, contenta doceri." This quote from Manilius’s poem "Astronomica" (3.39) explains that technical or scientific subjects do not lend themselves to flowery poetic language.</note>

Many believe that **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of the "Natural History."</note> refers to this Manilius where he speaks of the obelisk: for Manilius, with great ingenuity, placed a gilded ball at the summit of the obelisk <note>This refers to the Obelisk of Montecitorio, which Augustus brought from Heliopolis to Rome to serve as a giant sun-dial (gnomon) for the "Solarium Augusti."</note>, by the shadow of which the moments of the hours were observed. For this invention, he was held in high esteem.

**BOOK SECOND.**

### OCTAVIAN CAESAR AUGUSTUS, son of Octavius.
<margin>3,921</margin> <note>This year likely follows the *Anno Mundi* calendar, dating from the creation of the world, commonly used in 16th-century historical texts.</note>

**Octavius**, a senator and son of **Atia**, the nephew of **Julius Caesar** on his sister's side and his adopted son, reigned with **Marc Antony** and **Lepidus** for twelve years, and alone for forty-four: in total fifty-six years. Having held the power of a tribune for thirty-seven years, he set aside the title of Triumvir <term>Triumvir: One of three men holding joint power; here referring to the Second Triumvirate of Rome.</term>, and calling himself only consul, after having won over the soldiers with gifts and the people by providing them with food, he transferred to his own person the duties and responsibilities of both the Senate and the laws and magistrates, as there was no one at that time to offer any resistance. He established himself as his uncle's heir, and to better elevate his dominion, he raised **Claudius Marcellus**, his sister's son, to the Curule Aedileship <term>Curule Aedileship: A high-ranking Roman magistracy responsible for public buildings, festivals, and the grain supply.</term>. He put an end to five civil wars: first against **Marc Antony** near **Modena**, and another time near the promontory of **Actium**; then against **Cassius** and **Brutus**, the murderers of his uncle, at the fields of **Philippi**; then at **Perugia** against the two brothers of Antony; the second-to-last at sea in **Sicily** against the son of **Pompey**; and finally, he subdued **Dalmatia**, **Aquitaine**, **Slavonia**, **Hungary**, **Raetia** and **Vindelicis**, the **Salassi** <note>An ancient Alpine tribe located in what is now the Aosta Valley.</note>, **Armenia**, and the kingdom of **Galatia**, which he turned into a Roman province. He pacified the Empire, restoring it to a state of great tranquility and flourishing peace that then reigned throughout the entire world; and never were the Roman people so happy and powerful as under his Empire. He was not at all given to debauchery, although it is said that in his youth he had committed some acts of adultery, not for his pleasure, but for certain reasons <note>Historical sources often suggest these "reasons" were political, used to gather information or forge alliances.</note>. He was moderate in his diet, clothing, and furnishings; kind, temperate, honorable, civil, and patient. It is true that he had been a great gambler and much addicted to the infamous game of dice; because of which, during the Sicilian war, there was written and published about him this

# PROSOPOGRAPHY

### epigram:

> *After being twice defeated at sea and losing his ships,* <note>original: *Postquam bis classe victus naues perdidit*</note>
> *So that he might finally win, he plays dice constantly.* <note>original: *Aliquando ut vincat, ludit assiduè alea.* This satirical verse mocks Augustus, suggesting that because he was a poor naval commander, he turned to gambling with dice to find a victory.</note>

He had four wives: the first, **Servilia**, daughter of **Publius Servilius**, who was twice consul; the second, **Claudia**, daughter of **Publius Clodius**; **Scribonia**, with whom he had his daughter **Julia**; and **Livia Drusilla**. He established laws to punish those who did not marry, in order to increase the public treasury by this means; he was also the first to oversee legal proceedings regarding defamatory libels <term>libelles diffamatoires: Written materials intended to damage someone's reputation, which Augustus began to regulate as criminal offenses.</term>. While deliberating whether he should establish the use of **codicils** <term>codicilles: A legal document used to make additions or changes to a will without rewriting the entire document.</term>, which was previously not customary, he took the advice of **C. Trebatius Testa**, a legal consultant. Trebatius advised him to accept this practice as it did not conflict with the law and was very useful to citizens during long journeys; in cases where someone could not make a formal testament or wished to add to one they had already made, the codicil would be considered valid. He held learned men in high esteem, honoring and supporting them. He gave **Hortalus**, the son of the orator **Hortensius**, 25,000 crowns <note>original: *escuz*. The author uses the French "écu" to represent a significant sum of Roman currency.</note> to enable him to marry. He died of dysentery at **Nola**.

**Antonius Musa**, a Greek by nationality, came to Rome, which had not had a physician or surgeon for 403 years and 10 months. While there, he cured **Augustus** of sciatica in his knee; because of this, the Romans erected a porphyry statue in his honor. Afterward, when Musa wished to perform surgery—cutting feet and hands, removing rotted flesh, and sometimes applying fire through cauteries—the Romans, who had not yet seen such cruelty practiced, stoned him and dragged his body throughout the city. <note>This anecdote reflects the Roman public's historical suspicion of Greek medical practices, which often seemed violent or invasive compared to traditional Roman remedies.</note>

**A. Ofilius**, a legal consultant, wrote several books on civil law. He was the first to leave behind writings regarding the law of the twentieth <note>original: *legib. vicef.* (Lex Vicesima), referring to a 5% tax on inheritances.</note> and on jurisdiction, and was the first to compose a Praetorian Edict <term>edict. prat.: The *Edictum Praetoris*, a set of legal formulas and rules issued by a magistrate to govern their year in office.</term>.

Falcidius, a tribune of the people, establishes a law by which a father is permitted to dispose of his property at his pleasure and leave it to strangers, provided that he sets aside a fourth part which he is bound to leave to his heirs by natural right. This law is named after him, the <term>Falcidian Law</term> <note>Lex Falcidia (40 BC): A Roman law ensuring that legal heirs received at least 25% of an estate, preventing a testator from giving everything away to others.</note>, just as during this same period the Pompeian and Papian laws take their names from their authors.

This refers to the Nazarite vow mentioned in the Bible (Numbers 6), where the hair was left uncut as a sign of devotion; it was a common medieval tradition to depict Jesus this way.</note> He has a face without any wrinkle or blemish, which a moderate redness gracefully embellishes. In his nose and his mouth there is nothing at all to criticize. His eyes are clear and like green, or of a color where azure and water are mixed; and he has a thick beard, not long, of the same color as the hair, but forked in the middle. He has arms and hands most delightful to see; he is terrible when rebuking, sweet and amiable when admonishing, joyful in all gravity; he was never seen to laugh, but indeed to groan and weep, and he is also slow to speak, composed and modest: in short, perfect in beauty above all the sons of men.

The "manly robe" assumed by Roman youths around age 14-16 to signify their transition to adulthood and citizenship.</note>, held all the magistracies and honors one after another: he was Quaestor, Praetor, Consul, and Tribune, then commander of the army in Cantabria <note>A region in Northern Spain.</note>. He governed Gaul for one year. He later led five great wars, from which he brought back victory. He was adopted by Caesar <note>Referring to the Emperor Augustus.</note> after the deaths of Gaius and Lucius. # BOOK THREE

...by the means and persuasion of his mother Drusilla, <note>Historical records usually refer to her as Livia Drusilla, the wife of Augustus and mother of Tiberius.</note> he was taken as a colleague of the empire and a companion of the tribunate. And Augustus being dead, his son, who had been sent into exile on the island of Planasia, is killed; <note>This refers to Agrippa Postumus, the grandson and adopted son of Augustus, who was seen as a rival to Tiberius.</note> thus Tiberius takes the empire at the supplications and urgent prayers of the people. For he feigned a desire not to accept it and refused it, telling them that one did not know what a "great beast" an empire was.

At the beginning, he shows himself very liberal, modest, and humane, even to the point of making great bows to the senate; though he was of a wicked nature, a deceiver, and accustomed to thinking one thing and saying another. In the end, he becomes lecherous and given to all manner of vices and wickednesses: he has himself served at the table by naked girls, and besides this, he loves wine too much. On account of this, he is called by the mockery *Caldius Biberius Mero*, instead of his name *Claudius Tiberius Nero*. <note>original: "Caldius Biberius Mero." This is a Latin pun: *calidus* (hot), *bibere* (to drink), and *merum* (undiluted wine), essentially calling him a "hot drinker of pure wine."</note> Through his laziness, he allows the loss of Armenia, which the Parthians win, and Moesia to the Dacians; and the Germans conquer the Gauls from him. Furthermore, he never paid his soldiers and built nothing; and by having the wealthiest citizens killed, he stole their goods. He is poisoned by his nephew Caligula at the age of 78, after having held the empire for 23 years.

**Judas Iscariot**, one of the disciples of Jesus Christ, betrays his master and delivers him into the hands of the Jews for thirty pieces of silver; then, moved by repentance and despair, he hangs himself.

**Caiaphas** and **Annas**, High Priests of the Jews, greedy men. Caiaphas prophesies, saying in the middle of the assembly that it was necessary for one man to die for all the people. He will be removed from his office by Vitellius, the governor of Syria.

**Herod Antipas**, tetrarch of Galilee, brother of Ar... <note>The text cuts off, likely referring to Archelaus.</note>

<margin>Year after the birth of Jesus Christ, 31.</margin>
...Herod <note>Likely Herod Antipas, the Tetrarch of Galilee.</note> had Saint John the Baptist beheaded because he reproached him for keeping the wife of his brother Philip while he was still living, and for having had children by her. This is also the same Herod before whom Jesus Christ was brought, and whom he clothed in a white robe as a sign of mockery. In the end, he will be banished to Lyon and will lose his Tetrarchy. <note>Herod Antipas was indeed exiled to Gaul (Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges or Lyon) in 39 AD.</note>

<margin>33</margin>
In the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, Jesus Christ, for our salvation, is placed on the cross in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate "of Lyon," <note>There is a long-standing local tradition in France that Pontius Pilate was born in or exiled to the city of Lyon.</note> the governor of Judea for the Emperor; Pilate will later kill himself during the time of Caligula.

Jesus Christ rises again in glory three days after his death.

Dionysius the Areopagite, <note>A judge of the Areopagus in Athens who was converted by St. Paul; later tradition often conflated him with the author of mystical Christian texts.</note> a philosopher studying in Athens, seeing the darkness over the earth in broad daylight, the earth trembling, and the stones splitting, said: "Either this entire universal machine will perish at this hour, or else the Creator of it suffers."

The Augustal Games <note>Games held in honor of Augustus Caesar.</note> are celebrated in Rome.

The Tiber overflows because of continual rains.

The office of proconsul, having been abolished in the provinces of Macedonia and Achaia, is transferred to the Emperor because of the excessively heavy charges and taxes.

Ordinances are issued against the players or jesters in the theaters, as well as against the spectators.

Vonones, King of the Parthians.

Libo Drusus, <note>Marcus Scribonius Libo Drusus, a Roman senator accused of conspiracy and practicing magic.</note> the great-grand-nephew of Pompey and cousin of the Caesars, consults diviners on how he might attain the Empire, and if he might possess enough wealth to cover the Appian Way as far as Brindisi; he is accused before Tiberius. In the end, he kills himself, and his goods are divided among his accusers.

Pomponius Flaccus <note>A Roman general and close friend of Tiberius.</note> ordains days for holding processions.

> **Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.**
And immediately leaving their nets, they followed him. Jesus Christ afterwards gave to Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is to say (as he himself interprets it) sovereign power in the church to bind and loose on earth, according to what is said in the 16th chapter of Saint Matthew <note>Matthew 16:19. In Christian tradition, "binding and loosing" refers to the authority to make binding halakhic decisions or to forgive sins.</note>. While the Gospels mention both Annas and Caiaphas, Peter's denials are a central part of the Passion narrative.</note>: then, by the crowing of the cock, he remembered the word of his master, and going outside with great repentance, he wept bitterly. He raised a girl from the dead and healed a poor lame man. After the resurrection of our Savior, he converted 3,000 men to the faith of Jesus Christ through a single sermon. He proclaimed the Gospel in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and Bithynia, as he declares in his epistles. Afterward, he was Bishop of Rome. Finally, under the Empire of Nero, he was hung on a cross, head downwards and feet upwards, because he wished to die in this way, judging himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Creator. See Irenaeus and Tertullian, Eusebius, Dorotheus, Saint Jerome, Nicephorus: and for the rest, the book of Acts.

->[Ja]mes was very intimate with and beloved by Jesus Christ, and was often called by him to witness the great mysteries, alongside Peter and John, such as at the Transfiguration <note>The event where Jesus was seen in a glorified state on a mountain.</note> and when the daughter of the leader of the synagogue was raised from the dead <note>Referring to the raising of Jairus's daughter.</note>. He put the scribes and doctors of the law to confusion with valid arguments, and disputed so well against Hermogenes, the magician and heretic (of whom Saint Paul makes mention in 2 Timothy, chapters 1 and 2 <note>original: "2. à Timot. 1. & 2. cha." Saint Luke mentions this in Acts 12, saying: "King Herod killed James, the brother of John, with the sword."</note>

## SAINT THOMAS.

<image-desc>An oval engraved portrait of Saint Thomas the Apostle. He is depicted as a bearded man in robes, holding a long staff. In the background, a detailed cityscape with a prominent church or cathedral is visible. The oval is framed by a border containing the Latin inscription: "Saint Thomas, Apostle of Jesus Christ" <note>original: "D. THOMAS I. CH. APOSTOL."</note>.</image-desc>

THOMAS, called Didymus <note>From the Greek *didymos*, meaning "twin."</note> by our Lord, which is to say, Twin, was called to the Apostolic office along with the other eleven. He would not believe that Jesus was resurrected without seeing him, for he was not with the others when He appeared to them; but soon after, he believed and was a witness to His resurrection—not merely for having heard it said or having seen it only, but having touched the wound in His side and spoken to Him. He proclaimed the Gospel to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, and also (according to Dorotheus, Bishop of Tyre) to the Germans, Hyrcanians, and Bactrians. He died pierced by spears in several parts of his body by four soldiers who had been ordered to do so by King Misdaeus <note>original: "Mesdee." Historically identified with Mazdai, a king in India described in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas.</note> in a city of Greater India.

### SAINT MATTHEW.

<image-desc>An oval engraved portrait of Saint Matthew seated at a desk and writing in a book. To his left, a winged angel—his symbolic attribute—stands and points toward the text. MATTHEW, surnamed Levi, son of Alphaeus, was a publican <note>A "publican" was a person responsible for collecting taxes for the Roman Empire, a profession often despised in Jewish society.</note>, seated at the place of receipts, exchange, or banks. He was called by Jesus Christ as He passed by there, joining the number of His disciples, and in the end attained the Apostolic dignity. 

He came to preach in Ethiopia, which had fallen to him in the division of countries made among the Apostles. In a city of this province called Naddauer, he uncovered the deceptions and ruses of Zaroes and Arfexat, magicians whom Eglippe, the king of that place, worshipped as gods, believing them to be such. He was the first to write the Gospel in Judea, using Hebrew letters and words. The name of the person who translated it into Greek is not known for certain. Saint Jerome <note>original: "Sainct Hierofme." Jerome was a 4th-century scholar best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says that the Hebrew text written by Saint Matthew is in Caesarea, in the library built with great diligence by Pamphilus the martyr. SIMON the Canaanite, brother of Jude and James, whom some have called brothers of the Lord <note>The "brothers of the Lord" mentioned in the Gospels are traditionally interpreted by Western Church scholars as cousins or close kinsmen of Jesus, rather than siblings.</note>, all three natives of Cana in Galilee, was of the company of Jesus and one of the twelve. # SAINT JUDE.

<image-desc>An oval engraved portrait of Saint Jude (Thaddaeus). JUDE, otherwise known as Thaddaeus, also an Apostle of our Savior, preached the kingdom of heaven through Jesus Christ throughout all Mesopotamia, and suffered death on a cross under Abgar <note>original: "Augare." Abgar V was the King of Edessa; tradition often links him to the early spread of Christianity in the region.</note>, king of the Edessenes, in a city called Beryte <note>The ancient name for modern-day Beirut, Lebanon.</note>. He left in writing the short epistle which is among the seven catholic <note>In this context, "catholic" refers to the "General" or "Universal" Epistles of the New Testament, which were addressed to the Church at large rather than specific congregations.</note> letters; and because he takes testimony therein from the apocryphal book of Enoch, it is rejected by some. Nonetheless, Saint Jerome says that from all antiquity and long usage it has been received and approved by the Church, and placed among the number of the Holy Scriptures.

## SAINT JAMES.

<image-desc>An oval engraving of Saint James the Just. JAMES, brother of the Lord according to the flesh, and surnamed the Just, was (after the passion of Jesus Christ) appointed by the Apostles as Bishop of Jerusalem. He is the one who wrote a single epistle, placed among the seven catholic <note>In this context, "catholic" refers to the "General" or "Universal" Epistles of the New Testament, addressed to the Church at large.</note> letters received by the Church. Hegesippus, who lived near the time of the Apostles, discourses in this manner concerning James in the fifth book of his commentaries: James, brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, took charge of the Church of Jerusalem. He was holy from his mother's womb; he never drank wine nor any other beverage that could intoxicate; he never ate meat, nor cut his hair; he never used steam baths nor ointments. To him alone was it permitted to enter the place called the *Holy of Holies* <note>original: "Sancta Sanctorum"</note>, which is the Sanctuary. He wore no woolen clothes, but only linen. He died at Sebaste <note>Sebaste was a common name for several cities in the ancient world, including Samaria in Judea and a city in Phrygia.</note>.

# SAINT LUKE.

<image-desc>An oval engraved portrait of Saint Luke. He is shown as an elderly bearded man in robes and a cap, seated at a desk writing. An ox, his symbolic animal, is visible to his left. To his right, a winged child or angel assists him by holding an open book. The scene is framed within an oval border bearing the Latin inscription "Saint Luke the Evangelist." <note>original Latin: "D. LVCAS EVANGELISTA."</note></image-desc>

LUKE, a physician from Antioch, was learned in Greek literature; he accompanied Saint Paul on all his travels. "Luke, the beloved physician" (says Saint Paul to the Colossians) "greets you." And writing to Timothy, "Luke alone is with me." He wrote the Gospel in the Greek language, just as he had heard it from Saint Paul and the other Apostles; he testifies to this at the beginning of his Gospel, saying thus to Theophilus <note>Theophilus is the person to whom the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles are addressed; the name in Greek means "Friend of God."</note>, "Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word." <note>original: "Comme nous ont baillé ceux qui dez le commencement les auoyent veu, & auoyent esté ministres de la parolle." This refers to the prologue of the Gospel of Luke.</note> Furthermore, he set down in writing the Acts of the Apostles, according to what he himself had seen. He lived for 84 years. See Epiphanius. <note>Saint Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a prominent Church Father and bishop who wrote extensively on the lives of the biblical figures.</note>

## SAINT MARK.

<image-desc>An oval-framed engraving of Saint Mark the Evangelist. Mark is depicted as an elderly bearded man sitting at a desk, focused on writing in a book with a quill. He is dressed in flowing robes and has a subtle halo. Behind him to the left, his traditional symbol, a lion, rests under a stone archway. A small landscape is visible in the background. The Latin inscription "Saint Mark, Evangelist" <note>original Latin: "D. MARCVS, EVANGELISTA."</note> follows the curve of the top of the oval border.</image-desc>

MARK, a disciple and interpreter of Saint Peter, wrote the Gospel succinctly according to what he had heard Saint Peter recite. He was asked to do this by his brothers in Rome. Saint Peter approved of it, and by his own authority, he gave it to the church to be read, just as Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 150–215 AD) who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note> writes in the sixth book of the *Hypotyposes* <note>original: "Hipotiposes." This refers to a lost work by Clement titled "Outlines" or "Sketches."</note>. Saint Peter, in his first epistle, uses the name "Babylon" figuratively (according to Saint Jerome <note>A prominent Church Father and translator of the Vulgate Bible (c. 347–420 AD).</note>) to signify Rome, saying: "The church that is at Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you; and so doth Marcus my son." <note>This quote is from 1 Peter 5:13.</note> Mark then went to Egypt, and being the first to announce Jesus Christ in Alexandria, he established a church there with such great doctrine and self-discipline <note>original: "continence." Referring here to a life of asceticism and moral restraint.</note> that the converts to Christ imitated his way of life. He preached from Egypt as far as Pentapolis <note>A region of five cities in North Africa, specifically in modern-day Libya.</note>. He died in the 8th year of the reign of Nero <note>Approximately 61 or 62 AD.</note>, and was buried in Alexandria.

## OF THE FOUR EVANGELISTS
->in general.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'L' featuring a seated human figure in a robe, set within a frame of architectural elements and floral scrolls.</image-desc>THE four Evangelists had been predicted by Ezekiel in the vision of the four animals <note>Referencing Ezekiel 1:5–10, where the prophet sees four "living creatures" with four faces.</note>. The first face, of a man or Angel, signified Saint Matthew, who began to write as if concerning a man, thus: 
> The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham, etc. <note>Matthew 1:1. Matthew is symbolized by a man because he begins with the human genealogy of Christ.</note>
The second face, of a lion, signifies Saint Mark, in which is heard the voice of the lion crying in the desert: 
> Prepare the way of the Lord. <note>Mark 1:3. The lion represents the desert's roar and the royalty of Christ.</note>
The third face, of the young ox <note>original: "bouueau."</note>, demonstrates that Saint Luke took his origin from Zechariah the priest and sacrificer, as Saint Jerome <note>A prominent scholar and Father of the Church (c. 347–420 AD).</note> interprets it. The fourth face, namely that of the eagle, denotes Saint John, who, having taken the wings of an eagle and soaring higher, disputes profoundly regarding the eternal word of God, thus: 
> In the beginning was the Word, etc. <note>John 1:1. The eagle represents the spiritual heights of John’s theology.</note>
Furthermore, Saint John similarly introduced in his Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> four animals full of eyes, saying: 
> The first was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third like a man, and the fourth like a flying eagle. <note>Revelation 4:7.</note> 
From this and from what follows afterward in the text, it is demonstrated that these four Evangelists alone must be received and approved (for many have made gospels) and the others rejected as apocryphal <note>From the Greek for "hidden," referring to texts of doubtful authenticity or those not included in the official biblical canon.</note>.

## PHILO THE JEW.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Philo of Alexandria, depicted as an older man with a long beard and a turban-like head covering. The circular border contains the Latin inscription: PHILO IVDAEVS PHIL. NAT. ALEX. <note>Philo the Jew, Natural Philosopher of Alexandria.</note></image-desc>

Philo the Jew, a native of Alexandria, learned in all disciplines, abundant in vocabulary, rich in maxims <note>original: "sentences." In this context, it refers to pithy observations or moral dictates.</note>, and exalted in the interpretation of the divine scriptures, flourished during the time of Gaius Caesar <note>Better known as the Emperor Caligula (reigned 37–41 AD).</note>, about whose wickedness he wrote a book, which he recited in Rome before the entire Senate during the reign of Claudius. He made the acquaintance of Saint Peter, becoming his friend as well as that of Mark, his disciple. On this occasion, he gave great praise to the Christians and to the church of Alexandria, where Saint Mark was bishop. He imitated Plato in the elegance of his speech; and his style was so similar to that of Plato that it was said (and a proverb has come of it), *Either Plato philonizes, or Philo platonizes* <note>original Greek: "ἤ πλάτων φιλωνίζει, ἢ φίλων πλατωνίζει." This phrase highlights the seamless blending of Jewish theology with Platonic philosophy in Philo's work.</note>: as if one meant to say, either Plato imitates Philo, or Philo imitates Plato. He wrote several books, among which those translated into Latin by Sigismund Gelenius <note>A renowned humanist scholar (1497–1554) known for his Latin translations of ancient Greek texts.</note> are: *On the Antiquities of the Bible*, *On Hebrew Names*, *On the World*, *Commentaries on Genesis and Exodus*, *On the Life of Moses*, *On the Confusion of Tongues*, *On Special Laws*, *On the Embassy to Gaius*, *Alle-
gories*

### CONTINUATION OF THE CHRONICLE.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' featuring a seated figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
<margin>The Year of Christ 42.</margin>
TIBERIUS CLAUDIUS DRUSUS, son of Drusus and uncle of Gaius Caligula, a native of Lyon, held the empire for 14 years, having attained it at the age of fifty. He is the first of the Caesars who won the loyalty of the soldiers by means of wages <note>This refers to the *donativum*, a practice where the Emperor gave cash gifts to the soldiers (particularly the Praetorian Guard) to ensure their political support.</note>. He completed the two aqueducts to bring two springs to Rome, begun by Caligula: he had this water named after himself, the Claudian fountain <note>The Aqua Claudia, one of the four great aqueducts of ancient Rome.</note>: for the sumptuous construction of which he spent quite sixty thousand talents of gold (as Pliny says) worth, according to Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French scholar who calculated the value of ancient currencies in his work *De Asse*.</note>, one million, three hundred eighty-five thousand, and five hundred *écus* <note>A French gold coin.</note>. He was poisoned by a truffle by Agrippina his wife, daughter of his brother Germanicus, and this through the treason and at the provocation of Nero. He died at the age of 64.

Peter the Apostle, first bishop of Rome.

Simon the Sorcerer <note>Also known as Simon Magus.</note>, seeing that through the laying on of hands by the Apostles the people received the Holy Spirit, offered them money, saying: "Give me this power" (Acts 8). Since then, all those who trade sacred dignities for money are called Simoniacs after his name.

Pliny the Elder, Pomponius Mela, and Columella flourish during this time.

# VALERIA MESSALINA
## *A paragon of all lewdness.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' depicting a seated figure in classical or scholarly robes, gesturing toward an open book or tablet.</image-desc>

THE Valerii, as Seneca testifies in the book *On the Brevity of Life* <note>original: "au liure de la briefueté de la vie"; a reference to Seneca's *De Brevitate Vitae*</note>, were originally surnamed Messanins, for having conquered the city of Messana <note>Modern-day Messina in Sicily</note>: afterwards, the word having been corrupted, they were called Messalinus: from which name, as the men of this family were named Valerii Messalini, so the women were named Messalinas. From this family came Valeria Messalina, daughter of Barbatus Messalla, cousin of Claudius the Emperor. This woman, after the death of Aelia Paetina, was the fifth wife <note>Historically, Messalina is usually considered the third wife of Claudius; the author may be counting earlier betrothals or using a specific chronological source.</note> of the said Claudius, and had by him two children, one male named Britannicus, the other female named Octavia. Being the wife of an Emperor, she demonstrated a singular example of all crimes and wickednesses: in which vices, however, there was no virtue mixed. But she principally far surpassed all the women who lived before her, and after, and even until our own time, in two things: in lewdness and greed. As for her greed, she was so strongly devoted to amassing money, even by base means, to then give it away lavishly to her adulterers, that if anyone wished to obtain something from the Emperor—such as obtaining some magistracy <term>magistrat: a high-ranking public office in Rome</term> or legation <term>legation: a diplomatic mission or embassy</term>, being the head of an army, being placed and registered among the number of Roman citizens, or having deserved death, sought to be pardoned—he easily obtained all things through her by means of money. Now she was of a spirit so abject and base because of

By night, she would leave her husband alone in bed to go disguised to the brothel to abandon her body to whoever wanted it; then she would bring the stench of this debauchery back to her husband’s bed. Juvenal, in his sixth Satire, notes her lewdness thus:

> <note>original Latin: "Respice rivales divorum: Claudius audi, Quæ tulerit..."</note> Behold the rivals of the gods: hear, Claudius, what he endured. When his wife sensed her husband was asleep, she dared to prefer a common mat to the Palatine bed. Taking up the hood of a nocturnal harlot, the august Empress would leave with no more than a single female companion. Hiding her black hair under a yellow wig, she entered the warm brothel with its old patchwork curtain and went to her own empty cell. There, she stood with bare, gilded breasts, using the false name Lycisca, and displayed the belly that bore you, noble Britannicus <note>Britannicus was the son of Claudius and Messalina; the poet uses this to emphasize the shame of her actions</note>. She welcomed those entering with charms and asked for their coins. Soon, when the pimp was dismissing his girls, she departed sadly, but she was the very last to close her cell, still burning with the tension of her stiffened lust. Exhausted by men, but not yet satisfied, she withdrew. With her cheeks darkened and dirty, fouled by the smoke of the brothel’s lamp, she brought the smell of the brothel back to the imperial pillow. And should I speak of spells, and brewed poison given to a stepson? They do even worse things when driven by the power of their sex; they sin least through their lust.

# BOOK THREE.

She similarly forced other illustrious women to follow this course and the same way of life, and commanded that several of them be violated within the palace, even in the presence of their husbands; these men, in exchange for this, obtained riches, honors, and magistracies <note>high government offices</note> from her. She burned with such lewd lust that whomever was pleasing to her was either constrained to have company with her, or he was put to death.

Furthermore, Sabinus—who in the time of Gaius Caesar Caligula had been governor of the Celts <note>The Roman provinces in Gaul</note>—was condemned to death by the said Claudius and by the Senate for having had an affair with her, yet he was delivered by her own intervention. Certainly, I must not omit or keep silent the words of Sextus Aurelius Victor <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note>, so that one may more clearly understand what kind of woman Messalina was.

> Messalina (he says), the wife of the Emperor Claudius, exercised what was almost a right to adultery, first in secret and soon after publicly. Many who abstained from this out of fear were extinguished <note>meaning their lives or careers were ended</note>. Furthermore, being more cruelly inflamed, she set up alongside herself all the most noble women, the newly married, and the virgins in the manner of harlots, and men were forced to be present there. If anyone held such things in horror, she would charge him with some crime and exercise marvelous cruelty against him and against his entire family; so much so that she seemed more to be a man ruling under the Emperor than a wife married to the Emperor.

Is it possible to find, or even imagine, greater wickednesses in a woman than those of Messalina? Who, not content with having tried to strip him of the empire by every means, being privy to his secrets, remarried out of burning lust to another during the lifetime of her husband, having so thoroughly bamboozled <note>original: "embabouyné"; to trick or make a fool of someone</note> him that he seemed to be a slave under her, who was the mistress. ...is worse than the most cruel animal that exists on the earth. Is there one more superb and proud than the lion among those that walk on four feet? A wicked woman is even more so. The lion and the dragon are lesser in evil. The lions feared Daniel in the pit and did him no harm; yet Jezebel <note>The biblical Queen of Israel who famously persecuted the prophets of Yahweh</note> caused the death of the righteous Naboth <note>A man framed and executed by Jezebel so her husband, King Ahab, could seize his vineyard</note>. By woman, wars are waged, wise men are lost, saints are slain, and cities are burned. Through them, many end their lives. Sin and death proceeded from her <note>An allusion to Eve and the Fall of Man</note>. The rich become poor; the beautiful, ugly; the strong, weak; the truthful, liars; the diligent, lazy; the chaste, lustful; and the humble, proud. If she is not sober and modest, but only beautiful, her beauty is like a **whitened sepulcher** <note>A biblical metaphor from Matthew 23:27 for hypocrisy: something beautiful outside but dead and decaying within</note>, well-polished on the outside, and inside filled with rot and stench; or like the **apothecary boxes**, painted on the outside with gold and azure, but inside all full of poison and bitter drugs. Thus she causes a precipice and ruin for those who contemplate her external beauty, and gives such venom through her alluring eyes that those who look upon her are trapped and die from it. Wherefore Saint John Chrysostome <note>An early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful oratory; "Chrysostom" means "golden-mouthed"</note> rightly speaks of her thus: "What is woman but the enemy of friendship, an inevitable punishment, a necessary evil, a natural temptation, a desirable calamity, a domestic danger, and a delectable torment?" Saint Jerome <note>The priest and scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> calls her the way of iniquity, saying: *A harmful race is woman, the gate of the devil, the way of iniquity, and the sting of a scorpion* <note>original: "Nociuum genus fæmina, ianua diaboli, via iniquitatis, scorpionis percussio."</note>.
