# BOOK THIRD.

...but <note>The text continues from the previous page's metaphor about apothecary boxes being full of poisons.</note> when interrogated as to what a wicked woman was, he replied: "She is the confusion of man, an insatiable animal, an endless war, a continual damage, a hindrance to good works, the shipwreck of the lustful and immoderate man, a very heavy burden, and a drain of all evils." Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and biographer (c. 46 – 119 AD) widely read in the Renaissance for his moral essays</note> calls her an untamable animal, on account of her fickleness and fury. This is why the poets have depicted the Furies <note>In Greek and Roman mythology, the Furies (Eumenides) were female deities of vengeance who personified anger</note> as women, since women are more prone and subject to fury than men. Hence Virgil <note>The Roman epic poet, author of the *Aeneid*</note> describes that when Alecto <note>One of the three Furies</note> wants the stag of the shepherd Tyrrheus to die in Ascanius's hunt, she causes the fury to come to the female dogs and not to the males. The reason is that, a woman being of lesser heart and understanding, she can thus resist passions and disturbances less, there being nothing but total variation within her. In short, I could not sufficiently declare the specific inconstancy of many women, so full of it are their hearts. Petrarch <note>The Italian poet and scholar Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), famous for his sonnets to his beloved Laura</note> knew this well enough, even though love (which blinds lovers) had made him a slave to his lady Laura, singing thus of their fragility:

# CORNUTUS THE PHILOSOPHER

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of a bearded man in profile, wearing a classical robe. The text "CORNVTVS PHILOSOPHVS" is inscribed around the inner edge of the circle.</image-desc>

CORNUTUS, also called Phurnutus, was a philosopher so amiable and humane that he drew disciples to himself much more through his gentleness than through his doctrine. He wrote several books on Philosophy and rhetoric, the names of which you may see in Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>. The poet Persius, his disciple, studied moral philosophy under him in Rome, as he testifies in his fifth Satire:
> I placed myself under you: you took up my tender years, Cornutus, in your Socratic bosom. <note>original Latin: "Me tibi supposui: teneros tu suscipis annos / Socratico Cornute sinu." From Persius, *Satires* 5.36-37. This passage reflects the deep bond between the student and his mentor.</note>

Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a late 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note> makes mention of him in his notes on the ninth book of the *Aeneid*. Nero had him put to death along with the philosopher Musonius in Rome. <note>While the author states they were put to death, historical records suggest that Cornutus and Musonius Rufus were actually banished by Nero around 65 AD.</note>

—abandoned to all execrable vices. He takes women by force; he knows his mother carnally; <note>A reference to the rumors of incest between Nero and his mother, Agrippina the Younger.</note> he despoils the temples; he pillages and robs everyone. He is wasteful, becomes cruel, and poisons Britannicus. <note>Britannicus was the son of Emperor Claudius and Nero's rival to the throne; he was poisoned in 55 AD.</note> He is the first persecutor of the Church. He has his mother killed and her body opened in his presence without any horror. <note>A legendary and gruesome detail often found in medieval accounts, suggesting Nero wished to see the womb that bore him.</note> He has his aunt Lepida killed, as well as Seneca, his schoolmaster. <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher who had been Nero's tutor.</note> He has Rome set on fire, and taking pleasure in watching it from the Maecenatian tower, <note>The Tower of Maecenas on the Esquiline Hill, from which legend says Nero watched the Great Fire of Rome in 64 AD.</note> he sings, dressed as a mountebank, <note>original: "bateleur," referring to a street performer or stage player, highlighting the contemporary scandal of an Emperor performing in public.</note> of the sack and burning of Troy. > *Wife, father, and mother have condemned me to death.* <note>original Latin: "Morti me coniunx, pater & mater damnarunt." This refers to the ghosts of his wife Octavia, his adoptive father Claudius, and his mother Agrippina, all of whom he murdered.</note>

Meaning to say of himself that the shades and souls of his wife Octavia, of his mother, and of Claudius (who had adopted him)—all of whom he had put to death, even Claudius by poison, in order to hold dominion and the Empire—were justly demanding vengeance against him by righteous judgment, and were calling him to a miserable death. Driven out of Rome, he kills himself at the age of 30, having held the empire for 14 years. With this Nero, the lineage of the Caesars fails. <note>Nero was the last emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.</note>

Persius the Satirical poet; Seneca the philosopher, orator, and poet; and Lucan the poet flourished.

**AULUS VITELLIUS**, raised in the brothels of Capri, <note>original: "bordeaux de Capree." This refers to the island where Emperor Tiberius retreated; Vitellius was said to have been one of the youths serving Tiberius's infamous appetites.</note> vicious, gluttonous, and devoted to his belly, was sent by Galba into Upper Germany to command the Roman army. He seized the empire, over which he ruled for only eight months; for as Vespasian was elected and declared emperor, Vitellius saw himself abandoned by everyone. Having hidden himself in a cave in Rome, he was dragged out once the army entered the city. Being recognized, they tied his hands and tore his robe; with a rope around his neck, they dragged him through the city, where the people threw mud in his face. He was mocked while enduring an infinity of outrages; finally, he was torn to pieces and then thrown into the Tiber, aged fifty-five years.

**Apollinaris**, a martyr killed at Ravenna. <note>Saint Apollinaris of Ravenna is traditionally considered the first bishop of Ravenna; he is said to have been a disciple of Saint Peter.</note>

**Apollonius of Tyana**, an Asian philosopher, not content with equaling the philosophers of his own country in knowledge, and moved by a desire to learn, traveled toward the Persians, Scythians, Massagetae, and as far as India, then to the Brahmans <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of India.</note>. From there he went to the Elamites, Babylonians, Chaldeans, Medes, Parthians, Assyrians, Phoenicians, Arabs, and Palestinians; then to Egypt, and afterward to Ethiopia to hear the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked philosophers," ancient ascetic thinkers known for their rigorous self-discipline.</note>. From all these regions he returned more learned than he had been before going there. See his life in the works of Philostratus. <note>Philostratus was a Greek scholar who wrote a famous, though largely legendary, biography of Apollonius in the 3rd century AD.</note>

**Caelius Sabinus**, a jurist <note>The original uses "I.C." for *Iuris Consultus*, a professional legal expert in ancient Rome.</note>, put into writing *On the Edicts of the Curule Aediles* <note>original: "De edictis aedilium curulium." The Aediles were Roman officials responsible for public buildings and market regulations.</note>, where he treats *On the Laws of Slave Sales* <note>original: "De venalium servorum legibus."</note>.

## EPICTETUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of the philosopher Epictetus in profile, facing right. He is depicted with a beard and wearing a cap. The circular border contains the Latin inscription: "EPICTETVS PHIL. HIER."</image-desc>

**Epictetus of Hierapolis**, a noble philosopher of the Stoic sect, was lame. And although he was very poor, he nevertheless took so little account of the goods of fortune—called "externals"—that in his house there was no door, and inside one would have found nothing other than a wretched bed. He was a slave in Rome to Epaphroditus <note>A powerful freedman and secretary to the Emperor Nero.</note>

...who was familiar with Nero: he lived until the time of Marcus Antoninus. Arrian wrote a volume on his life and character, which by the injury of time has not reached our hands; he also gathered from his books the best parts, like a beautiful flower, and compiled them into a volume titled *Enchiridion* <note>The *Enchiridion*, or "Manual," remains one of the most famous summaries of Stoic ethics. Two Greek verses were written about him, which subtly imply that the gods are not entirely hateful or hostile toward those who pass the course of their lives amidst various calamities and miseries:

> I, Epictetus, was born a slave, and lame of body,
> and as poor as Irus, yet beloved by the immortals.

which I translated in the past as follows:
> Born a slave, I am Epictetus, and in body, lame,
> And poorer than Irus: yet loved by the gods.
> <note>original French: "Epictete serf né, suis, & de corps, boiteux, Et plus pauure qu'Irus : aymé pourtant des dieux." Irus was the proverbial beggar of Homer's *Odyssey*.</note>

Plague in Rome.

Fire burned the mountain in Campania <note>The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.</note>, and within Rome the temples of Serapis, Neptune, and Jupiter Capitolinus, the baths of Agrippa, the porticos of Pompey, the Theater of Balbus, the house of Octavia, and the library.

<margin>Year 82</margin>
**DOMITIAN**, brother of Titus, a very wicked man and quite different from his father and brother; he wished to be called "Lord and God" by his subjects. He persecutes the Christians; banishes all mathematicians and philosophers from Rome; hosts magnificent spectacles and games; and institutes the Secular Games, which were held every hundred years <note>The *Ludi Saeculares* were ancient Roman religious celebrations involving sacrifices and theatrical performances, marking the end of a *saeculum*, or the maximum span of a human life.</note>. He takes pleasure in catching flies after retiring to some secret place, piercing and skewering them with a sharp iron tool <note>This famous anecdote from Suetonius was often used to illustrate Domitian's cruelty and idle nature.</note>. He forbade the planting of more vineyards because of a shortage of grain and an abundance of wine. He has statues of himself erected; he holds the empire for 15 years, at the end of which, in the 45th year of his life, he is killed by a conspiracy of his household servants.

Shortly before the death of Domitian, a crow was heard to speak at the Capitol and say, "All things will go well" <note>original Latin: *Bene erit*, or Greek: *Estai panta kalos*. Historians recorded this as a rare "prophetic" omen occurring in 96 AD.</note>. This was a prodigy presaging the future and approaching rule of Nerva and Trajan, who were renowned for their clemency and gentleness.

Arruntius Stella of Padua, an elegiac poet, writes epigrams and a poem on the victory obtained by Domitian against the Sarmatians <note>The Sarmatians were nomadic tribes from the Iranian-speaking peoples who frequently clashed with Rome's Danube frontier.</note>.

Statius the poet writes the *Thebaid* <note>An epic poem in twelve books chronicling the struggle between the brothers Eteocles and Polynices for the throne of Thebes.</note>.

Trogus the historian <note>Likely Pompeius Trogus, whose universal history survives primarily through the epitome by Justin.</note>.

**ANACLETUS**, Bishop of Rome, holds the see <note>The transcription notes a macron over the 'e' in *tiet* indicating the omitted 'n' in *tient*, the French word for "holds."</note> for 12 years <note>Anacletus, or Cletus, is traditionally counted as the third Bishop of Rome.</note>.

Aristarchus and Priscus, martyrs.

Paul, Bishop of Narbonne.

Eutropius, Bishop of Aquitaine.

**CLEMENT** the Roman, Bishop of Rome, holds the see for 9 years.

Saint John the Apostle writes the Gospel.

## JUVENAL

<image-desc>Circular medallion containing a profile portrait of a bearded man facing left, wearing a soft cap or cowl. The inscription around the border reads: "Decimus Junius Juvenalis, Satirist" <note>original Latin: *DEC. IVNIVS IVVENALIS SATIRIC.*</note></image-desc>

IV. Decimus Juvenal, a native of Aquinum <note>A town in central Italy, now known as Aquino.</note>, was a poet and a disciple of the grammarian Fronto. Following the example and imitation of Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, the 2nd-century BC inventor of Roman poetic satire.</note>, he composed five books of Satires, of which we enjoy only sixteen; the rest have been lost. He was very well-versed in satirical poetry, which took its beginning from the "Old Comedy" of the Greeks. He proved himself to be more biting, harsh, and violent in the accusation and condemnation of vices than Lucilius, Horace, or any other satirical poet had ever been. Martial was one of his closest friends. He was banished to Pentapolis in Egypt <note>Biographical traditions of Juvenal vary; some sources suggest he was exiled to the frontier of Egypt as a military command in his old age as a form of "honorable" punishment for mocking a court favorite.</note> at the age of 80, where he ended his days.

->Iavolenus and T. Aristo, Jurisconsults<-
<note>Iavolenus Priscus and Titius Aristo were renowned legal experts and advisors to the Emperors Trajan and Hadrian.</note>

He provides for the nourishment of poor children at public expense. He restores afflicted cities, and to provide for such great expenses, he sells his own clothing, his gold and silver plate, his furniture, and his inherited estates. <meta>This page continues the famous ghost story of the philosopher Athenodorus, originally recounted by Pliny the Younger. The previous page ended with the description of a haunted house in Athens where, in the silence of the night, one heard...</meta>

<page-num>298</page-num>
<header>PROSOPOGRAPHY</header>

...heard a sound of iron chains, first from afar, then from closer by. Immediately there appeared the likeness of an old man, very thin, ugly, and filthy, having a very long beard and hair standing on end and hideous. He wore irons on his feet and hands, such as those placed upon criminal prisoners, and he rattled them so loudly that the inhabitants of that house could not sleep for fear and distress, but stayed awake all night, from which they became ill, and finally death followed, because their fear always increased; for by day also, although such a phantom <note>original: *idole*—from the Latin *idolon*, meaning an apparition or specter</note> or likeness did not show itself, it nevertheless seemed to the inhabitants that they saw it, which caused them even greater terror. Wherefore the master of the house was constrained to leave it entirely to this monster and phantom, as no one wished to live there, and he had it proclaimed and put up for public notice <term>criee</term> <note>A public announcement or auction, often used for selling or leasing property.</note> to sell or rent it to someone who might not have known of such misfortune.

Now there came to Athens a philosopher named Athenodorus, who, having read the sign and also learned the price of the house, inquired why it was being offered so cheaply. Having learned everything, and notwithstanding such an apparition, he nonetheless rented it with all the more eagerness. When night came, he commanded his servants to prepare for him the first room or the front part of the house, and had pen, ink, and paper brought to him for writing, along with a light <note>original: *du feu*—literally "fire," but referring to the flame of a candle or lamp used for work.</note>. This being done, he commanded them to retire to another wing and part of the house; then he set himself attentively to writing, so that his mind, wandering here and there or empty of occupation, might not conceive and imagine such a figure out of vain fear. At the beginning of the night, he heard nothing. Soon after, he heard the rattling of irons on feet and hands, making a noise. He did not lift

[he did] not [lift] his eyes at all, and did not stop writing, strengthening his courage <note>original: *couraige*—here meaning his mental resolve or spirit</note> all the more, and lending an ear. Then this sound began to increase more and more, and the likeness of the old man approached as far as the entrance of the door, then into the chamber. He looked and recognized the old man, just as he had been told and as he had been described to him. The old man was standing there, making a sign with his finger to call the philosopher. He, on the contrary, made a sign with his hand that he should wait a little: and once again set himself to writing. The phantom, for its part, approached as far as the table, and did not cease to rattle and make noise around and near the head of the philosopher, who was writing. Athenodorus gazed at it again and saw it making the sign as before. Therefore, without delay, he took the light <note>original: *le feu*—likely a candle or oil lamp</note> and followed it. This old man walked quite slowly and heavily, as if burdened by chains and iron bonds; when he had gone down to the lower courtyard of the house, suddenly the likeness of the old man vanished, leaving the philosopher there, who, with leaves and herbs, marked the spot where the phantom had disappeared. The next day he went to the magistrates of the city, advising them to have the marked spot dug up. This was done. And there were found in the earth bones, chained or bound in iron, which the body—having rotted in the earth over the course of time—had left bare and gnawed by those iron bonds. The magistrates had them all gathered and buried publicly: and since then, no such spirit was ever seen or heard in that house again.

For sometimes God's will is revealed to those who sleep through dreams, and the soul, sharing in divinity, sometimes foresees the future through a freer movement when the body rests. Macrobius <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman philosopher whose commentary on the "Dream of Scipio" became the standard textbook for dream interpretation in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> identifies five types of dreams: three true and two false. These are: *oneiros* <note>original: ὄνειρος</note>, a symbolic dream; *horama* <note>original: ὅραμα</note>, a prophetic vision; and *chrematismos* <note>original: χρηματισμός</note>, an oracle. These are the true ones. Then there are *enypnion* <note>original: ἐνύπνιον</note>, a daydream (which the Latins call *insomnium* <note>original: "insomnium," referring to a dream caused by mental or physical distress</note>); and *phantasma* <note>original: φάντασμα</note>, a phantom or false imagination, which creates an apparent impression different from what it actually is. 

There are dreams that come to pass, and others that do not. Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the famous Italian humanist and poet</note> recounts that a man dreamed he was bitten to death by the marble lion placed in front of a temple. The next day, passing before the statue of the lion, he recounted his dream to his companions who walked with him, with great laughter. Having put his hand into the open mouth of the stone lion, saying, "Here is my enemy of the night," a scorpion, which was hidden inside, bit him and wounded him mortally. 

The last two types of dreams we mentioned have no power of divination. For *enypnion* <note>original: ἐνύπνιον</note> arises from the thoughts, worries, and business one had while awake, which one remembers later while sleeping. *Phantasma* <note>original: φάντασμα</note> proceeds from the quality of the humors <note>In traditional medicine, the "four humors"—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were thought to influence health and mind; an imbalance could cause vivid hallucinations</note>, such as *ephialtes* <note>original: ἐφιάλτης</note>, called by the Latins *Incubus* <note>original: "Incubus," a term for a nightmare or a demon believed to weigh down the sleeper</note>, which belongs to this same category. But the first three contain divination within themselves. *Oneiros* <note>original: ὄνειρος</note> presents the truth to us under other forms, such as Pharaoh's dream of the seven years, represented by the seven cows <note>A reference to the Biblical story in Genesis 41, where Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dream of seven fat and seven lean cows as years of plenty and famine</note>. *Horama* <note>original: ὅραμα</note> shows clearly to the spirit

# ON THE INSTITUTION
## of Lent.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or religious figure, at a desk within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>

Lent, called in Latin *Quadragesima* <note>original: "Quadragefima", referring to the forty-day period</note>, by reason of the forty days and as many nights that our Savior fasted in the deserts without eating or drinking, was instituted for several good causes. First, in this time we represent the people of Israel who lived in the desert for forty years, after which they celebrated Passover <note>original: "Paſque"</note>, just as we, after having fasted forty days following the example of Jesus Christ, celebrate our New Passover <note>original: "Paſque nou-uelle"; here referring to Easter and the Eucharist</note> which he instituted and left as a pledge <note>term: "arres" (earnest money); a symbolic down payment or guarantee of a future promise</note> of his alliance with us. A Passover certainly very different from the ancient one: for instead of the paschal lamb, we receive his precious and most worthy body in memory of him and of his passion.

But before presenting oneself at the table of the Lord, one must prepare throughout all of Lent, called a time of penance <note>original: "penitence"</note>, the fruits of which are: abstinence, fasting, prayer <note>original: "oraifon"</note>, spiritual contemplation, alms, weeping, tears, and other works of mercy. Furthermore, by nature man is more inclined and moved to lust in the spring, when all his strengths are renewed, more than in all other seasons: for which reason, to restrain and hold short this fleshly appetite, the wise men of old ordained such a fast during this time. Wherefore it is necessary to abstain and fast better from vices than from meats (although the abundance of these is the match <note>original: "allumette"; the kindling or spark that starts a fire</note> and maintenance of sins): for what does it profit to exhaust the body through abstinence if the heart is swollen with pride? What praise shall we acquire through a pale complexion by dint of fasting, if we are

As long as Eve fasted and abstained from the forbidden fruit, she remained a virgin: but after she had broken and violated the fast, she fell into misery, was subject to the corruptions of lust, and was cast out of the earthly paradise. Moses, having fasted forty days and as many nights on Mount Sinai, spoke with God: and the people of Israel, being full <note>original: "saoul"; meaning glutted or overfed</note>, forged meanwhile the idol of the golden calf, and lost the labor of so many days through gluttony. Saul, in the first book of Kings, says: Cursed be he who eats bread until the evening, and until I am avenged of my enemies.

In the temple of *Eleusis* in *Athens* were written three precepts of *Triptolemus* <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology who was taught the craft of agriculture by Demeter</note>, namely: to Worship the gods, Honor parents, and Not live on flesh. *Dicaearchus* <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note>, in his books on antiquities, writes that in the time of *Saturn* <note>The mythical Golden Age of peace and plenty</note>, all meats being rejected, people lived indiscriminately on all kinds of fruits or grains. *Orpheus* (says *Saint Jerome*) detests in his verses the custom of eating flesh. *Chaeremon* the Stoic recounts of the life of the ancient priests of *Egypt*, that having left behind all the cares and affairs of the world, they remained always within the temple, where they contemplated the nature of things, the causes, the effects, and the logic of the stars. They never associated with women, nor ever saw their parents or children. From the time they began to devote themselves to divine service, they always abstained from eating flesh and drinking wine, and even from eggs and milk—saying that an egg is liquid flesh, and milk is blood that has merely changed color. *Saint Paul* in the *Epistle to the Romans, chapter 14*, writes concerning food as follows: One believes that he may eat all kinds of foods, and another, who is weak, eats herbs. Let him who eats not despise him who does not eat, and let him who does not eat not judge him who eats: for God has accepted him. And toward the end of the same chapter: Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. It is true that all things are clean: but it is bad for the man who eats and gives offense. It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother might be offended.

### G A L E N

<image-desc>A circular woodcut medallion portrait of Galen, the physician of Pergamon. He is depicted in profile facing right, wearing a soft cap and a scholarly robe. The circular border contains the English translation of the Latin inscription: GALEN, PHYSICIAN OF PERGAMON.</image-desc>

Galen the philosopher, and the most excellent of all physicians, was a native of Pergamon, a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, near the river Caicus. This city has been subject to the Emperor of Rome since the time of King Attalus <note>Attalus III, the last King of Pergamon, who bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman Republic in 133 BC</note>. Galen himself testifies to this in these words, translated by Laguna <note>Andrés Laguna, a prominent 16th-century Spanish physician who translated Galen's works into Spanish and commented on them in Latin</note>: "This remedy is not numbered among those first composed by me; rather, it was made many years ago by our king Attalus, ruler of the people of Pergamon, a man devoted to the study of all types of medicine." <note>Original Latin: *Hoc medicamentum non ex eorum numero est, quæ à me primùm composita sunt: sed iam annis multis ante, à rege nostro, Pergamensibus imperante, Attalo, viro omnigenorum medicaminum studioso.*</note> He flourished during the reigns of the Emperors Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, and Pertinax, in Rome, where he arrived after having studied at Smyrna and Corinth, traveled through Egypt and across all Syria-Palestine, and sailed to Lemnos and Cyprus. # DIALOGUE BETWEEN A PHYSICIAN AND
## *a Lawyer, on the dignity of their art.*

<image-desc>Decorative floral drop cap initial 'A'.</image-desc>
A Lawyer and a Physician, both eager for honor, were in a dispute over which of them should take precedence; and they wished to argue over the excellence of their respective arts. "We are," said the Physician, "ordained by the Most High, who says: *Honor the Physician* <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1: "Honor the physician for the need thou hast of him: for the Most High hath created him."</note>. There have been kings who, not disdaining the art, were its professors: Sabor and Gyges, Physicians of the Medes; Sabiel, of the Arabs; Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, famous for his study of poisons and his namesake antidote, "mithridatum."</note>, of the Persians; Hermes, of the Egyptians; and Mesue <note>Johannes Mesue, the name attributed to influential 8th and 10th-century Persian/Syrian medical writers.</note>, nephew of the King of Damascus. What is more, the Angel Raphael, according to the Hebrew truth <note>The Hebrew versions of the Book of Tobit, in which the Archangel Raphael provides instructions for making medicine from a fish.</note>, made use of it. God is the author of health: nature is God's instrument: and the Physician is the minister of both. This science, after Theology, holds a place higher than the science of law; and of the three types of goods—those of the spirit, the body, and fortune—it preserves and maintains the first two better, healing the suffering spirit and the body, which take precedence over the goods of fortune (which are perishable), which lawyers and legal counselors only try to maintain." The lawyer, for his reasons, said: "The law is very necessary and profitable, and without it the human state would not

Regarding medicine, it is found in the commentaries of the Greeks that the good King of Judah, Hezekiah—who rooted out idolatry, restored the true worship of the one God, and who had no equal in piety in that kingdom before or after him—found in the temple of Jerusalem a book by Solomon dealing with the cure of all kinds of diseases, which he removed from there so that the memory of it might be extinguished; this is of great significance and seems to detract from the dignity of the physician. 

"That," replied the physician, "will not be found in the entire Bible; and if it were so, God did not permit this book to come forward, but rather, using Hezekiah, wished to have it abolished so as not to increase superstition among the Jewish people, foreseeing that their posterity would abuse this knowledge and give all the praise to the book rather than to Him, who taught Solomon the secrets contained therein. It is useless to say that for this reason He took away the art, or wished that there be no physician; He only wants humans to admire Him in His works, and that they use this art for His glory and their salvation. ### BOOK THREE

[heals] Hezekiah's wound with figs <note>A reference to 2 Kings 20, where the prophet Isaiah heals King Hezekiah using a poultice of figs, demonstrating that God works through physical means.</note>. Nevertheless, although the Most High God created both [the physician and the medicine], He does not want us to place our trust in them during illness as if expecting health from them alone, but in Him who grants it through the physician and the medicine that He employs. Therefore, one must have recourse to Him, implore His aid, and in fear use reverently the things He has placed upon the earth, neither speaking ill of this divine gift nor of this art so beneficial to humankind. Now, if we run from house to house and town to town (as you say), in this we are observing God's commandment to visit the sick. "I was sick," He says, "and you visited me; for this cause, possess the kingdom prepared for you by my Father."

"It is quite the opposite," added the lawyer, "for you physicians are greedy to the core, and charity is dead within you. If a poor man is sick and without money, he is abandoned by physicians—that is to say, they do not visit him at all—whereby it becomes necessary for the Great Physician, God, to take charge and care of him."

"It is the lawyers," said the physician, "who are filled with extreme greed. Jason Maynus <note>Giasone del Maino (1435–1519), an influential Italian jurist known for his immense wealth and his legal commentaries.</note>, one of your most excellent <term>Jurisconsults</term> <note>A professional legal expert or jurist.</note>, sold his consultations dearly and at an excessive price, so greedy was he; likewise, he was such a gambler in his youth that he even wagered his own legal code written on parchment."

### THIRD BOOK

...born from the flowers of rhetoric; and the most excellent of yours are barbaric to the ultimate degree, such as **Bartholus**, **Baldus**, and others. <note>Bartholus de Saxoferrato and Baldus de Ubaldis were the most famous medieval legal commentators. "Many elegant and discreet persons," replied the lawyer, "have never been offended by the lessons of **Bartholus**, **Baldus**, **Jason**, and others who are coarse and rough in language, and to whom they are ordinarily frequent and devoted. ## HERACLIDES LYC.

<image-desc>Circular portrait medallion of Heraclides Lycius, depicted as a bearded man in profile facing right. The border of the medallion contains the Latin text: HERACLIDES LYCIVS SOPH. <note>original Latin: "Heraclides Lycius, Sophist."</note></image-desc>

HERACLIDES the Sophist <note>A Greek rhetorician of the 2nd century AD, known for his work in the Second Sophistic movement.</note> was of a coarse mind and unkempt in his clothing; nevertheless, through diligence, assiduity, and great labor—and having often drunk deeply of the smoke of the lamps in his study <note>A common historical metaphor for staying up late to study by oil lamp.</note>—he reached the point that great personages judged him worthy to be counted among the number of eloquent orators, calling him "most elegant." This is a remarkable thing in him, seeing as history denotes him a great glutton: for study and gluttony are very contrary things. A pleasant account is made of this, since every man instructed by such experience knows that there is nothing that continual labor cannot overcome, and when one applies oneself stubbornly to a task, one will eventually achieve it. Having thus written a book titled *In Praise of Labor* <note>original Greek: πόνου ἐγκώμιον (*ponou enkomion*)</note>, it happened by chance that while walking one day with his book in his hands in Naucratis, a city of Egypt, he encountered Ptolemy <note>Likely referring to a scholar or local dignitary, as the historic Pharaohs were long gone by Heraclides' time.</note>, who was also very studious. When asked by him what book he had brought to light, Heraclides replied it was *In Praise of Labor*. Ptolemy took the book, and having erased the first letter "p" <note>original Greek letter: π</note>, there remained *In Praise of the Ass* <note>original Greek: ὄνου ἐγκώμιον (*onou enkomion*). The joke relies on the fact that removing the 'p' from *ponos* (labor) leaves *onos* (donkey or ass).</note>, which is to say nothing other than *The Praise of the...* 

<summary>This page provides a biographical sketch of Heraclides Lycius, a 2nd-century Sophist known for his tireless work ethic despite his personal lack of refinement and gluttonous habits. It concludes with a humorous anecdote about a pun made on the title of his book by a contemporary named Ptolemy.</summary>

# HERACLIDES OF LYCIA

<image-desc>A circular medallion portrait of a bearded man in profile, facing right. He wears a simple robe. The circular border of the medallion contains the Latin inscription: HERACLIDES THE LYCIAN, SOPHIST.</image-desc>

Heraclides the sophist <note>Heraclides of Lycia (fl. 2nd century AD) was a prominent teacher of rhetoric in Athens, known for his rivalries with other intellectuals.</note> was of a coarse spirit and unkempt in his dress; nevertheless, through diligence, assiduity, and great labor—and having often breathed in the smoke of the lamps during his studies <note>A reference to the classical idiom "to smell of the lamp," meaning a work produced by long hours of study at night.</note>—he reached such a point that great personages judged him worthy to be numbered among the eloquent orators, calling him most elegant. This is a remarkable thing in him, given that history describes him as a great glutton: for study and gluttony are very contrary things. A pleasant tale is told of this, for every man instructed by such experience knows that there is nothing that continual labor cannot overcome, and when one persists in something, they will eventually succeed. Thus, having written a book titled *The Praise of Toil* <note>original: "πόνου ἐγκώμιον" (*ponou enkōmion*)</note>, it happened by chance that while walking one day with his book in his hands in Naucratis <note>A Greek city in the Nile Delta of Egypt, a center for trade and learning.</note>, a city in Egypt, he met Ptolemy <note>Likely Ptolemy of Naucratis, a fellow sophist and rival known for his wit.</note>, who was also very studious. When asked what book he had published, he replied that it was *The Praise of Toil*. Ptolemy took the book, and having erased the first letter "p" <note>original: "π" (the Greek letter pi)</note>, there remained *The Praise of the Ass* <note>original: "ὄνου ἐγκώμιον" (*onou enkōmion*). By removing the first letter, Ptolemy turned "toil" (*ponos*) into "donkey" (*onos*), mocking Heraclides's industriousness as mere stupidity.</note>, which is to say nothing other than The Praise

Teaching another time at Smyrna during the time of the empire of Severus, he came to Rome; wanting to harangue <note>To deliver a formal, lengthy public speech.</note> unexpectedly and on the spot before the Emperor, and without having otherwise thought about it, he was astonished by the nobility and presence of so many great personages who were listening to him. He remained mute, and suddenly lost his speech without knowing what he should say, nor how to continue and pursue his discourse. And one must not marvel at this: for we read of Demosthenes, prince of the Greek orators, that wanting to harangue Philip the King, son of Amyntas, he was so astonished at the beginning of his oration that he fell silent as if he were mute, terrified (as is believable) by the majesty of such a man. ### L. SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS,
the sixth persecutor of the church, but otherwise a good and valiant prince. After the death of Julian <note>Didius Julianus, who was emperor for only nine weeks in 193 AD.</note>, he was named emperor in Illyria by the soldiers; at the same time, Pescennius Niger was likewise named emperor by the army of Syria which he led. Occupying the empire, Severus cast him out from the region of the East, and Clodius Albinus from the country of France <note>original: "France," referring here to Roman Gaul.</note>. He conquered the Parthians, the Arabs, and the Adiabenians. He died of gout (some say of old age) in England <note>Severus died in Eboracum, modern-day York, in 211 AD.</note> at the age of 70 years, having reigned 18 years.

**BASSIANUS CARACALLA**, so named because of a long robe reaching to his heels, which he brought from Gaul <note>original: "France," referring to the *caracalla*, a hooded Celtic cloak</note> and gave to the people of Rome. He was the son of Severus and a native of Lyon, for his father Severus was sent there on an embassy. He married his stepmother <note>Julia Domna. Historical sources are conflicted; she was his mother, but rumors of an incestuous marriage were common in ancient histories.</note>; he killed his brother Geta; and had the head removed of Papinian, the quaestor <note>A high-ranking Roman official responsible for legal and financial administration.</note> and great Jurist. He was killed at Carrhae, a city in Mesopotamia, while he wanted to relieve himself <note>original: "aller à la ſelle," literally "go to the stool."</note> by untying his laces <note>original: "defliant ſes eguilletes," referring to the ties that fastened his clothing.</note>, having held the empire with all cruelty for 7 years.

Origen lived during the time of Severus and Caracalla, or (according to Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a German Benedictine abbot and scholar (1462–1516).</note>) during the reign of Valerian. He corrected the translation of the Bible of the 70 interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, adding everything they had omitted and explaining the mysteries in which they had shown themselves obscure.

Papinian the Jurist wrote *Responses, Book 19; Questions, 37; Definitions, 2; on Adultery, 1; on the Edict of the Curule Aediles, 1; Digest, 19.* Caracalla commanding him to deliver an oration for him before the Senate and before the people, by which the murder of his brother Geta might be excused or refuted, he responded to him that parricide could not be as easily excused as committed. The Emperor begged him again to make an invective against his slain brother and recite all his vices. This the jurist refused to do, saying that it is another parricide to accuse the slain innocent. **OPELLIUS MACRINUS** of Mauritania, born of a low and obscure lineage, was learned in law but otherwise detestable, dissolute, and cunning. ## ALEXANDER SEVERUS
reigned peacefully without bloodshed for 13 years, 3 months, and 7 days. A good prince, he favored the Christians. He detested theft and had thieves punished. He forbade the selling of public offices and did not wish for women of ill-repute to greet his mother. He overcame the King of Persia in war, enriching his soldiers with the spoils. He often had this sentence on his lips:

> Do not do to another what you would not wish done to yourself.

He was killed in France <note>Historically the Roman province of Gaul</note> by his soldiers, with Maximinus being the leader of this enterprise.

**MAXIMIN**, a native of Thrace, 8 feet and one finger tall, from a shepherd becomes emperor. Persecutes the Christians. Often drinks in a single day (if one may trust Julius Capitolinus <note>A historian listed as one of the authors of the *Augustan History*</note>) the eighth part of a *muid* of wine <term>muid: a large ancient liquid measure; an eighth would be roughly 30–35 liters</term>; eats forty pounds of meat; collects the sweat flowing abundantly from his body in a cup; trains the legions in hunting and wrestling; throws five or six soldiers to the ground at once while wrestling; his thumb is so thick that, in place of a ring, he wears his wife's gold bracelet upon it; has fingers so strong that he breaks topaz stones and medium-sized trees in the middle, such that through the great and diverse experience of his strength, some call him Antaeus, Hercules, and others Milo of Croton <note>Antaeus and Hercules were mythological giants/heroes; Milo was a legendary six-time Olympic wrestling champion</note>; and for the cruelty he uses against everyone, notably against the gentlemen, he is nicknamed Cyclops, Busiris, Phalaris, Typhon, and Geryon <note>All names of legendary monsters or cruel tyrants from antiquity</note>: for he had ordered all his relatives killed to erase the memory of his lineage, poverty, and low status. Comes to Italy to lay siege to Aquileia, where his camp begins to starve, and having put certain captains to death, being hated by all, he is killed with his son in his tent at the age of 60, having held the empire for 3 years.

**MAXIMINUS**, a native of Thrace, 8 feet and one inch tall, rose from being a shepherd to become emperor. He persecuted the Christians. He often drank in a single day (if one may believe Julius Capitolinus <note>A supposed author of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies</note>) the eighth part of a *muid* of wine <term>muid: An ancient measure of capacity; 1/8th of a muid would be roughly 35 liters or 9 gallons</term>; ate forty pounds of meat; and collected in a cup the sweat from his body which flowed abundantly. He trained the legions in hunting and wrestling, and while wrestling would throw five or six soldiers at once. His thumb was so large that he wore his wife's gold bracelet as a ring. His fingers were so strong that he could break topaz stones and small trees through the middle; so that, because of the great and diverse experience of his strength, some called him Antaeus or Hercules <note>Mythological heroes known for their strength</note>, others Milo of Croton <note>A famous Greek wrestler from the 6th century BC</note>. For the cruelty he used against everyone, and especially against the nobility, he was nicknamed Cyclops, Busiris, Phalaris, Typhon, and Gyges <note>All names associated with tyranny or monstrous behavior in antiquity</note>. He had all his relatives killed to erase the memory of his low birth, poverty, and common status. He came to Italy to lay siege to Aquileia, where his camp began to suffer from famine. Having put certain captains to death and being hated by everyone, he was killed along with his son in his tent at the age of 60, having held the empire for 3 years.

**DIOCLETIAN**, of low birth, with **MAXIMIAN** surnamed Herculius, holds the empire for 22 years.

### BOOK THREE

...good men of holy life) to whom and to his successors the Emperor Constantine gave great wealth, nearly all the imperial power, several provinces and cities, and the imperial palace along with the city of Rome. Oh, what a wicked donation! At the time it was made, a voice was heard in heaven by several great personages, saying: "Today, a most wicked venom of the Asp <note>A reference to a legendary "voice from heaven" that supposedly cried out when the Church first received land and power, warning that poison had been introduced into the faith.</note> has been sown in the Church of God." Dante, the Florentine poet, in the 19th canto of Hell <note>The original text says the 20th canto, but this famous passage actually appears in Canto 19 of the *Inferno*.</note>, complains of it in this way:

> *Ah, Constantine, of how much ill was mothered,*
> *Not by your conversion, but by that dowry*
> *Which the first wealthy father took from you.*
<note>original: "Ah Constantino de quanto mal fu Madre / Non la tua conuersion, ma quella dote / Che da te prese il primo ricco padre."</note>

And John, a Doctor of Paris <note>Refers to Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a famous French scholar and Chancellor of the University of Paris who wrote extensively on Church reform.</note>, in his treatise on the power of the Pope, recounts that in the time of Boniface VIII, a certain cardinal of the Cistercian order said at the conclusion of his sermon that just as—and by the same degrees—the clergy rose to possess temporal wealth, they would likewise descend again to the poverty of Sylvester. And to prove his saying, he cited several authorities from Holy Scripture. Now (says Nicolas Bohier <note>A prominent 16th-century French jurist known for his legal commentaries.</note>), we see that this time has arrived; namely, that the patrimony and temporal property of the clergy is returning to the laity. Pierre de Ferrariis, a legal practitioner who lived more than 140 years ago, speaks of it in these terms: *Foolish are the emperors who, enticed by these clergymen, granted such things.* <note>original: "Fatui imperatores qui inescati ab istis ecclesiasticis talia concesserint."</note> And a little later, speaking of the Pope: *And truly, unless a good emperor intervenes, all things will devolve to the Church. But I hope that just as it was acquired, so also shall it one day be lost.* <note>original: "Et profecto nisi bonus prouideat imperator, omnia deuoluent in ecclesiam. Sed spero quemadmodum ille acquisiuit, ita & aliquando deperdet."</note> And elsewhere: *And thus it is necessary that shortly all the goods of the laity be subjected to the dominion of the clergy, unless a good emperor provides, who revokes the donation of Constantine, and makes a law that the status of all clergy [be returned] to the status of mendi—* <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "mendi-" likely refers to "mendicity" or "mendicancy," meaning a state of begging or apostolic poverty.</note>

## P O P E  S Y L V E S T E R .

CONSTANTINE the Great, son of Constantius and Helen, held the empire with Maxentius and Licinius for thirty years in total; he conquered and dispossessed them. Then, reigning alone, he received the faith of Jesus Christ and strove to advance it as much as he possibly could. He gave the city of Rome to Pope Sylvester and transferred the seat of Rome to Greece <note>This refers to the founding of Constantinople, often called the "New Rome," in the Greek-speaking East.</note>. Upon this, I will say by way of digression that undoubtedly the Church does not err; but since Sylvester, some pastors, having perverted the good order through their ambition, have not entered the sheepfold <note>A biblical metaphor for the Church community, based on John 10:1.</note> through the door, as they are not caring for their flock. So much so that since wealth entered the Church, avarice immediately took its place, and as the root of all evils, it has spoiled everything. The first popes were men of good character; thus, the Church of God flourished. Saint Peter, Linus, Cletus, Clement, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, and several others—most of whom were killed by persecutors for planting the Gospel and instructing the people in the faith of Jesus Christ, being by this means martyrs—were all people of good life and condition until Sylvester (Although there have been found after him...)

### *Paul & Anthony, or Saint Anthony the Egyptian abbot, the first hermits.*

# MEMORABLE STORY
### *of an encounter that Saint Anthony had in the desert.*

Saint Jerome <note>Sophronius Eusebius Hieronymus (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and writing the lives of early saints.</note>, in the life of Paul the first hermit which he described, recounts how Saint Anthony, traveling all alone through the deserts of Egypt seeking Paul, encountered a monster that had the face of a man, a hooked nose, two horns on its forehead, and from the navel downward was supported on two feet similar to those of a goat. The holy man, astonished by such a sight, arming himself with the shield of faith and the <term>breastplate</term><note>The original French uses "halecret," a type of light corselet or armor worn in the 16th century.</note> of hope, adjured it in the name of the Almighty to tell him who it was. The creature answered him: "I am a mortal man like you, and one of the inhabitants of this desert, whom the deluded <term>Gentiles</term><note>Refers to non-Christian pagans of antiquity.</note> and antiquity, deceived by vain error, once worshipped under the names of Fauns, Satyrs, and Incubi <note>In Roman mythology, Fauns and Satyrs were nature spirits; Incubi were traditionally seen as spirits or demons that haunted sleepers. Here, they are portrayed as physical creatures acknowledging the Christian God.</note>. I have been sent here on behalf of the whole troupe of my companions, so that you might pray to our common God for us, whom we have known to have formerly come for the salvation of the world, and whose fame is spread throughout all the earth." At these words, Saint Anthony abundantly watered his face with tears, which (as indicators of his heart) the greatness of his joy caused to flow from his eyes; for he rejoiced greatly in the glory of Jesus Christ and in the ruin of Satan. So much so that, marvelling at such words, he said, striking the ground with his staff: "Woe unto you, O Alexandria, who instead of God, worship monsters! Woe unto you, harlot city, where so many false gods flock! What is..."

## DIDYMUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Didymus the Blind, a scholar from Alexandria. He is depicted in profile with a beard and a hood. The Latin inscription "DIDYMVS ALEXAN." is printed along the inner circular border of the frame.</image-desc>

Didymus, having lost his sight to ophthalmia <note>A general historical term for severe inflammation of the eye.</note>, or (as Sabellicus <note>Marcus Antonius Coccius Sabellicus (1436–1506), a Venetian historian and scholar.</note> says) having been blind since his infancy, grew up and learned his first letters and elements so well by placing his fingers upon characters engraved in tablets and books, that through constant study he gained knowledge of geometry, dialectics, and mathematics: in which sciences he wrote of notable and rare things. He became a learned and distinguished theologian. He was the teacher of Saint Jerome. He wrote several books in Greek, including seven on the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Saint esprit." These were later translated into Latin as "De Spiritu Sancto."</note>, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, and two against the Arians <note>A Christological sect that held that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note>. He wrote commentaries on Job, Isaiah <note>original: "Esaye"</note>, Hosea <note>original: "Osee"</note>, Zechariah <note>original: "Zacharie"</note>, the Psalms, the Gospel of Saint Matthew, of Saint John, and the Catholic Epistles. # THEMISTIUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of a bearded man, identified as Themistius, wearing a flat cap and scholar's robes. The circular border contains the inscription: THEMISTIUS THE PHILOSOPHER.</image-desc>

Themistius Euphrades <note>His epithet "Euphrades" means "the eloquent." He was a statesman and philosopher who served several Roman emperors.</note>, of the Peripatetic sect <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle’s philosophy; the name comes from the Greek word for "walking" or "itinerant," as Aristotle often taught while walking.</note>, wrote several books in the Greek language, namely: *Paraphrases of Aristotle's Posterior Analytics*, *On Physics* <note>original: "De naturali auscultatione"</note>, *On the Soul*, *On Memory and Recollection*, *On Divination through Dreams*, *On Sleep and Waking*, and *On Dreams*. These Paraphrases were translated into Latin by Ermolao Barbaro <note>A renowned 15th-century Italian humanist and diplomat who sought to restore the original meaning of Aristotle's texts.</note>. Sozomen <note>A 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note> makes mention in the *Tripartite History* of a book by Themistius addressed to the Emperor Valens; and he who wrote *The Light of the Soul* <note>original: "Lumen animae," a popular 14th-century theological and scientific encyclopedia.</note> cites the *Summary of Natural Beings* by Themistius.

SIRICIUS, a Roman and Pope, held the seat for fourteen years <note>Pope Siricius reigned from 384 to 399 AD. He is known for being the first to issue decretals—formal rulings on church discipline.</note>.

## DIDYMUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of a bearded man wearing a scholar's hood or cap. Around the inner border of the circle, the Latin inscription reads: "DIDYMUS OF ALEXANDRIA."</image-desc>

Didymus, having lost his eyes to ophthalmia <note>A general historical term for severe inflammation of the eye or conjunctiva.</note>, or (as Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), an influential Venetian historian often cited in Renaissance biographies.</note> says) having been blind from his infancy, grew up and learned his first letters or elements so well—by placing his fingers on the characters engraved in tablets and books—that through constant study he gained knowledge of <term>geometry|The branch of mathematics dealing with points, lines, and shapes</term>, <term>dialectics|The art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions through logical argument</term>, and mathematics. In these sciences, he wrote of notable and rare things, and became a learned and distinguished theologian. He was the teacher of Saint Jerome. He wrote many books in Greek, including seven on the Holy Spirit (translated into Latin by Saint Jerome) and two against the Arians <note>A group in the early Church who followed the teachings of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being rather than co-eternal with God the Father.</note>. He wrote commentaries on Job, Isaiah, Hosea, Zechariah, the Psalms, the Gospels of Saint Matthew and Saint John, and the General Epistles. He is [described as] the Bishop of Alexandria <note>Historically, Didymus was the leader of the prestigious Catechetical School of Alexandria; the text's identification of him as "Bishop" may be a common period error or a loose use of the title.</note>. By the student, one can know the quality of the teacher's doctrine.

VALENTINIAN, VALENS his brother, and GRATIAN his son—who was learned and skilled in arms—held the empire for a total of 13 years.

## THEMISTIUS.

## BASIL.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut portrait of Saint Basil (Basilius) dressed in heavy monastic robes, standing with his right hand raised in a gesture of blessing. The oval border contains the inscription "BASILI ORDO". Stylized vegetation or small trees are depicted on either side of the figure within the frame.</image-desc>

<margin>380</margin>
Basil, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, established a monastic order in the East with a specific rule of life in the year of Jesus Christ 380. By this rule, he required those who wished to join his community to vow chastity and poverty after they had lived there for one year. He lived solitarily with his brothers in a monastery with great austerity of life, possessing no goods. He wrote the *Monastic Institutions* <note>original: "l'institution monachale," often referred to as the "Rules" of Saint Basil, which remain foundational for Eastern Orthodox monasticism.</note>, translated by Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and scholar who translated many Greek theological works into Latin for Western audiences.</note>, and the rest of his works were translated by Raphael Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a Renaissance humanist from Volterra noted for his encyclopedic writings.</note> or by Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius (1500–1558), a German humanist and physician who translated many ancient Greek medical and theological texts.</note>.

## SAINT AUGUSTINE.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of a bearded man with a miter, representing Saint Augustine. The circular border contains the Latin inscription: "Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo." <note>original: "D. AVGVSTINVS EPS HIPPONENSIS."</note></image-desc>

AUGUSTINE, a native of Carthage or (according to some) Tagaste in Africa, was converted to the faith and baptized by Saint Ambrose in the year 389. He first proclaimed the faith of Jesus Christ at Hippo, a city now called Bone <note>Known today as Annaba, Algeria.</note>, where he was bishop. He was a great friend of Saint Jerome, as can be seen through their letters. *“At all times indeed (Saint Jerome writes to Saint Augustine) I have revered your blessedness with the honor that is fitting; and I have loved the Lord the Savior dwelling in you, etc.”* <note>original: "Omni quidem tempore... beatitudinem tuam eo quo decet honore veneratus sum: & habitantem in te dilexi dominum saluatorem, &c."</note> and in the signature: *“To the holy and most blessed Lord Augustine, Jerome.”* <note>original: "Domino sancto ac beatissimo Augustino Hieronimus."</note> Saint Augustine, for his part, acknowledges the great doctrine of Saint Jerome, writing to him thus: *“I have asked and I ask our God, brother Jerome, that he would grant that this which I write to you, consulting you on these things of which I am ignorant, be fruitful for us. Since—”* <note>original: "Deum nostrum rogaui & rogo, frater Hieronime, vt hoc quod ad te scribo, consules te de his quæ nescio, fructuosum esse nobis velit. Quan-"</note>

# ARCADIUS.

<image-desc>An oval engraved portrait of the Byzantine Emperor Arcadius. He is depicted in royal robes, wearing a crown, holding a globus cruciger <note>A cross-topped orb representing worldwide Christian dominion.</note> in his right hand and a long scepter in his left. The inscription "ARCADIVS IMPERATOR" <note>Emperor Arcadius</note> runs along the upper curve of the oval. In the background, there are architectural structures representing a city with towers and domes.</image-desc>

ARCADIUS & HONORIUS, brothers and sons <note>original: "f", abbreviation for "fils"</note> of the Emperor Theodosius, reigned 31 years. These two are often mentioned in the *Digests* <note>The *Digest* is a major part of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the body of Roman law compiled under Justinian.</note>, where they are called *Divine brothers* <note>original: "Diui fratres"</note>. Arcadius governed in the West, and Honorius in the East <note>The author has reversed their historical roles: Arcadius ruled the Eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople, while Honorius ruled the Western Roman Empire from Milan and later Ravenna.</note>. At his death, their father had appointed guardians for them: Rufinus for Arcadius, and Stilicho for Honorius. It was at this time that the Franks, leaving their country called Franconia, in a part of Germany, crossed the Rhine, staying at Trier and the surrounding areas for about three years. During this time, Stilicho—intending during the troubles to seize the Roman Empire from Honorius in order to join it to his own house and invest <note>To formally give a title or rank to someone.</note> his son with it—incited without cause the Vandals, Alans, Suebi, and Burgundians to come and destroy the land of the Gauls.

but in the end, he and his son Eucherius, considered enemies of Honorius, were killed. Rufinus, on the other hand, being ambitious, sent word to Alaric, King of the Goths, with presents of gold and silver, that he should come to wage war against Arcadius, in the hope that fear would cause this young prince to abandon the empire, which he would then seize for himself. But as God does not permit such woven wickedness and treason to come to fruition against those he has chosen to rule, the secret enterprises of Rufinus were discovered; the soldiers cut off his head and his right hand (his designs having been frustrated) and carried them to Constantinople. This is a fine example and history for the present time, of how God by his grace has so well preserved our King Charles <note>Referring to Charles IX of France (reigned 1560–1574), who faced multiple civil wars during the French Wars of Religion.</note>, so that amidst so many affairs and troubles that have surrounded him from all parts of his kingdom during his youth, he has triumphed four times, remaining victorious over his enemies. The greatest argument for this is that he loves God, for which reason God loves him. Arcadius, likewise, was so burning with honor for God and devoted to the holy faith that he was the first to have the sign of the cross engraved on one side of the coinage, in memory of the passion of Jesus Christ our Savior, and to keep it regularly before one's eyes; because of this, currency has always been marked with a cross from then until the present. God also held him in his protection, making him reign fortunately.

## ARCADIUS.

<image-desc>A circular portrait engraving of Emperor Arcadius. He is depicted standing, wearing a crown and a fur-lined mantle over his shoulders, and holding a scepter in his right hand. In the background are two fortified cities with towers and domes. Above him, an inscription within the circle reads: "ARCADIVS IMPERATOR."</image-desc>

ARCADIUS and HONORIUS, brothers and sons of the emperor Theodosius, reigned for 31 years. Mention of them is often made in the Digests <note>The *Digest*, a massive collection of legal opinions from Roman jurists compiled under the Emperor Justinian.</note>, where they are called the *Divine Brothers* <note>original: "Diui fratres"</note>. Arcadius governed in the West, and Honorius in the East <note>The author here reverses their historical roles; Arcadius ruled the Eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople, while Honorius ruled the Western Roman Empire.</note>. 

Their father, at the time of his death, had appointed guardians for them: Rufinus for Arcadius, and Stilicho for Honorius. It was during this time that the Franks <note>original: "François"</note>, abandoning their country called Franconia in a part of Germany, crossed the Rhine, staying at Trier and the surrounding areas for about three years. At that same time Stilicho—who intended, amidst the troubles, to seize the Roman Empire from Honorius in order to join it to his own house and invest his son with it—incited without any provocation the Vandals, Alans, Sueves, and Burgundians to come and destroy the lands of the Gauls.

# PROSOPOGRAPHY,

### ->KINGS OF FRANCE.<-

**PHARAMOND** succeeds Marcomir, Duke of the Franks, his father: he is the first King of France, and the author of the **Salic Law** <note>The ancient civil law code of the Salian Franks; in later centuries, it became famous for its rule excluding women from inheriting the throne.</note>. He reigns along the Rhine for 11 years.

**Visigoths** (Western Goths) and **Ostrogoths** (Eastern Goths). Some Visigoths are called **Balthi** <note>original: "Balthi"</note> for their prowess, while others are called **Amali** after Amalus, a great king and warlord.

**CELESTINE**, a native of Campania, Pope, adds the **Gradual** and the **Offertory** to the Mass. He sends **Patrick** to the Scots <note>In the 5th century, the term "Scoti" primarily referred to the Gaelic people of Ireland.</note> who had received the faith of Jesus Christ. He holds the seat for 9 years, 10 months, and 9 days.

The **Council of Ephesus** <note>Held in 431 AD, this ecumenical council focused on the nature of Christ.</note> is held against the heresy of **Nestorius**, Bishop of Constantinople.

**John of Damascus** <note>Also known as John Damascene. Though listed here in the 5th-century timeline, he actually lived much later, in the 7th and 8th centuries; the author of this manuscript has placed him out of chronological order.</note>.

# PROSPER.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait medallion of Prosper of Reggio in profile, facing right, wearing ecclesiastical robes. The circular border is inscribed with the text: PROSPER BISHOP OF REGGIO.</image-desc>

**PROSPER**, Bishop of Reggio <note>Specifically Reggio Calabria, located at the southern tip of the Italian "boot." Historical accounts often conflate Prosper of Aquitaine, the theologian, with the Saint Prosper who was Bishop of Reggio Emilia.</note>, formerly a great city near Sicily, at one of the extremities of Calabria—distinct from the Reggio near Parma <note>Reggio Emilia</note>—and a native of the province of Aquitaine, succeeded to the bishopric after Faventius. He was a fine poet and orator. He wrote in Latin:
*On the Contemplative Life* <note>original: "De vita contemplatiua"; this work is now often attributed to Julianus Pomerius.</note>.
*On Free Will* <note>original: "De libero arbitrio."</note>.
*Answers to the Chapters of the Gauls* <note>original: "Ad capitula Gallorum responsiones."</note>.
*To the Objections of the Vincentians* <note>original: "Ad obiecta Vincentianorum"; a defense against the criticisms of Vincent of Lérins regarding the theology of Saint Augustine.</note>.
*To the Extracts of the Genoese* <note>original: "Ad excerpta Genuensium."</note>.
*Against Cassian, on Free Will* <note>original: "Contra Cassianum, de libero arbitrio"; a polemic against John Cassian.</note>.
*Chronicle of Histories* <note>original: "Chronicon historiarum."</note>.
*On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "De illustribus viris."</note>.
*On the Providence of God* <note>original: "De prouidentia Dei."</note>.
*On the Captivity of Rome* <note>original: "De captiuitate Romæ."</note>.
*A Great Summary of 330 Propositions* <note>original: "Summam grandem 330. propositionum."</note>.
*Letters to Various People* <note>original: "Epistol. ad diuersos."</note>.
*Epigrams* <note>original: "Epigrammata."</note>.
*Poem on the Ungrateful* <note>original: "De ingratis poëma"; his most famous work, defending Augustinian grace against those he deemed "ungrateful" for God's gift.</note>.
All of which were printed in Lyon by Gryphius <note>Sebastian Gryphius (c. 1492–1556), a highly influential German bookseller and printer who worked in Lyon and specialized in humanist and classical texts.</note>.

**CLODION THE HAIRY**, son of Pharamond, and second king of France, ordained that the Franks should wear long hair as a sign of their liberty <note>This tradition gave rise to the term "the long-haired kings" (reges criniti), a distinctive mark of the Merovingian dynasty.</note>. **Suthphard**, king of the Huns <note>The text uses "Hunnois ou Hongres" (Huns or Hungarians), reflecting a common early modern belief that these groups were the same.</note>, made war against the Burgundians, who, having been baptized, were victorious.

**Genseric**, king of the Vandals.

He held the seat for 21 years, 1 month, and 29 days.

<margin>450</margin> **MEROVECH**, king of France, succeeded Clodion. With the help of Aetius, the vice-emperor or lieutenant of the Emperor Valentinian, he overcame Attila, king of the Huns, at that cruel battle fought on the Catalaunian Plains, in which two hundred thousand men died between the two sides. He reigned for 10 years.

...by fire and blood into extreme ruin: sacking, after **Padua**, **Vicenza**, **Verona**, **Brescia**, **Bergamo**, **Milan**, and **Pavia**, not without a great slaughter of people. So much so that in a battle he fought against **Theodoric**, king of the Visigoths, and **Aetius**, a small stream swelled so greatly with blood that dead bodies floated upon it. Not to be omitted here is a miracle: as he arrived at **Modena** with his army, **Geminian**, bishop of the place <note>St. Geminianus, the patron saint of Modena.</note>, trusting in the help of God, came before him and asked him who he was. "I am," Attila replied, "the Scourge of God." And I," Geminian replied, "am the servant of God." And after these words, he had the gates opened for him. At this, Attila, terrified and fearing the wrath of God, passed through the city without doing any harm or damage whatsoever. Deliberating on going to Rome, **Pope Leo** came to humble himself before him and obtained from this cruel tyrant (not without a great miracle) that he leave Italy and return to **Hungary**, where he led **Honoria**, sister of the Emperor **Valentinian**, whom the said Emperor had been constrained to give to him in marriage. He died at a feast from a flow of blood coming out of his nose. Thus, he who was so covetous of human blood, having caused it to be shed abundantly in the places where he passed, was suffocated by losing all of his own. See **Paul the Deacon** <note>An 8th-century historian whose *History of the Lombards* is a primary source for this period.</note>.

After the demolition of so many cities in Italy by Attila, **Venice** was built, which would eventually surpass Rome.

**Aurelius**, father of **Arthur**, king of Britain <note>The text uses "Bretaigne," which in this context refers to Great Britain.</note>, along with his brother **Uther Pendragon**, brothers of the King of England, besieged **Vortigern** (who had seized the kingdom) in a tower, where he was burned along with his people.

**Merlin** the great enchanter, born (if it is permissible to believe the historian Antoninus) of an **Incubus demon** <note>In medieval folklore, an incubus was a demon in male form that sought to father children with human women; Merlin's magical powers were often attributed to this supernatural parentage.</note>.

<header>FOURTH BOOK</header>

MARCIAN holds the empire in the East, or at Constantinople, for 7 years, while Valentinian is at Rome. He assembles the Council of Chalcedon <note>The Fourth Ecumenical Council, held in 451 AD, which defined the dual nature of Christ.</note> against the heretics Dioscorus and Eutyches, at the command of Pope Leo. Marcian is present at this fourth synodal assembly against Eutyches, where he says:

> We wish to be present at the synod for the purpose of confirming the faith, not to display power, following the example of the most religious prince Constantine; so that once the truth is discovered, the multitude, drawn away by wicked doctrines, may no longer be in discord: judging it more fitting that its articles be firmly established by the synod according to the rules, rather than being decreed by our own law. <note>Original Latin: "Nos ad fidem confirmandã, non ad potentiam oftendendam, exemplo religiofisfimi principis Conftantini, fynodo intereffe volumus : vt inuenta veritate, non vltra multitudo prauis doctrinis attracta, difcordet: decorum iudicantes capitula eius regulariter potius firmari per fynodum, quàm noftra lege fanciri."</note>

Words worthy of a Christian prince.

Germain, bishop of Auxerre, and Severus, bishop of Trier, are sent to England to strike down the Pelagian heresy <note>A theological doctrine that denied original sin and emphasized human free will over divine grace.</note>.

Theodoret the Syrian writes against Eutyches, and ten books of ecclesiastical history.

Anianus, Lupus, and Nicasius, bishops <note>Aignan of Orléans, Lupus of Troyes, and Nicasius of Reims, notable 5th-century Gallic saints.</note>.

Genevieve, virgin <note>The patron saint of Paris, credited with saving the city from Attila's Huns through prayer.</note>.

The eleven thousand virgins <note>The legendary companions of Saint Ursula, martyred by the Huns.</note>.

<margin>460</margin>
CHILDERIC, son of Merovech, is driven from the kingdom for his debauchery; later he recovers it and reigns for 26 years. He fights a battle near Orléans against Odoacer, king of the Saxons.

After Emperor Valentinian in the West, or at Rome, Avitus the senator rules for 4 years, then Severian, and after him ANTHEMIUS.

<margin>461</margin>
LEON, the first of the Greeks, holds the empire in Constantinople for 17 years.

<margin>465</margin>
HILARY, of Sardinia, pope, holds the see for 6 years, 2 months, and 10 days.

The Visigoths, together with Spain, occupy Aquitaine.

SIMPLICIUS, a native of Tivoli, becomes Pope and holds the see for 18 years, 1 month, and 8 days. <note>Pope Simplicius (reigned 468–483) oversaw the church during the final collapse of the Western Roman Empire.</note>

Arthur, King of Britain, has his knights sit with him at a round table during his meals, so that no envy might arise among them regarding a first or last place or rank, as if he considered them all equals and companions. <note>The author includes the legendary King Arthur alongside historical figures, reflecting the medieval tradition that treated Arthurian romance as genuine British history.</note>

<margin>478</margin>
ZENO the Isaurian, Emperor of Constantinople, is buried alive by his wife Ariadne. He holds the empire for 17 years. <note>Zeno was an Eastern Roman Emperor. The story of his being buried alive while unconscious—and his wife refusing to open the tomb—was a popular historical anecdote of the time.</note>

After Anthemius Caesar at Rome, Libius Severus succeeded, and after him, Glycerius; following him was his nephew <note>Likely referring to Julius Nepos, who was Glycerius’s successor, though the familial relationship was more complex than "nephew."</note>, who was driven out by force. In his place came Augustulus, under whom the Empire of Rome was seized by Odoacer, and much later transported to France. <note>Romulus Augustulus is traditionally considered the last Western Roman Emperor. The "transport to France" refers to the *Translatio Imperii*, the political theory that the authority of the Roman Emperors eventually passed to Charlemagne and the French monarchy.</note>

# FULGENTIUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut medallion featuring a portrait of Saint Fulgentius. The cleric is shown in a three-quarter view, tonsured and wearing a hooded ecclesiastical garment. **FULGENTIUS** Placiades <note>Known to history as Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe (c. 467–533 AD). The name "Placiades" likely refers to his full name, Fabius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius.</note>, a native of Telepte <note>A city in the Roman province of Africa, in modern-day Tunisia.</note> and a man of great learning, descended from the noble lineage of Carthaginian Senators, was the bishop of Ruspe, a city in Africa. He was sent into exile in Sardinia along with 120 other bishops by Thrasamund, King of the Vandals <note>The Vandals, who ruled North Africa at the time, were Arian Christians. Thrasamund persecuted the Nicene (Catholic) clergy, frequently exiling bishops who opposed his theological views.</note>. He wrote several good and learned books, which are:

*On the Grace of God and Free Will, 7 books.* <note>original: "De gratia Dei & libero arbitrio"</note>

*On the Remission of Sins, 2 [books].* <note>original: "De remifsione peccatorum"</note>
*Dispute with King Thrasamund, 1 [book].* <note>original: "Altercat. cum Trasemundo rege"</note>
*Rule for a True Life, 1 [book].* <note>original: "Regul. veræ vitæ"</note>
*On Marital Continence, 1 [book].* <note>original: "De continentia coniugali"</note>
*On Virginity, dedicated to Proba, 1 [book].* <note>original: "De Virginitate ad Probam"</note>
*On Charity, 1 [book].* <note>original: "De charitate"</note>
*On Penance, 1 [book].* <note>original: "De penitentia"</note>
*On Faith, dedicated to Donatus, 1 [book].* <note>original: "De fide ad Donatum"</note>
*On the Mystery of the Mediator, 3 [books].* <note>original: "De misterio mediatoris"; this refers to Christ as the mediator between God and humanity.</note>
*Letters to Various People.* <note>original: "Epistol. ad diuersos"</note>
*On Predestination, 3 [books].* <note>original: "De predestinatione"</note>

**SYMMACHUS**, of Sardinia, was elected pope after Anastasius. He ordered the singing of *Glory to God in the highest* <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis Deo"</note> on Sundays and feast days, which Telesphorus <note>An early 2nd-century pope traditionally credited with introducing the Gloria into the liturgy.</note> had first established to be said on Christmas day only. A schism occurred in the church through which several murders took place, not only of the laity, but of the clergy; for while Symmachus had been created pope in the church of Saint John Lateran, another called Lawrence <note>Laurentius (died c. 507), an archpriest supported by a pro-Byzantine faction.</note> was likewise elected pope, or antipope, in the church of Saint Mary Major, by which the people were divided. Some senators favored Symmachus, others inclined toward Lawrence: but after having debated enough, they consented and resolved to send to Ravenna to see Theodoric, King of the Goths—distinct from the one mentioned previously <note>Theodoric the Great (reigned 493–526), the Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy from Ravenna.</note>—then reigning in Italy, to give his judgment.
