## BOETHIUS

<image-desc>An oval engraved portrait of the philosopher Boethius. He is depicted as an older man with a beard, wearing a distinctive head covering (turban or chaperon), seated and looking down while holding a stylus or pen and a book. Several other books are scattered on the floor around him and on a shelf behind him. The oval border is inscribed with the Latin text: BOETHIVS MANLIVS SEVERINVS PH. OR. PO. <note>The abbreviation stands for "Philosopher, Orator, Poet."</note></image-desc>

Boethius, ordinary consul of Rome, an excellent philosopher, orator, and poet, a Catholic, subtle and quick-witted, was an intimate friend of Saint Benedict, so much so that he frequently dined with him at Monte Cassino. Theodoric, King of the Goths, had him strangled at Pavia. Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and scholar famous for his works on history and bibliography.</note> says otherwise: that by the command of Theodoric his throat was cut in the prison at Ravenna; and after his death, he was placed in the catalog of Saints under the name of Severinus. His works include:

*On the Holy Trinity* <note>original: "De sancta Trinitate"</note>
*On the Unity of the Trinity* <note>original: "De vnitate Trinitatis"</note>
*On the Two Natures in Christ* <note>original: "De duabus naturis in Christo"</note>
*On the Faith* <note>original: "De fide"</note>
*On Unity and the One* <note>original: "De vnitate & vno"</note>
*On the Introduction of Porphyry* <note>original: "De Isagogis Porphirij." This refers to Boethius's commentary on the "Isagoge," a standard medieval textbook on logic.</note>

## ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'B' featuring a figure, possibly a cherub or saint, amidst floral or garden-like patterns.</image-desc>
BENEDICT, abbot, native of Nursia <note>modern Norcia, Italy</note>, an ancient city of the Sabines in the Duchy of Spoleto, prince and founder of the monks in the West, was a man of good conduct and holy life. From his order, many learned and saintly figures have emerged: of whom there have been 18 popes, two hundred cardinals, sixteen hundred archbishops, four thousand bishops, fifteen thousand and seventy abbots—flourishing through their doctrine and writings—and fifteen thousand six hundred who have been canonized or entered into the catalog of saints. Likewise, the Rule of Saint Benedict, contained in 73 chapters, so strict and severe that it could not be more so, was inviolably kept

I will recite the verses that d'Espence <note>Claude d'Espence (1511–1571), a French theologian and scholar who wrote about Church reform.</note> wrote regarding the difference between the monks of the past and those of the present in a poem of his titled *Godo*.

> *Then monasticism was heaven; the wilderness was paradise:* <note>original Latin: "Tunc cælum monachiſmus erat: paradiſus, heremus."</note>
> *A place of hospitality for the liberal arts, for languages, for good*
> *Manners, and a most pleasing station for the sacred Muses.*
> *Not yet in those times were there lazy brothers*
> *With bellies protruding a foot and a half, or living in idleness.* <note>original: "Sexquipede extabant, vel agebant otia ventres." A satirical reference to the girth of overfed monks.</note>
> *None yet, under the appearance of righteousness and the shadow of virtue,*
> *Or by prayers offered without the mind, or by a muffled murmur,*
> *Devoured the wealth of the poor commoners, widows, and children.*
> *The idle drone did not yet sit full at the manger,*
> *Nor did any sleep by the cup, or snore loudly,*
> *Or vomit: the river and the grain were enough for the monk.* <note>original: "Fluuiúſque Ceréſque." Ceres was the goddess of agriculture, here symbolizing bread.</note>
> *Scarcely anything else than to taste the juice of Bacchus* <note>original: "laticem Lyæum." Lyaeus is a title for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note>
> *On rare occasions, or to eat but little meat from the fields.*

**JUSTIN**, a swineherd in Thrace who later became emperor, held the empire—which he had acquired by fraud—for 7 years. He appointed Justinian, who was his nephew, as his successor.

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>575</margin> **JUSTINIAN II** <note>The text refers to him as Justinian, but the dates and the 12-year reign identify him as Justin II, the nephew and successor of Justinian the Great</note> is crowned emperor by his grandfather; he falls into the Pelagian heresy and dies from an ailment of the feet <note>original: "douleur des pieds"</note>, having held the empire for 12 years.

**SOPHIA**, wife of Justin.

**CHARIBERT** <note>original: "Cherebert"</note>, otherwise known as Aribert, a slave to women and abandoned to his pleasures, holds the kingdom of France <note>The Merovingian realm of the Franks</note> with his brothers for 9 years.

<margin>574</margin> **CHILPERIC**, son of Clothar, strangles Galswintha his wife, daughter of the King of Spain, and marries Fredegund, who makes him impose several unaccustomed taxes upon the people. He is killed by the command of the aforementioned Fredegund, an adulteress, having been King of France for 14 years.

<margin>577</margin> **TIBERIUS II CONSTANTINE**, a charitable and God-loving emperor, makes peace with the Lombards who had long held Rome. He holds the empire in Constantinople for 7 years.

**JOHN**, first patriarch of Constantinople <note>Likely referring to John III Scholasticus</note>.

**BENEDICT I**, a Roman, Pope, holds the see for 4 years.

<margin>581</margin> **PELAGIUS II**, a Roman, succeeds him and holds the see for 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days.

The Goths dwelling in Spain abandon the Arian heresy <note>A theological belief that Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father, declared heretical by the early Church</note> and return to the faith.

<margin>584</margin> **MAURICE**, a Cappadocian, once a simple notary, then a captain of the guard, later son-in-law to Tiberius, and finally successor to the empire; he drives the Huns out of their lands into the deserts, along with the Scythians of Moesia and the Lombards; he is killed with all his lineage by Phocas, governor of Scythia, having held the empire for 20 years and lived for 63.

The Tiber River, having overflowed, knocks down several houses in Rome and rises as high as the city walls.

# GREGORY.

<image-desc>A circular medallion portrait of Pope Gregory the Great in profile, facing right. He is depicted as tonsured and wearing clerical vestments. The Latin inscription around the border reads: "The Lord Gregory, 62nd Roman Pontiff."</image-desc>

<margin>591</margin>
GREGORY, son of Gordian and Silvia <note>The OCR reads "Suie," a truncation of Silvia, his mother</note>, noble Roman citizens, reached in his youth the height of philosophy through frequent study. And although he was of very noble lineage and had very wealthy parents, he nevertheless <note>original: "voulut po[urtant]"</note> wanted to separate himself from the world and leave all his goods behind to <note>original: "p[our]"</note> enter a religious life. After the death of his father, he had <note>original: "f[it]"</note> six monasteries built in Sicily; and setting aside his garments <note>original: "veſtem[ents]"</note> enriched with gold, pearls, and precious stones, he took up a simple and [humble] monastic habit. And when Pelagius had died of the plague <note>original: "pe[ste]"</note>, being elected pope by the voice of the clergy and of all the people <note>original: "p[eu]ple"</note>, with the consent of the Emperor Maurice—although he <note>original: "q[u’il]"</note> did not wish to take such a burden, considering it too great <note>original: "gran[de]"</note> in respect to his capacity—he accepted it against his will, through the continual urging of everyone. He augmented the Mass with several ceremonies, such as singing the "Lord have mercy" <note>original: "kirye eleyſon," the Greek prayer used in the Latin rite</note> nine times <note>original: "fo[is]"</note> and the *Alleluia*, except during Lent; [ordered] to say in the Canon of the Mass: *And dispose our days in your peace,* etc. <note>original: "Diéſque nostros in tua pace diſponas," a line Gregory famously added to the 'Hanc Igitur' prayer</note>; and to recite...

# PROSOPOGRAPHY

### [LEO III]
[The Emperor Leo III] images, because he has the images of the churches torn down and burned, in favor of two Jews: he holds the empire in Constantinople for 25 years. <note>Leo III "the Isaurian" (r. 717–741) initiated the First Iconoclasm, the systematic destruction of religious icons.</note>

The Saracens keep Constantinople besieged for three years under the leadership of Maslama <note>original: "Masgalde," likely Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik</note>. Three hundred thousand citizens die within the city from famine and plague.

**CLOTAIRE IV**, uncle of Dagobert II <note>Historically the son or relative of Theuderic III; "Dagobert II" here refers to the previous page's Dagobert III</note>, crowned king by **Charles Martel**, who had defeated Chilperic, who was supported by Eudes, Duke of Guyenne <note>Aquitaine</note>. He reigns for 2 years, having only the name of king, under the authority of Martel. <note>Clotaire IV was a "puppet king" installed by Martel to legitimize his own power as Mayor of the Palace.</note>

**CHILPERIC II**, second after the death of Clotaire, is summoned by **Charles Martel** to come from Gascony to France. Eudes, Duke of Aquitaine, sends him back with part of the treasures of France: he is established as king by the aforementioned Martel, always under his authority, and reigns for 5 years.

<margin>726</margin> **URSO HYPATO**, Duke of Venice, hardens the youth and increases the number of soldiers. He is killed by the people as the author of the war of the Heracleans with the Equilians, after having governed for eleven years. <note>Urso was the third Doge of Venice; his reign ended in a violent civil conflict between rival city factions.</note>

<margin>726</margin> **THEUDERIC IV** <note>original: "Theodoric, second"</note>, nicknamed "Cala" <note>likely referring to the Abbey of Chelles where he was raised</note>, made King of France through the means of **Charles Martel**, Mayor of the Palace, a powerful knight, leader and governor of France, who overcomes 400,000 Saracens, and defeats 370,000 of them near Tours, losing only 1,500 of his own men: who also conquers from Gerard of Roussillon, Count of Burgundy, the cities of Marseille, Arles, and all of Provence, Nîmes, Béziers, and Montpellier, which belonged to the said County. <note>This entry combines the Battle of Tours (732) with Martel's later campaigns to consolidate southern France.</note>

Domenico Leone succeeds Urso Hypato in the Duchy of Venice: Felice Cornicula, Julianus Hypatus, Diodato Ipato <note>original: "Zian Britiat"</note>, Dukes of Venice. <note>These figures were "Magistri Militum" (Masters of the Soldiers) who ruled Venice during a five-year interregnum following Urso's murder.</note>

**CHARLEMAGNE**, or Charles the Great, having remained King of France for 32 years, is elected Emperor of Rome. He has five councils assembled in France: at Mainz, Reims, Tours, Châlons, and Arles. # CARDINALS.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration depicting a Cardinal in his traditional robes and broad-brimmed hat, standing in a landscape with a building in the background. The name of the Cardinals takes its origin from the plural Latin word *Cardines* <note>original: "Cardines"</note>, which means the hinges of a door, which support it, close it, and make it turn; for by the counsel and authority of the cardinal—that is to say, the principal—priests, all of <term>Christendom</term> <note>original: "Crestienté"</note> seems to be supported. Because of this, the following phrase and manner of speaking is used in the Latin language: *The matter turns on this hinge* <note>original: "In eo rei cardine vertitur"</note>, to mean "Everything depends on that," or, "The whole matter proceeds from there." And although the word "cardinal" was not used in ancient times, there are nonetheless good and sufficient reasons why these great pillars of the church have been so named. # CARDINALS.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration depicting a Cardinal in ecclesiastical robes and a broad-brimmed hat, holding a book, set against a landscape with a fortified castle in the background. The oval border contains the Latin inscription: CARDINALIS A CARDINE DICTVS <note>original: "CARDINALIS A CARDINE DICTVS," meaning "A Cardinal is so named from a hinge."</note>.</image-desc>

The name of the **Cardinals** took its origin from the plural *Cardines* in Latin, that is to say, the hinges of a door, which support it, close it, and make it turn: for by the counsel and authority of the <term>cardinal priests</term> <note>At this time, "cardinal" was both a title and an adjective meaning "principal" or "pivotal."</note>, that is to say, the principal ones, all of **Christendom** seems to be supported. Whence in the Latin language this following phrase and manner of speaking is in use: *In eo rei cardine vertitur* <note>original: "In eo rei cardine vertitur," meaning "It turns on that hinge of the matter."</note>, to say, "The whole thing depends on that," or, "The entire matter proceeds from there." And although the word "cardinal" was not used in ancient times, nevertheless there are good and sufficient reasons why these great columns of the church have been so named. In the first place, **Gregory the Great** in his epistles, speaking often of bishops, calls "cardinal priests" those who are greater and excel—

excel over the others.

**André Barbatias** <note>Andrea Barbazza (c. 1410–1479), a famous Sicilian doctor of canon and civil law.</note>, to please the prudent and learned **Cardinal Bessarion** <note>Basilios Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and Catholic cardinal who was a key figure in the Renaissance revival of Greek letters.</note>, composed a short commentary on this subject, alleging at its beginning that which is written in the first book of Kings <note>Known in modern Bibles as 1 Samuel 2:8.</note>, chapter two: *For the pillars of the earth belong to the Lord, and he has set the world upon them* <note>original: "Domini enim sunt cardines terræ: & posuit super eos orbem." The Latin "cardines" means both "pillars" and "hinges."</note>. Which passage the doctor **Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Susa (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canonist known as "Hostiensis" because he was the Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia.</note> has interpreted to symbolize our cardinals, saying: "Just as the door is governed by the hinge, so the Roman Church is guided by the counsel of the cardinals." See for a moment the ridiculous dispute of **Barbatias** in his treatise, as if this text alleged by him did not refer just as well to the bishops and priests inferior to these, who in worldly dominion and grandeur have governed the Church with the Bishop of Rome for more than a thousand years before this title of "Cardinal"—along with the <term>red hat</term> <note>The *galero*, a broad-brimmed red hat with tassels, which became the distinctive symbol of a cardinal's rank.</note> so renowned and held in such high esteem—was even known. The saying of **Guido the Archdeacon** <note>Guido de Baysio (c. 1250–1313), an influential canon lawyer.</note> should be more pertinent. In the past (he says), in each church the principal priests—such as the <term>curates</term>, the bishops, or others having the charge of souls—were called "cardinals," which is to say, "first" or "principal." And to provide a reason for his claim, he alleges a text from **Deuteronomy** concerning the Levite priests. This name of "cardinal," therefore, was in use before this current institution, but not in such a fashion; and it was not given to such men as those who possess it today with their riches, pomp, and ostentation. **Gregory the Great** bears witness to what its status was in several places in his writings. In the first book of his epistles, he writes thus to the company and assembly of priests on the island of **Corsica**: *For this reason, since the church of Aleria and Sagona has long been destitute of the help of a priest, we have deemed it necessary to [send] Martin...* <note>original: "Ea de re quoniam ecclesia Alariensis Sagonensis, sacerdotis diu est auxilio destituta, necessarium duximus Martinum..." This refers to a letter where Gregory appoints a "cardinal" priest to a vacant see, using the term in its original sense of being "incardinated" or permanently assigned to a church.</note>

Now, **Boniface III** <note>Pope in 607 AD.</note> having obtained from the **Emperor Phocas** <note>Byzantine Emperor (r. 602–610) who recognized the primacy of the Roman See.</note> that the Pope of Rome should be the head of all other churches and should hold preeminence forever, his successors—authorized and obeyed without controversy more than before—to further bolster their authority, raised in dignity the priests of Rome who were closest and nearest to them, giving them this title of **Cardinals**. And little by little through favor, having regard for wealth or pleasure rather than merit, they increased their number, so much so that the other principal priests (poor though they may be) who still retained the name of cardinal, such as those of **Ravenna** and **Compostela**, have become ridiculous and subjects of mockery to those other "great lords," no less than a man who takes the name of the **King of Yvetot** <note>A French proverbial reference to a minor lord whose "kingdom" was a tiny, tax-exempt seigneury; used here to mock titles without power.</note>, even though it is a tiny kingdom. 

Now, I remember having read in **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), one of the most influential jurists of the Middle Ages.</note> on the law *additos*, at the end of the **Code** <note>The Code of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law.</note> under the title of *appeals*, that the Cardinals have this privilege among others: that if they encounter someone being led to be hanged or executed by some other form of punishment, such a person is delivered from death by this encounter alone.

### ORDER OF THE CARTHUSIANS

<image-desc>An oval woodcut emblem depicting a Carthusian monk standing in a landscape. At the time when Bruno, a native of Cologne and a man excellent in doctrine, was a professor of theology in Paris, it happened that a canon who was a friend of his passed away. Those of this religious order are dressed in a **hair shirt** <note>A garment made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a form of bodily penance.</note>, a large black cloak, and a white robe underneath it, with a hood or **cowl** <note>original: "quoqueluchon," a pointed hood.</note> pointed at the top of the head. They never eat meat. They eat without company, except on certain feast days when they dine together. None of them is permitted to leave their monastery, except for the **procurator** <note>The monk responsible for the monastery's external business and supplies.</note> alone. They maintain perpetual silence except when praying, saying their hours, and performing divine service; and they do not speak to one another at all. Women are forbidden from entering their church; for it is recorded that Hugh, prior of the Chartreuse after Bruno, did not see a woman for 50 years, and did not wish to see one for the remainder of his life.

A man who constantly gazes at the faces of women remains in chastity just as straw remains in fire. <note>original Latin: "Sic manet in castitate homo facie intuens assidue mulierũ, sicut manet palea stans in igne."</note>

Man and woman are the fire and the straw. There is no safety in sleeping near a serpent. Perhaps it will not bite; yet it is also possible it will bite. In this so great a battle between the flesh and the spirit, no one can be victorious unless he flees; no one else shall bring back a total victory, except he who runs away. And this combat cannot be sustained except through abstinence, fasting, and by force of keeping watch. *Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation,* says our Savior. But where must one flee? To the deserts, to solitary places? O happy solitude, in which are born those stones from which the city of the great king is built in the **Book of Revelation** <note>original: "Apocalypfe"; the final book of the New Testament, describing the New Jerusalem.</note>.

<header>BOOK FOUR.</header>

## CALIXTUS II
A Burgundian, having been created Pope in France upon the death of Gelasius, comes to Rome to contest the position against the antipope Gregory <note>Gregory VIII, who was supported by the Emperor</note>. Once captured, Gregory is mounted upon a donkey facing backward <note>a traditional medieval ritual of public humiliation</note>; and Calixtus, gaining the friendship and favor of the Emperor Henry, secures the see to the great shame of Gregory, and holds it for 6 years.

The kingdoms of Portugal, Naples, and Sicily begin.

Ordelaffo Falier, Doge of Venice, travels to Syria with Godfrey of Bouillon. He dies in Dalmatia fighting against the Hungarians, after having governed for 19 years.

Venice is half-destroyed by an unfortunate fire.

Domenico Michiel, Doge of Venice, a very eloquent man, makes a voyage to the Holy Land: he takes from the Turks the islands of Rhodes, Chios, Samos, Mytilene, and Andros.

<margin>1125</margin>
## HONORIUS II
A native of Imola, Pope, holds the see for 5 years.

Guy, Count of Forez, for a long time usurps the title and possession of the Abbey of Savigny in the Lyonnais, according to the custom then common among princes and lords who seized church property located in their neighborhood. However, King Louis the Fat, returning from his expedition to Auvergne—which he had undertaken against the Count of Auvergne and others who were persecuting churchmen—leads the said Guy to renounce the said abbey. Guy returns it into the hands of His Majesty while he is passing through Montbrison, specifically within the Church of the Magdalene outside the town, in the year 1129.

### ORDER OF THE TEMPLARS.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut medallion featuring a bearded figure in a hooded habit with a cross on the breast, holding a staff topped with a cross. To the right of the figure, a small stone building is visible. The Latin inscription "ORDER OF THE TEMPLARS" <note>original: "ORDO TEMPLARIORVM"</note> is printed within the upper curve of the oval border.</image-desc>

THE <term>Templars</term> <note>The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon</note> were first established to ensure the safety of travelers and pilgrims who went to visit the <term>Holy Sepulchre</term> <note>The tomb in Jerusalem where Jesus is said to have been buried and resurrected</note>, and to protect them from the danger of the countless robbers and <term>Assassins</term> <note>referring to the Nizari Ismaili state, whose members were known to the Crusaders as "Assassins"</note> who controlled the port of <term>Jaffa</term> <note>original: "Zaff"</note> and other passes, while the soldiers and other Christians were occupied in various other places warring against the infidels. And persevering in this holy combat and beneficial practice, a significant number of knights withdrew into a sacred temple with the consent of the local abbot, and for this reason were called Templars. The King and the Patriarch of Jerusalem, finding this work holy and laudable, had them provided with everything they needed: so much so that from day to day their numbers increased; they remained nine years in this place without having a specific rule or habit <note>the formal monastic regulations and distinctive clothing that would later define the order</note>.

Guigon, <term>count</term> <note>Comte</note> of Forez, after several quarrels, makes an exchange with Guichard, <term>archbishop</term> <note>Archevêque</note> of Lyon, and the cathedral chapter, concerning the rights, jurisdiction, and homages that they held in one another's lands.

<margin>1182</margin>
He took the cross <note>became a crusader</note> in the year 1182 at the Abbey of Cîteaux, along with the Marquis Boniface of Montferrat, to go to Jerusalem; but later, plans having changed, the enterprise turned toward Constantinople <note>This refers to the Fourth Crusade, which was famously diverted from the Holy Land to the conquest of the Byzantine capital in 1204</note>. He granted a privilege to the subjects of the commanders of Saint John of Jerusalem <note>The Knights Hospitaller</note> within his lands, stating that they shall no longer be required to come equipped for the expeditions or armies that he or his successors might assemble hereafter against their enemies.

<margin>1211</margin>
Guigon, <term>count</term> of Forez, son of the aforementioned and of Wimere, marched with a great force in the service of King Philip Augustus, called the Conqueror, against Ferrand, <term>count</term> of Flanders. Since then, he led a large army against the "Heretic of Avignon" <note>original: "Bugre d'Avignon". The term "Bugre" (Bulgarian) was a common medieval slur used to describe Cathar heretics or their associates during the Albigensian Crusade</note>, uncle of the said Ferrand, who was coming down through Provence to destroy the lands of Lyonnais and Forez; he gave battle to him on the very same day that the King had given it to the said Ferrand at Bouvines <note>The Battle of Bouvines (1214) was a definitive victory for the French Crown</note>, from which he brought back victory and took the said Heretic prisoner, whom he brought to Paris. He had the Abbey of Valbenoîte in Forez rebuilt anew, after having confirmed the gifts made to it by his grandfather and father. In the year 1211, he ordered the first foundation of the Church of Our Lady of Montbrison, where he established thirteen <term>canons</term> <note>Chanoines: clergy members belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church</note>, by the authority of the <term>archbishop</term> of Lyon, his uncle, to whom he gave the castle and lordship of Moing, with its appurtenances and dependencies, the tithe of Verrières, and sixty strong pounds <note>Liures forts: a specific high-value currency of the period</note>, to be taken every year from the market of Montbrison. Overtaken by death, he was unable to begin the construction of the said church.

He understands the Greek, Latin, Italian, Teutonic or Germanic, and Arabic languages very well. He recovers Jerusalem and fortifies it. He makes a truce with the Sultan for 9 years. He harbors a hatred for the popes. He is the first to bring those pernicious names into Italy: the **Guelphs** and **Ghibellines**, two divided factions that cause a civil war so cruel that a great abundance of human blood is shed, and innumerable sackings and killings are committed without any mercy. He holds the side of the Ghibellines, and Pope Gregory IX that of the Guelphs <note>The Guelphs supported the Papacy, while the Ghibellines supported the Imperial authority</note>. He is killed by his bastard son, or according to the sayings of some, poisoned through the schemes of the Pope, having held the empire for 35 years.

# OF THOSE OF THE ORDER OF THE
## Trinity: and the Friars Minor.

<image-desc>An oval engraved emblem featuring a standing monk in a landscape. The monk is dressed in a long, hooded habit with a cross visible on the front. He is gesturing with his right hand toward a fortified city with a prominent domed building and a tower. To the left are rugged mountains. The emblem is framed by an oval border with the inscription "ORDER OF THE HOLY TRINITY" <note>original Latin: "RELIGIO S. TRINITATIS."</note></image-desc>

THE ORDER of the monks of the Trinity had its beginning in the time of Pope Innocent III <note>Innocent III reigned from 1198 to 1216 and was one of the most powerful popes of the Middle Ages, known for authorizing the great mendicant orders.</note> by a man named John de Matha <note>Saint John of Matha (1160–1213), a French saint who founded the Trinitarians.</note> and Felix the hermit <note>Saint Felix of Valois (1127–1212), who lived as a hermit in the forest of Galeresse before co-founding the order.</note>, both living solitary lives. Having been instructed by a revelation while they slept, they went to the said Innocent to ask him for a specific rule of life. The Holy Father ordained that they should wear a white habit with a red cross <note>While the text mentions a red cross, the Trinitarian cross is traditionally blue and red; the colors symbolized the Trinity.</note>, with the additional duty of providing for the ransom of Christian prisoners. For this reason, they were called the Religious of the Redemption of Captives. Afterward, these good people, to carry out this work of piety, traveled throughout the lands asking for and collecting alms, in order to use them for the deliverance of prisoners who needed to be ransomed from the hands of the infidels—

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<keywords>Order of the Holy Trinity, Trinitarians, Pope Innocent III, John de Matha, Felix of Valois, redemption of captives, religious orders, 13th century history</keywords>

<header>BOOK FOUR.</header>

...oners. At this same time, Saint Francis established his order of the Friars Minor <note>The Order of Friars Minor (OFM), founded by St. Francis of Assisi around 1209.</note>, whom he named thus for the sake of humility; for, girded with a rope and going barefoot, they considered themselves the least of all. This is not something they do at this hour, for everything has gone from bad to worse. Lorenzo Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457) was a famous Italian humanist and critic known for his sharp wit and for proving the "Donation of Constantine" was a forgery.</note>, a mocker to the very end, while walking in the church of the Cordeliers <term>French name for the Franciscans, referring to the knotted rope cord (corde) they wore as a belt.</term> in Naples, saw an image of Saint Francis sitting in the middle of the four Doctors <note>The Four Great Doctors of the Western Church: Saints Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory the Great.</note>. Calling over a friar, he asked him: "Why has Saint Francis been placed in the rank of the Doctors, since he was a layman and without formal education?" Indeed, one does not see works of his as one does by Bonaventure <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Franciscan theologian and philosopher known as the "Seraphic Doctor."</note> and others who have written. The friar asserted that Saint Francis was the greatest of all the doctors. To which Valla replied: "And how can he be 'great' <note>original: "grand" (great/large), playing on the Latin 'major'.</note> when he has always been placed in the number of the 'minors'?" <note>Valla is making a linguistic pun: Francis cannot be a "Great" (Major) Doctor if he is the head of the "Minor" (lesser) friars.</note> Now, although the Friars Minor have vowed humility, calling themselves in the past the least of all in name and in deed, the fact remains that you see some among them so proud that if you do not call them "Our Master" or "Monsieur the Doctor," you lose their good graces. This favor, once converted into hatred, will lead them to try to avenge themselves in some way—if they can do no worse, they will defame you from the pulpit and practically point you out with their finger. In former times, it would have been better to be banished than to be in the bad graces of one of these Friars Minor. I do not say this of all of them; but they have a great need to be reformed by their Provincials <term>A high-ranking superior in a religious order who oversees a specific geographic territory or "province."</term>, among whom there are many learned men, and they should be forbidden from preaching humorous tales and trifles on Easter Day itself, which they have been accustomed to intermingle in their sermons <note>This refers to the "Risus Paschalis" (Easter Laughter), a tradition where preachers used jokes and funny stories to make the congregation laugh after the somber season of Lent.</note>. One sees that they are already beginning to correct this. And if they follow the rule of Saint Francis, their founder, they will give no occasion...

## SAINT LOUIS,
had the church of Saint-Denis in France built anew and restored; he ransomed from the Venetians the Crown of Thorns and other relics pledged by Baldwin <note>Baldwin II, the last Latin Emperor of Constantinople, who had pawned the Crown of Thorns to Venetian bankers to fund the defense of his empire.</note>; he placed them in the **Sainte-Chapelle** in Paris, which he had built. He undertook the journey against the Saracens <term>A medieval term for Muslims, particularly those in the Holy Land or North Africa.</term>; ransomed Christian slaves in great numbers; had the house of the **Quinze-Vingts** <note>The "Fifteen-Twenties," named because it housed 300 (15 x 20) people; it remains a famous hospital for the blind in Paris today.</note> built in Paris to support 300 knights who returned from overseas with him and whose eyes had been put out by the Saracens. He founded the house of the **Filles-Dieu** <term>A religious order for reformed women ("Daughters of God").</term>, the Beguines, the **Blancs-Manteaux** <note>The "White Capes," a religious order.</note> formerly called the Guillemins, Sainte-Croix-de-la-Bretonnerie, and the Carthusians <note>The Chartreux, an austere monastic order.</note> outside the Saint-Michel gate. He chased the bankers out of France, and banished jesters and jokers from his court. He made good ordinances, notably against those who blaspheme the name of God. He reigned for 44 years.

Those of Turin took prisoner Thomas, Count of Savoy, their lord.

## NICHOLAS OF LYRA

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Nicolas de Lyra in profile, facing right. He is depicted as a tonsured monk with a short beard, wearing a hooded habit. The portrait is enclosed in a double-ruled circular frame containing the Latin inscription: NICOLAVS DE LYRA. ANG. MIN.</image-desc>

NICHOLAS of Lyra, English <note>Although the text calls him "Anglois" (English), Nicholas was actually born in Lyre, Normandy. This was a common confusion in early modern historiography.</note>, of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>, wrote commentaries on all the books of the Old and New Testament, printed under the title of the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>original: "Glosa ordinaria." Nicholas's "Postillae" were so influential they were often printed alongside the standard medieval biblical commentary.</note>, and several other works. Some detractors say of him, "Lyra raves" <note>original: "De Lyra delirat." A famous Latin pun playing on his name and the word for delirium/madness.</note>, for "names often suit their subjects" <note>original: "Conueniunt rebus nomina sæpe suis." A Latin proverb suggesting a person's name reflects their character.</note>. They claim that his moral gloss corrupts all the beautiful text, and that it is like a velvet robe trimmed with coarse wool <term>bureau: a thick, rough, inexpensive woolen cloth often worn by the poor or lower clergy</term>. But such slanderers, unsound of mind, could not approach the least of his perfections. In any case, he was a learned man, and I wish that all the Franciscans <term>cordeliers: another name for the Friars Minor, referring to the knotted cord they wore as a belt</term> were like him.

### BARTOLUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Bartolus de Saxoferrato in profile, facing right, wearing a hood and academic or legal robes. The Latin inscription around the border of the medallion reads: BARTOLUS OF SASSOFERRATO, JURISCONSULT <note>original: "BARTHOLVS DE SAXO FERRATO IVR. C."</note></image-desc>

BARTOLUS was born in the year of our salvation 1309. As a young child, he was taught by Peter of Assisi; and having not yet even passed the age of 14, he applied his mind to the study of civil law in the city of Perugia <note>original: "Perufe."</note>. Six years later, having been a disciple of Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia, a famous jurist and poet.</note>, Butrigario <note>Jacopo Butrigario.</note>, and Rainerius <note>Ranieri Arsendi.</note>, he responded publicly on the law at Bologna with great honor. At the age of 21, he received the degree of doctor in the said city; and to apply the theory of law into usage and practice, he frequented the pleadings in the courts and at the bar for some time. He served as a wise judge and learned <term>Jurisconsult: A person who is an expert in the law and provides legal advice.</term> in the city of Tudertum, commonly called Todi. Leaving this heavy burden and magistracy, he returned to leafing through the volumes of law and diligently devoted himself to the study of the statutes. In this, he became so accomplished that they came to seek him to be a public lecturer of law at Pisa, where he wrote that beautiful <term>repetition: A formal, detailed lecture or academic exercise focusing on a specific legal text or law.</term> on the law *If he who, as a purchaser...* <note>original: "Si is qui pro emptore. ff. de vfucap." A reference to a specific section of the Roman Digest concerning the acquisition of property through long-term possession.</note> being at that time 25 years old. He later married in Perugia, in which place he demonstrated the doctrine of law, with such

**PHILIP THE FAIR** <note>Philip IV (1268–1314).</note>, King of France, had among other children a daughter named Isabella, who was married to Edward, second of that name, King of England, by whom she bore Edward III. This Edward III claimed the succession of the kingdom of France after Charles the Fair <note>Charles IV (1294–1328), the last direct Capetian king.</note>, his uncle and his mother’s brother, died without children—having nevertheless left Lady Joan of Évreux, his wife, pregnant. Edward said the throne belonged to him legitimately if any mishap befell his aunt while she was pregnant, or if the child died, or if it were a girl; otherwise, he claimed he should have the government of the kingdom and the guardianship of the posthumous child if it were a male. The French, on the contrary, said that the said Edward had no right there; for even if it were the case that women should succeed to the crown of France (which they do not), the daughters of the late kings Louis the Quarreler <note>original: "Loüis Hutin" (Louis X).</note> and Charles the Fair were more eligible to succeed than he. They also cited the <term>Salic Law</term> <note>A traditional law of the Salian Franks used here to argue that the French throne could not be inherited by or through a woman.</note>, by virtue of which women were deprived of the

Guy, Count of Forez, following his father John, spared nothing in his time to aid the kings of France, for whom he undertook several expeditions against the English: notably at the sieges of Cambrai and Tournai in 1339 and 1340; on the expedition to Gascony in 1345, where he recaptured a city of great importance to the King; and at the siege of Calais, where he was among the first to arrive. He raised an army in the year 1358 against a troop of English led by Robert Knolles <note>original: "Robert Canolle," a prominent English commander during the Hundred Years' War</note>, who had descended as far as Auvergne, from where, through his wise leadership, he drove them out without the loss of his own men. Regnaud de Forez, brother of Guy, was killed in the Battle of Brignais <note>original: "Brignes"</note>, at the age of 17.

Louis de Forez remained regent and governor of the County of Forez along with Lady Jeanne de Bourbon, daughter of Louis I, Duke of Bourbon, during the minority of the young Count John, her nephew and the son of the said Jeanne.

<header>FOURTH BOOK.</header>

## BALDUS.

<image-desc>A circular engraved medallion portrait of a man shown in profile facing right. He wears a scholar's cap and a layered robe. The Latin text inscribed within the circular border reads: Baldus of Perugia, Jurisconsult <note>original: "BALDVS PERVSINVS IC." IC is an abbreviation for Iureconsultus.</note>.</image-desc>

Baldus, a disciple and student of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential jurist of the Middle Ages.</note>, earned the name of a great legalist and learned Jurisconsult <term>Jurisconsult</term> <note>An expert in law who provides formal legal opinions; a title of high prestige in Roman and Civil law traditions.</note> of his time, and was held in high honor and reputation. Bartolus, Baldus, and Jason <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a later but equally famous legal scholar often grouped with the other two.</note> are named as the greatest doctors of law who have ever lived. Among them, Baldus holds the second place. He is called an "ungrateful disciple" because he was often opposed to the opinions of Bartolus, his master, attempting to correct him wherever he could. He wrote:
*On the Code*, Book 9 <note>original: "Super codice, lib. 9." This refers to the Code of Justinian, a cornerstone of Roman law.</note>.
*On the Old Digest*, Book 24 <note>original: "Super ff. veteris, lib. 24." The "Digest" (or Pandects) was a massive compilation of juristic writings; the "Old Digest" was the first section studied in medieval universities.</note>.
*On the Infortiatum*, Book 14 <note>original: "Super ff. inforciati, lib. 14." The "Infortiatum" was the middle section of the Digest.</note>.
*On the Use of Fiefs* <note>original: "De vsu feudorum." A foundational work on feudal law.</note>.
*On the Authentics* <note>original: "Super autentic." Referring to the "Authenticum," a collection of Justinian's new laws (Novels).</note>.
*On the second book of the Decretals* <note>original: "Super secundo decretalium." This refers to canon (church) law.</note>.
*Additions to the Mirror* <note>original: "Additiones speculi." Referring to the *Speculum Iudiciale*, a famous procedural manual by William Durand.</note>.
Many *Consilia* <term>Consilia</term> <note>original: "Consilia multa." These were formal legal opinions given by famous jurists to resolve specific court cases.</note>.

race having instigated a certain man, born for the ruin of himself and of humanity, to devise such a diabolical work, to be put into effect afterwards—an effect certainly miserable. This man then (says Polydore Vergil) kept sulfur in his house, ground into powder in a mortar to make some medicine; and having covered it with a stone, it happened that while striking his flint-stone afterward to get fire, a spark fell into the mortar. The matter therein being reduced to a flame of fire, it made the stone that served as a cover fly very high. By this example, he made a tube or cannon of iron, in which he put a certain powder composed of sulfur and other things, together with a stone; then, placing a burning coal at a hole that was at the end of the cannon where the sulfur appeared, the stone, shooting out through the great vehemence of the fire, gave a loud sound like a clap of thunder. Thus he invented this machine of war, and first showed the use of it to the Venetians in that war which was fought against the Genoese in the year 1380. This machine was called from then on a **Bombard**, a name composed from *Bombo* by onomatopoeia <note>A word formed by imitating the sound it describes.</note>, because of the noise and sound it makes, and from *Ardeo* <note>Latin: "to burn."</note>, because of that which burns; or from the Greek *bombos* <note>original: βόμβος</note>, which means "sound." At present it has changed its name, and various kinds of them are made through the cunning of Satan and the malice of men: such as, cannons, serpentines, bastard culverins, great culverins, medium culverins, falconets, field pieces, petronels <note>A portable firearm, intermediate between a pistol and an arquebus, fired from the chest.</note>, arquebuses with a serpentine wheel, hooked arquebuses, petards, pistols, pistolasses, and pistolets. Truly, you were far too much an enemy of life,
Whoever first discovered artillery.
Truly, you gave yourself renown for a cruel deed,
Whoever first invented the cannon.
And what? If you desired to be remembered,
Did your glory have to be bought with our deaths?
And what? Could you not otherwise prevent
Your name from dying, without it costing so much?
O cursed manner: cursed art, cursed master:
O wretched cannon: o wretched saltpeter:
O wretched powder! O wretched cannonballs!
O inhuman executioners of valiant men!
By you, the brave man falls to the ground as quickly
As does the greatest coward who was ever in war.
By you, many a strong man is struck down by the weak,
By you, the virtue of the French is no longer known.
There are Rolands and Renauds also, <note>References to the legendary chivalric heroes Roland (hero of the *Song of Roland*) and Renaud de Montauban, symbols of traditional knightly valor and physical strength.</note>
Whom terrifying fear never troubled.
But this cursed cannon murders them just as
It would a common scoundrel or some cowardly man.
And the upright and bold man can protect himself less
Than the fearful one, whose heart is debased.

## SENTENCE OF THE COUNCIL
### *of Constance against John Hus.*

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial letter 'L' featuring a woodcut illustration of a bearded man in robes, possibly a scholar or church official, seated at a desk or lectern with an open book.</image-desc>The holy and general Council of Constance, representing the Catholic Church, legitimately assembled with the Holy Spirit, for perpetual memory in the future, gives notice: Because (as truth bears witness) the bad tree is accustomed to bearing bad fruit, it has come to pass that John Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384) was an English theologian whose white-hot critiques of the papacy and emphasis on the Bible as the only authority paved the way for the later Reformation.</note> through his deadly doctrine—not in Jesus Christ through the Gospel, as the holy fathers of old fathered children, but against the holy faith of Jesus Christ—has produced pestilential children like a poisonous root. ...that, notwithstanding such condemnation and decree, contravening it with a bold audacity, he had dogmatized, held, and proposed his errors and several heresies condemned both by the church of Jesus Christ and formerly by several reverend fathers in God—archbishops, bishops, and doctors of theology from various kingdoms and provinces. He published certain articles listed below by the said Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English theologian whose critiques of the papacy heavily influenced Hus.</note> and others, in schools and sermons, insisting upon them and maintaining them as Catholic, while asserting that Wycliffe was an evangelical doctor <term>evangelical doctor: a title given to Wycliffe (Latin: *Doctor Evangelicus*) by his followers, emphasizing his reliance on the Gospels over church tradition</term> and a Catholic.

Some are scandalous, others offensive to pious ears, rash and seditious, and some of them notoriously heretical, having been rejected from time immemorial by the holy fathers and general councils; with an inhibition and prohibition to all persons from proposing or approving them in any way or manner whatsoever.

### THERE FOLLOWS THE TENOR OF
### *certain articles of Wycliffe condemned.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "S" featuring a child-like figure or angel nestled among scrolling foliage.</image-desc>Just as <note>original: "Sicut"</note> Christ is at once God and man, so the consecrated host is at once the body of Christ at least in figure, and true bread in nature. Or what sounds the same, true bread naturally, and the body of Christ figuratively. <note>original: "Sicut Christus est simul Deus & homo, sic hostia consecrata est simul corpus Christi ad minimum in figura, & verus panis in natura."</note>

Just as John was figuratively Elijah, and not personally, so the bread on the altar is figuratively the body of Christ. And this is a figurative expression, *This is my body*: just like that one, *John is Elijah*.

The fruit of that madness by which "accident without a subject" <term>accident without a subject: a philosophical concept used to explain how the appearance of bread (accidents) can remain while the actual substance of bread is gone</term> is feigned, would be to blaspheme against God, to scandalize the saints, and to mock the church through the language of accidents.

Those who define that the little children of the faithful dying without sacramental baptism will not be saved, are in this matter foolish and presumptuous.

The light and brief confirmation of bishops, when it is solemnized only by the said rites, was introduced by the prompting of the devil.

As for the oil with which bishops anoint children, and the linen cloth <note>This refers to the "chrism cloth" or *chrismale* used to cover the head of the newly confirmed</note> which is wrapped around the head, it seems that it is a trivial rite, unfounded in Scripture.

In these words, *You are clean, but not all* <note>A reference to Christ's words to the disciples in John 13:10</note>, the devil placed an unfaithful snare: for he introduced private and unfounded confession. And once it was known to the confessor, he established it as a law that the malice of the person thus confessed should not be revealed to the people.

It is a probable conjecture that such a person who lives rightly is a deacon or a priest. For just as I know that this person living holily...

...does, he is established by God in such an office or state.

The ancients, out of a desire for temporal things, from the hope of mutual assistance, or for the sake of excusing lust, even if they despair of having offspring, may be joined together in marriage.

These words, "I will take you as my wife," are more preferable in a marriage contract than these, "I take you as my wife," etc.; because by contracting with one through these words of the future, and afterwards with another through these words of the present <note>original: "Accipiam te in uxorem... Ego te accipio in uxorem". Wycliffe is arguing against the legalistic hair-splitting of the Church courts regarding betrothal versus immediate marriage vows.</note>.

The Pope, who falsely calls himself the "servant of the servants of God," holds no rank in the work of the Gospel, but only in a worldly one. Even if he is in any order, he is in the order of demons serving God in a most blameworthy manner.

The Pope is the patron of the Antichrist; not just that single person, but the whole multitude of popes since the time the Church was endowed with worldly wealth <note>This refers to the "Donation of Constantine," a document Wycliffe believed corrupted the Church by giving it political power and land.</note>.

Yet it is not inconsistent that Gregory and other popes, who in their lives did many good things of a general nature, finally repented.

There are twelve proctors and disciples of the Antichrist: the pope, cardinals, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, officials, deans, monks, "two-forked" <term>bifurcati canonici: literally "cloven-hoofed" or "two-horned" canons, likely a derogatory reference to their mitres or the divide between their religious and secular duties</term> canons, the false friars introduced recently and last of all, and pardoners <term>quæstores: officials authorized to raise money for the church, often through the sale of indulgences</term>.

Every essence has one person <term>suppositum: a philosophical term for an individual substance or person</term>, according to which another person equal to the first is produced. And this is an abiding action, the most perfect possible in nature.

Every essence, whether bodily or incorporeal, is common to three persons, and in all of them properties, accidents, and operations exist in common.

God can annihilate nothing, nor make the world larger or smaller, but He can create souls only up to a certain number and no further.

Every being is everywhere, since every being is God.

Everything that will happen, will happen with absolute necessity.

<page-num>463</page-num>
<header>BOOK FOUR.</header>

# HERE FOLLOWS THE TENOR OF
### *several articles of Jan Hus exactly as he wrote them in his own hand.*

---

There is only one holy universal Church, which is the assembly of all the predestined <note>original: "VNICA est sancta vniuersalis ecclesia, quae est praedestinatorum vniuersitas." Hus defined the Church not as the visible hierarchy of Rome, but as the invisible group of people chosen by God for salvation.</note>.

*Paul was never a member of the devil, even though he performed certain acts similar to the acts of the church of the malignant.*

*Those who are foreknown <note>original: "Praesciti". In Hus’s theology, this refers to those God knows will ultimately be damned, as opposed to the "predestined" who are saved.</note> are not parts of the Church, since no part of it will finally fall away from it, because the love of predestination, which binds the Church together, does not fail.*

*Peter is not, nor was he ever, the head of the holy Catholic Church.*

*No one acts as the vicar of Peter or of Christ unless he follows him in his character; for no other way of following is more relevant, nor does anyone receive delegated power from God in any other way. This is because that office of vicar requires both a conformity of character and the authority of the one who appoints him.*

*It is not necessary to believe that whoever is the Roman pontiff is the head of any particular holy church, unless God has predestined him.*

*Doctors who claim that someone who is to be corrected through ecclesiastical censure, if he refuses to be corrected, must be handed over to secular judgment, certainly follow in this the high priests, scribes, and Pharisees. These were the ones who handed Christ over to secular judgment when he would not obey them in all things, saying, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death" <note>John 18:31</note>. Such people are more grievous murderers than Pilate.*

*If a pope is wicked, and especially if he is one foreknown to be damned, then like the apostle Judas, he is a devil, a thief, and a robber, and he is not the head of the holy militant Church, since he is not even a member of it.*

*The pope ought not to be called "most holy," even according to his office.*

--- Page 543 ---
<meta>This page continues the list of theological articles for which Jan Hus was condemned at the Council of Constance. The catchword "quia" from the previous page begins the Latin text at the top of this page, which argues that office alone does not make one holy.</meta>

<page-num>464</page-num>
<header>PROSOPOGRAPHY</header>

*...because otherwise a king would have to be called "most holy" simply by virtue of his office, and executioners and heralds would be called holy; indeed, even the devil would have to be called holy, since he is an official of God.* <note>original: "quia aliàs rex deberet dici sanctissimus..." This article challenged the idea that religious or political titles automatically carry spiritual merit.</note>

*The condemnation of the forty-five articles of John Wycliffe made by the doctors is irrational, unjust, and poorly executed.* <note>original: "Condemnatio quadraginta quinque articulorum Ioannis Vvicleff..." Wycliffe was an English reformer whose writings deeply influenced Hus; the Council had already condemned Wycliffe's works.</note>

*No one is a civil lord, no one is a prelate, and no one is a bishop while he is in mortal sin:* <note>original: "Nullus est dominus ciuilis... dum est in peccato mortali." This was a particularly dangerous teaching to the authorities, as it suggested that a leader’s power was only valid if they remained in a state of grace.</note>

Jan Hus was questioned once again [to see] if he wished to hold and believe the contents of the said articles. He replied that as a priest (in the hope) of Jesus Christ, fearing to offend God and commit perjury, he did not support the articles produced by false witnesses in their testimony against him, which (as God is his witness) he had never preached or proposed as they had claimed. Then the deputies asked him if he would swear that he did not acknowledge the articles written in his own hand, contained in his books and confessed by him, and instead hold the contrary with the Church. He replied that in everything that had been duly extracted from his books and written by his hand, he stood firm; and, maintaining it as Catholic and true, he wished to live and die in this faith, which he would never deny so as not to scandalize those he had taught—choosing instead to be burned a thousand times over for it, if such a thing were possible.

Seeing this, Master Henry de Pyro, the promoter <note>A legal officer in an ecclesiastical court, acting as a prosecutor.</note> and procurator, requested in the name of the whole council that sentence be given against the said Jan Hus, concluding that he should be condemned to be degraded <note>term: "degraded"—The formal process of stripping a clergyman of his holy orders, effectively removing his status as a priest before he could be handed over to secular authorities for execution.</note> and his books publicly cast into the fire. This sentence, as contained hereafter, was given and pronounced word for word to the said Hus. And so that he might be delivered into the hands of secular justice, the Archbishop of Milan, the suffragan of the e- <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "suffragan" refers to a bishop who assists or is subordinate to an archbishop.</note>

# THE ART OF PRINTING.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration depicting a 15th or 16th-century printing shop. In the center is a wooden printing press with a banner across the top reading "THE ART OF TYPOGRAPHY" <note>original: "ARS TYPO GRAPHICA"</note>. To the left, a man sits at a desk working with type cases. In the center, a man operates the press by pulling a large lever. To the right, another figure stands, possibly inspecting a printed sheet. Various tools hang on the back wall, and the entire scene is framed by an oval border.</image-desc>

The art of printing books was first discovered in Mainz <note>original: "Magonce"</note> by a man named Johann Gutenberg <note>original: "Iean Gutembergius"</note>. It is an invention certainly divine, admirable, and worthy of memory, through the effect of which men can gain knowledge of all sciences and learn the deeds and exploits of emperors, kings, peoples, nations, republics, towns, and cities. Sebastian Gryphius <note>A celebrated 16th-century German printer who operated in Lyon, known for his high-quality editions of classical texts.</note>, who has since brought printing to its perfection, deserves the second place of honor after Gutenberg the inventor.

<margin>1413</margin>
Murad II <note>original: "Amurates"</note>, 7th Emperor of the Turks, established the <term>Janissaries</term> <note>An elite infantry unit that formed the Ottoman Sultan's household troops and bodyguards.</note>; he captured Thessaloniki from the Venetians; and after having overcome the Christians, he became a monk <note>This refers to Murad II’s historical abdications in 1444 and 1446 to join a religious retreat, though he was forced back into power.</note>.

<margin>1417</margin>
MARTIN V, pope, held the seat for 25 years.

<margin>1422</margin>
CHARLES VII, King of France, reigned for 38 years.

### PIUS II, a Sienese, Pope, a learned man who had been the chancellor to the Emperor Frederick, and was then called Aeneas Sylvius, holds the seat for 6 years. Here are some of his apophthegms <note>Apophthegms are concise, pointed sayings or maxims.</note> and sententious remarks.

*To investigate the course of the stars is more beautiful than it is useful.* <note>original: "Siderum cursus inuestigare pulchrius quàm vtile."</note>
*Neither can the greedy man be satisfied by money, nor the learned man by the knowledge of things.* <note>original: "Neque potest auarus pecunia explexi, neque doctus rerum cognitione."</note>
*He who is given more to know, greater doubts follow him.* <note>original: "Cui plura datum est nosse, hunc maiora sequuntur dubia."</note>
*Letters <note>Meaning literacy and education.</note> should be as silver to commoners, gold to the nobility, and gems to princes.* <note>original: "Plebeiis loco argenti esse debent literæ, nobilibus auri, gemmarum principibus."</note>
*Laws have power over the common people, but they fall silent before the powerful.* <note>original: "In plebem vim habent leges, in potentes obmutescunt."</note>
*More serious matters are decided by arms, not by laws.* <note>original: "Grauiores res armis decernuntur, non legibus."</note>
*As rivers flow into the sea, so do vices flow into the houses of the powerful.* <note>original: "Vt in mare flumina, ita in potentiorū ædes confluunt vitia."</note>
*Litigants are like little birds, the court is the threshing floor, the judges are the nets, and the fowlers are the legal advocates.* <note>original: "Litigatores auiculæ sunt, forum area, iudices retia, aucupes causarum patroni."</note>
*The burden of the papacy is heavy, but it is a blessing to him who carries it well.* <note>original: "Graue pontificis onus, sed illi beatum qui bene fert."</note>
*Marriage was taken away from priests for a great reason, but it ought to be restored for an even greater one.* <note>original: "Sacerdotibus magna ratione ademptum connubium, sed maiore quadam restituendum."</note>
*A wandering monk is a slave of the devil.* <note>original: "Vagus monachus mancipium diaboli."</note>
*Men should be given to honors <note>Referring to high offices or dignities.</note>, not honors to men.* <note>original: "Dignitatibus homines dandi, non dignitates hominibus."</note>
*He nourishes an enemy within himself who forgives his son <note>Pius II suggests that failing to discipline a son creates a future adversary.</note>.* <note>original: "Hostem in se nutrit qui filio ignoscit."</note>
*Vices are covered by generosity and exposed by greed.* <note>original: "Vitia liberalitate teguntur, nudantur auaritia."</note>
*Death is sweet to the good, but harsh to the wicked.* <note>original: "Dulcis mors bonis, iniquis dura."</note>

Charles, fifth duke of Bourbon and Auvergne, count of Clermont and Forez, lord of Beaujeu and Château-Chinon, peer and chamberlain of France, is married to Agnes of Burgundy, daughter to John, duke of Burgundy. He passed away in the year 1456, and she in 1476.

Louis Pontan, a most learned <term>jurisconsult</term> <note>A scholar of law who provides expert legal opinions.</note>, is of such a great and incredible memory that he recites by heart not only the beginning of the laws, but the contents of all the laws. He died of the plague at the Council of Basel <note>A major ecclesiastical council held in Switzerland starting in 1431.</note>, aged 30 years.

## MARSILIO FICINO.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Marsilio Ficino. He is depicted in profile or three-quarter view, wearing a soft cap and a high-collared garment. The circular frame contains the Latin inscription: MARSILIO FICINO FIOREN.</image-desc>

Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was one of the most influential humanist philosophers of the Italian Renaissance and the head of the Florentine Platonic Academy.</note> of Florence translated all the works of Plato from Greek into Latin, which he illustrated with arguments that serve as commentaries; he also translated Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercure Trismegiste." A legendary figure believed in the Renaissance to be an ancient Egyptian sage and the author of the *Hermetic Corpus*.</note> and Plotinus, upon whom he wrote learned commentaries. Additionally, he translated the book on death by Xenocrates the Platonist; the short works of Speusippus, Alcinous, and Pythagoras; the books of *Mystical Theology* and *The Divine Names* by Saint Dionysius the Areopagite; the *Theophrastus* of Aeneas the Platonist <note>Aeneas of Gaza, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist.</note>; and he compiled a summary in two chapters of the Greek book by Athenagoras the Philosopher, *On the Resurrection*. The other books created from his own invention and arrangement are:
*Remarkable Theology.* <note>original Latin: "Theologia notabilis." This refers to his masterpiece, the *Platonic Theology*, where he sought to harmonize Christian doctrine with Platonic philosophy.</note>
*On Intellect and Intelligence.*
*On Plato's Symposium.* <note>original: "In convivium Platonis." This work, also known as *De Amore*, was highly influential in defining "Platonic love" for the Renaissance.</note>
*Several books of Letters.*
*On the Triple Life.* <note>original: "De triplici vita." A famous treatise on health and longevity, especially for scholars, blending medicine, philosophy, and astrology.</note>
*An Apology for Medicine and Astrology.*
*Antidote for Epidemics and the Preservation of Good Health.*
*On Magic and the Magi.*

Apology for his book on light. <note>original: "Apologia in suum librum de lumine." In this work, Ficino defends his metaphysical theories regarding light as a manifestation of the divine.</note>

Eighteen books on the immortality of souls and eternal happiness, dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici. <note>original: "De animorum immortalite & æterna felicitate lib. 18, ad Laurentium Medicem." He died in the year 1503.

# SABELLICO.

<image-desc>A circular portrait engraving of Marcantonio Sabellico (M. Antonius Sabellicus). He is shown in profile facing right, wearing a scholarly cap and gown. The circular frame contains the translated text: "Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, Poet" at the top and an abbreviated honorific at the base.</image-desc>

MARC Antony Sabellico, a great historian, orator, and poet, and a close friend of Hermolao Barbaro and Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano and Hermolao Barbaro were leading scholars of the Italian Renaissance; their friendship with Sabellico highlights his high standing in the "Republic of Letters."</note>, wrote in elegant Latin:

Five Enneads of historical rhapsodies from the foundation of the world. <note>original: "Rapsodiæ historiarum ab orbe condito Enneades quinque." An "Ennead" is a group of nine books. This was Sabellico's attempt at a universal history.</note>

Also six Enneads of rhapsodies. <note>original: "Item Rapsodiæ Enneades sex." These additional books continued his monumental historical project.</note>

Three Decades and three books of the fourth Decade on Venetian history from the founding of the city. <note>original: "Rerum Venetarum ab urbe condita Decades tres, & quartæ lib. 3." This work earned him the position of official historian of the Venetian Republic.</note>

Twenty-nine books of Supplements. <note>original: "Supplementi lib. 29."</note>

Ten books of Examples. <note>original: "Exemplorum lib. 10." A collection of moral and historical anecdotes intended for rhetorical use.</note>

Six books on the antiquity of Aquileia. <note>original: "De Aquileiæ antiquitate lib. 6." Aquileia was an important Roman city in northeastern Italy.</note>

Three books on the location of the city of Venice. <note>original: "De Venetæ vrbis situ lib. 3."</note>

On the Venetian magistrates. <note>original: "De Venetis magistratibus."</note>

On the office of the praetor. <note>original: "De prætoris officio."</note>

A dialogue on the office of the scribe. <note>original: "De officio scribæ dialog."</note>

A dialogue on the restoration of the Latin language. <note>original: "De Latinæ linguæ reparatione dialog." A typical humanist work championing the return to classical Latin purity.</note>

Twelve books of familiar letters. <note>original: "Epistolarum familiarium lib. 12."</note>

Twelve Orations. <note>original: "Orationes, 12."</note>

Various poems. <note>original: "Poëmata varia."</note>

<margin>1498</margin>
LOUIS, twelfth of that name, previously Duke of Orleans <note>Louis XII succeeded his cousin Charles VIII in 1498. He was known as the "Father of the People" despite his long wars in Italy.</note>

[Or]leans & of Valois, succeeded to the kingdom of France as the closest and most able to succeed; father of the country and shepherd of the people, he reigned for 17 years. He married Anne of Brittany, widow of King Charles the Eighth <note>By marrying Charles VIII's widow, Louis XII ensured that the Duchy of Brittany remained tied to the French crown.</note>, and conquered the Duchy of Milan, which belonged to him <note>Louis claimed Milan through his grandmother, Valentina Visconti.</note> and which was occupied by the Sforzas. He had Ludovico Sforza <note>The Duke of Milan, known as "Il Moro."</note> led as a prisoner to Bourges, after Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, the colonel of his army in Italy, had chased him from Milan.

The French retook Genoa, which had revolted, and then made war against the Venetians.

An illness called whooping cough <note>In the early 16th century, the term *coqueluche* was used to describe a major respiratory epidemic, likely a form of influenza, that affected much of the population.</note>.

The Spanish at Ravenna, where the Duke of Nemours was killed <note>Gaston de Foix, Duke of Nemours, was a brilliant young commander who died at the moment of victory at the Battle of Ravenna in 1512.</note>.

Captain Bayard <note>Pierre Terrail, Seigneur de Bayard, famously known as "the knight without fear and beyond reproach" (*le chevalier sans peur et sans reproche*).</note>, the lords of Aubigny and of La Palice: great lords and brave captains on the side of King Louis.

Gonzalo Fernández <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba.</note>, a Spaniard surnomed the "Great Captain," a valiant man.

The King of Spain takes Pamplona and a part of the Kingdom of Navarre.

**ALEXANDER the Sixth**, Pope, held the See for 10 years.

Cesare Borgia, called "Valentinois" <note>Cesare was the Duke of Valentinois, a title granted to him by Louis XII.</note>, son of Pope Alexander, left the cardinal’s hat to take up the helmet: he conquered Romagna and the county of Spoleto, making himself lord of them; he carried for his motto: *Either Caesar or nothing* <note>original: "Aut Cæsar aut nihil"</note>.

Leonardo Loredan governed in Venice for 19 years and 8 months.

Philip, Archduke of Austria and King of Aragon by his wife <note>Philip I, known as "the Handsome," who married Joanna the Mad of Castile and Aragon.</note>, obtained the Kingdom of Castile: he rendered homage to King Louis the Twelfth for the counties of Flanders and Artois.

# FOURTH BOOK. 483
## GIROLAMO SAVONAROLA.

<image-desc>A circular portrait medallion of Girolamo Savonarola in profile, facing right. He is depicted wearing a hooded monastic habit. The inscription within the border of the medallion reads: "Brother Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, Master of Divinity" <note>original: "F. HIERONYMVS SAVONAROLA FER. M. D."</note></image-desc>

**GIROLAMO** Savonarola <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498) was a Dominican friar and influential preacher in Florence, known for his attempts at moral reform and his eventual execution during the conflict with the papacy.</note> of Ferrara, of the order of the Friars Preachers <note>The Dominican Order.</note>, a most ardent preacher and full of charity, was, by the envy of Pope Alexander <note>Pope Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia), who excommunicated Savonarola in 1497.</note>—a magician and wicked man <note>The author uses strong polemical language typical of the period, accusing the Pope of sorcery and corruption.</note>—condemned to be burned with two of his companions, in the year 1499 <note>While the text states 1499, Savonarola was historically executed on May 23, 1498.</note>. His works are:

Lenten Sermons <note>original: "Quadrageſimale"</note>.

Commentary on the penitential psalms <note>original: "Commentum ſuper pſalmos penitentiales"</note>.

Prophecies, in which he predicted many things concerning this our age and the commotion of kingdoms <note>original: "Prophætia qua multa de hoc noſtro æuo regnorúm-que commotione prædixit"</note>.

A Short Commentary: That the sect of the Muslims is devoid of all reason, etc. <note>original: "Commentatiuncula. Mahumetanorum ſectam om-ni ratione carere, &c."</note>.

A Treatise in which all the sciences are divided <note>original: "Tractatus in quo diuiduntur omnes ſcientiæ"</note>.

Meditations on the psalms, "Have mercy on me" <note>Psalm 51.</note>, and "In thee, O Lord, have I put my trust" <note>Psalm 31 or 71. Savonarola wrote these famous meditations while in prison.</note> <note>original: "Meditationes in pſalmos, miſerere mei, & in te do-mine ſperaui"</note>.

Exposition of the psalm "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel" <note>Psalm 80 (79 in the Latin Vulgate).</note> <note>original: "Expoſitio pſalmi qui regis Iſraël intende"</note>. A Compendium of all philosophy <note>original: "Compen-dium philoſophiæ totius"</note>.

A work on the division, order, and utility of all sciences <note>original: "Opus de diuiſione, ordine, vtilitate omnium ſcien-tiarum"</note>.

An Apology for poetry <note>original: "Apologeticus in poëticem"</note>.

A Compendium of logic <note>original: "Compendium logices"</note>.

# JOHANNES STOEFFLER.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Johannes Stoeffler in profile, facing right. He wears a scholar's cap and a fur-lined robe. **Johannes Stoeffler**, an astrologer, has written:
*A Work of Ephemerides from the beginning of the year of Christ 1533, for the next twenty years following.* <note>original: "Opus ephemeridum à capite anni Christi 1533, in alios viginti proximè subsequentes." Ephemerides are tables providing the positions of celestial bodies at specific intervals.</note>
Likewise, *Two books on the composition or construction of various Astrolabes.* <note>original: "variorum Astrolabiorum compositionis seu fabricæ lib. 2."</note> *Commentaries on the Sphere of Proclus Diadochus.* <note>original: "In Procli Diadochi Sphæram comment." Proclus was a Greek philosopher whose work on the "Sphere" was a standard astronomical textbook.</note> *The Great Roman Calendar.* <note>original: "Calendarium romanum magnum."</note>

His astronomical tables were printed in Germany in folio format in the year 1514.

**Henry VIII**, King of England, takes the city of Tournai; he creates terrible tragedies against his wives and the clergy. <note>This refers to the English King’s eventual break with the Catholic Church and the executions of several of his wives and high-ranking officials like Thomas More.</note>

**Odet de Foix**, Lord of Lautrec, a valiant knight and governor for the King in Milan, then colonel of the army in Italy, who took Pavia and Alessandria.

**Charles de Montpensier**, son of Gilbert, Count of the said Montpensier, and of Claire de Gonzague, daughter to the Marquis of Mantua, is <term>Constable of France</term> <note>The highest military officer of the French crown, second only to the King.</note>, and Duke of Bourbonnais and Auvergne, and Count of Forez by means of **Suzanne**, the sole heiress of the said duchies and county. # ALBRECHT DÜRER.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait medal of Albrecht Dürer in profile, facing right. He is depicted with shoulder-length hair and a beard. An inscription runs along the inner border: IMAGE OF ALBRECHT DÜRER AT THE AGE OF 56 <note>original Latin: "IMAGO ALBERTI DVRER ÆTATIS SVÆ LVI"</note>.</image-desc>

ALBRECHT Dürer <note>original: "ALBERT Durer"</note>, an excellent painter and native of Nuremberg, has left to posterity examples and patterns from his own hand which are followed by the majority of talented painters, who derive their figures from the inventions of the said Albrecht. He wrote four books on geometric institutions in German <note>original: "Aleman"</note>, which were translated into Latin by a learned man. Likewise, *On the Building of Cities, Fortresses, and Castles* <note>original Latin: "*de Vrbibus, archibus, castellisque condendis*"</note>. Likewise, *On the Symmetry of Parts in the Upright Forms of Human Bodies, and on the Variety of Figures, and the Bending of Parts and Gestures of Images* <note>original Latin: "*de Symmetria partium in rectis formis humanorum corporum, & de varietate figurarum, & flexuris partium ac gestibus imaginum*"; this refers to Dürer's influential work on human proportion</note>.

## THE INVENTION OF BANKS.

<image-desc>An oval woodcut illustration depicting the interior of a 16th-century banking house or counting room. A man, likely a banker or clerk, is seated at a large wooden desk, writing in a large ledger book. On the desk are various items including an inkwell and several bound volumes. In the background, a leaded-glass window provides light, and an open doorway reveals another room with a shelf of books and a view of a street or building outside. On the floor in the foreground sit two large tied sacks, presumably filled with coin or valuables. The entire scene is framed by an oval border above a decorative ground.</image-desc>

At the beginning of the reign of King Francis, the first of that name <note>King Francis I, reigned 1515–1547</note>, banks were introduced in the city of Lyon by foreigners: a most damaging invention, tending only toward the total ruin of men, even though these "kind" bankers say that by their means human society is maintained. But I pray you, see what a thinly veiled cover this is. One can clearly recognize their claims to be false: for if a man takes money <note>original: "deniers," a common term for coins or currency</note> from them, he finds himself ensnared in such a way that it is a great rarity if he ever recovers. And if he gives money to them to make a profit and have (as they say) "money in the bank," after they have raised great sums of money, they depart for Spain or England, Sicily or Constantinople, or elsewhere; then you must go and search for them, or else wait for news of them until their return—which will be on the Greek Calends <note>original: "Calendes Grecques"; an idiom meaning "never," as the Greek calendar had no Calends</note>, or on the feast of Our Lady of May <note>another idiomatic expression for a date that will never come</note>.
