### THE LIFE OF A GREAT
### usurer.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring ornate floral vines and a small human figure intertwined with the foliage.</image-desc>
There are two ways to become rich (says <term>Bonaventure des Périers</term><note>A popular 16th-century French author and storyteller known for his satirical and often skeptical views on society</note>): diligence and small expenses; and these are considered good before God. But there are such wicked and miserable men who take a third path and practice it, saying that one only needs to turn one's back on God for five or six years to be rich forever. They establish a "supreme good" and blessedness for the son and heir, even though the father is damned for having acquired riches by hook or by crook. I knew one man who, from being a seller of pins and a humble basket-carrier <note>A street peddler who carries his wares in a basket</note> at the beginning, later found himself opulent with more than one hundred thousand **crowns** <note>original: "eſcuz," the gold écu, a major currency in Renaissance France</note>; and this was through usury—or more accurately, theft. For usury in **Latin** <note>original: "vſure en latin" (usura)</note> is equivalent to saying "the usage of things." The method of this usurer is that when some villager, a laborer of modest means, addresses him to get money as a loan, of...

Once this man had one foot in and was entered into the master’s ledger <note>original: "papier du sire" — the creditor's book of accounts</note>, he never came out with clean breeches <note>An idiom meaning he did not escape without loss or shame; essentially, he was "taken for a ride"</note>. The laborer, having kept the money for two months and spent it down to the last penny <note>original: "maille" — a small copper coin of very low value</note>, the question then becomes one of being paid, or at least making a show of it. The term having expired, "Well," says the creditor to his debtor, "shall we have our money?" 

"Sir, I beg you to wait a little longer, if you please. You certainly have the means to do so, and you well know that you will lose nothing with me—indeed, you cannot lose anything. I have the means to pay, but please do not take me so unawares. I will see to it that you are paid." 

"My friend, I am a merchant; my funds would be put to great profit elsewhere. I wish to be paid."

"Ah, you speak very well, and I esteem you for listening to reason. Very well, go fetch such-and-such a notary." 

The notary having arrived: "Write how this man binds himself to me for the sum of one hundred pounds <note>original: "livres"</note>, as a loan, payable at my request alone." The laborer, not the best manager in the world, buys all four for sixty livres, and yet they are not worth forty. And when he wants to go fetch them, the usurer points out to him that they will give much trouble to remove and bring down, to load and drive: possibly his wife, who runs a trade in goods and merchandise on her own, will buy them. ...money, makes a deal for the said fatback with the wife, which he sells to her for forty livres paid in cash, under the promise she makes to him to make her husband wait as long as he wishes. Then, all the other obligations, debts, and accounts—put together and reduced into a single sum—a fine contract of sale of the debtor's property is written for the profit of the usurer. From these goods, the seller divests himself <note>Legally transfers ownership</note> under a grace period granted to him to be able to repurchase the estates <term>heritages: inherited lands or permanent property</term> at a certain time; meanwhile, he holds them as a tenant from the other—the true lord and owner of them through his trickery—without (oh, strange occurrence) the obligations being in any way erased or cancelled. They remain always in force, without the contract of sale making any mention of them, which is so well-locked and sealed that all the laws "concerning the rescinding of a sale" <note>original: *de rescindenda venditione* — a title in the Roman Justinian Code regarding legal ways to cancel a sale</note> in the Code, nor the Pandects <note>A massive compendium of Roman legal writings</note> have the power to give the slightest right of rescission to the poor man, who cannot even say his hat is his own: for "he owes his very soul" <note>original: *Animam debet* — a Latin expression meaning to be hopelessly in debt</note>.

And if by chance the lands and meadows sold are worth more than the price contained in the sales, when the time to be able to repurchase is near and the seller asks for an extension of his ability to redeem <note>original: "reemere" — to buy back or redeem a property</note> (seeing that one always lives in hope, and some say nothing is needed but one stroke of good luck to be rich forever), it is then necessary to give the usurer ten crowns to grant this extension of the grace of repurchase. To secure these ten crowns, they draw up a sale of the surplus value of the sold estates. Some give, for this purpose, a hood <note>original: "chapperon" — a style of headgear; here used as a formal gift to seal a deal</note> to the wife, who asks for it for her "pins" <note>original: "espingles" — the custom of "pin money," a small gift given to a wife to secure her consent to a contract involving family property</note>, or else the price it might cost. And I believe that if she has kept all the hoods her husband has reserved for her, there would be more than five hundred of them: a quite large number...

The usurer, like a sponge, sucks up and draws in all the substance of the poor, and is worse than a thief. One cuts the throat of a single man in the woods; the other kills an entire family—wife and children—before the eyes of the people, making them languish, then die of the pain of hunger. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' featuring a standing figure within an ornate rectangular frame.</image-desc>CHRISTOPHE de Longueil, a Parisian and an illustrious figure, wrote in elegant Latin an oration in praise of King Saint Louis and the French; a countless number of orations and letters; another oration in praise of Pliny; various epigrams and elegies; commentaries on civil law; a comparison of civil law to the art of war; a history of herbs; commentaries on Pliny; and five orations in praise of the city of Rome. > Oh traveler, here beneath lies Longueil;
> What holds you back from deep mourning,
> When you hear that his life is finished?
> Have you not yet heard his fame
> Throughout the lands, which his remarkable renown
> Goes proclaiming with voice, trumpet, and clarion?

## JOHANNES OECOLAMPADIUS.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait of Johannes Oecolampadius shown in profile facing right. He has a long, flowing beard and wears a soft cap and a fur-collared robe. The circular border contains the inscription: JOHANNES OECOLAMPADIUS <note>original: "IOANNES OECOLAMPADIVS." The name is a "classicized" humanist version of his German birth name, Hussgen or Heussgen, meaning "house lamp."</note>.</image-desc>

JOHANNES Oecolampadius, a German and a follower of Luther, wrote several treatises, orations, sermons, and commentaries which have been printed in Basel and elsewhere. He translated from Greek into Latin those works of Saint John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father renowned for his preaching; his name means "golden-mouthed."</note> contained in the fifth volume of the Froben edition <note>Hieronymus Froben was a prominent printer in Basel who specialized in humanist and reformation texts.</note>; the text of Genesis according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament.</note>; Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and influential biblical commentator.</note> on the four gospels; several sermons of Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Great Cappadocians."</note>, and other minor works. He also brought to light several other books in the German vernacular. He died at the age of 39 <note>The text says 39, but Oecolampadius was actually 49 years old (1482–1531) when he passed away.</note>, a little after the death of Zwingli <note>Huldrych Zwingli, the primary leader of the Reformation in Switzerland, who died in battle shortly before Oecolampadius.</note>, his great friend, in the year 1531.

This is Erasmus, a native of Rotterdam, whose assiduity in study and the infinite number of books he published under his name make him admirable and worthy of being called a great orator and philosopher, just like Cicero. These works were partly printed by Froben <note>Johann Froben was a famous printer in Basel and a close friend of Erasmus.</note> in ten large folio volumes, and cost 26 livres tournois in blank <note>Books were often sold "in blank," meaning as unbound sheets of paper, allowing the buyer to commission their own binding.</note>. He died in Basel shortly after departing from Freiburg, at the age of seventy.

->Epitaph for Erasmus by George Buchanan <note>A Scottish historian and humanist scholar.</note>.<-
> *The great Erasmus, whom the great world echoes,* <note>original: "Ingens ingentem quem personat orbis Erasmus"</note>
> *This painted image brings you but half of him.*
> *But why not the whole? Cease your wondering, reader,*
> *For the whole earth itself cannot contain the entire man.*

<image-desc>Circular woodcut portrait of the printer Sebastian Gryphius shown in profile facing right. He has a beard and is wearing a flat cap and a fur-trimmed robe. The portrait is encircled by a border with the Latin inscription: SEBASTIANO GRYPHIO GERMANO ANNO AETATIS SVAE LVIII.</image-desc>

Sebastian Gryphius, a native of Reutlingen in Swabia, near Augsburg <note>original: "Auguste." This refers to the city of Augsburg, Germany.</note>, restored the art of printing in Lyon. This art, which was previously corrupted, he returned to its full integrity and embellished it.

->*Sebastian Gryphius,*<-
->*A German, and a Printer,*<-
->*Skilled in three languages and a most excellent man,*<-
->*Died at the peak of his years.*<- <note>original Latin: "Sebastianus Gryphius / Germanus, ac Typographus / Tri linguis & vir optimus / Climace Tulli mortuus." The reference to "Climace" likely alludes to his death at age 63, often called the "grand climacteric" in early modern thought.</note>

The poets of his time called him the excellent Tryphon <note>Tryphon was a famous bookseller in Ancient Rome mentioned by the poet Martial; the comparison highlights Gryphius's status as a premier publisher of classical texts.</note> of our age, of whom Martial makes mention. He was a refuge for learned people, diligent and curious in searching everywhere for good books that had been lost (or at least gone astray) through the ravages of time, so that once found, he might restore them and allow posterity to enjoy such a rare treasure. His son, Lord Antoine Gryphius, still has a good portion of these to print; and just as his father spared no expense to recover them and then faithfully bring them to light, so too is the son not stingy with his labor or his wealth in making them public. He died in the year 1556 at the age of 63.

# TRAGIC HISTORY OF A
->*Sicilian who preferred to die rather than be*<-
->*in the captivity of the Turk.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E within a square border, decorated with foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

IN the year 1551, Sultan Suleiman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent, who reigned from 1520 to 1566.</note>, Emperor of the Turks, greatly aggrieved by the loss of his city of Africa <note>Referring to the city of Mahdia in Tunisia, which was often called "Africa" in 16th-century geography.</note> and the castle of Szolnok <note>A fortress in Hungary.</note> recently taken from him by the Emperor Charles V and Ferdinand, King of the Romans, his brother, gathered a large and powerful army and many vessels and galleys at sea. This army was led by two of his Pashas, Dragut <note>Turgut Reis, a famous Ottoman admiral and privateer.</note> and Sinan <note>The text reads "Sala," likely referring to Sinan Pasha, who commanded the Ottoman fleet.</note>, as commanders and chiefs, in order to seek revenge by this means and, if possible, invade some lands belonging to the Christians and the Emperor. To execute this, they began to besiege Malta, and took Tripoli and the Isle of Gozo as the opening move of the game. The captains who were in Gozo held firm and endured the siege for several days, making every defense possible for them. But having lost hope of being rescued or of being able to resist such a great force, they concluded together to surrender themselves to the discretion and mercy of the enemy, which they did afterward. During this deliberation, after they had parleyed and surrendered, as the enemy was entering, there was a Sicilian man married to an honest woman of the place, having two daughters ready to be married, who were no less beautiful than they were virtuous. This man was not ignorant of the cruelties and execrable acts which these infidels are accustomed to practice toward Christian women and the men they take as slaves, for he himself had been in their hands for a period of

<header>PROSOPOGRAPHY</header>
<sig>xib</sig>

ten years, and during that time had well perceived their way of living <note>The text likely refers to a previous period of enslavement the man had already endured.</note>, he resolved to die rather than find himself again in foreign hands in captivity, and what is worse, to see the virginity of his daughters and the chastity of his wife defiled. For although chastity is the fortress of beauty, yet the enemies of the faith take by force what they cannot have by goodwill.

The Sicilian, therefore, being troubled in his mind and overcome by this fear, went to his house immediately after the decision that the leaders had made to surrender: where he had his two daughters come before him. "My daughters," (he said to them) "since fortune, or rather our misfortune, wills that we be stripped of our liberty, and that your honor—which you have kept until now—be ravished by these Turkish dogs, I want to know if you will prefer life to honor, or if you would rather leave it as prey than die with it. What I say to you, my children, is to make you certain that I, your mother, and you must today leave this world to go to the other: assuring you that if you go first, I will keep you company and follow you soon, preferring much more to save myself from servitude and deliver my kin from it, than to remain living as a captive."

The young girls, at the words of their sad father, were suddenly moved, and trembled with fear of death—as everyone flees the final period of life as much as they can, especially young people—and without answering a single word, they began to weep so hotly that a still <note>original: "alembic"; a chemical apparatus used for distilling liquids, here used as a metaphor for the flow of tears.</note> never distilled better than their eyes yielded tears. Seeing this, the Sicilian said, "No, no, leave these tears, and do not worry about dying, seeing that the death of men should not be fled, but rather desi[red]..."

[...lost their liberty] as a captive in Rome, bound and shackled, yet began to laugh at the gates of the prisons. The Athenians were once servants to the kings of Macedon; the city of Carthage was subject first to the Romans and later to the Vandals; this very Rome, mistress of the world, was subject to the Goths; and the "New Rome," which is now Constantinople, belongs to the Turk who makes his residence there.

Therefore, that which an excellent people and great kings have endured, we can with even greater reason suffer, according to the condition of human life which is subject to a thousand misfortunes. For why should a private person be angry at being submitted to the same laws to which emperors and kings are subjected? One must endure to endure <note>original: "Il faut endurer pour durer" — a French wordplay suggesting that one must suffer or tolerate hardship in order to last or survive</note>: for in enduring, we do battle against Fortune, who is very often defeated. Fire tests gold, the storm tests the master of the ship, and the difficulties of war demonstrate the strength of the colonel; furthermore, there is nothing so bitter that a stout heart cannot make it ripen through endurance. Even though we may be captives, we must have hope of regaining our liberty, and meanwhile take consolation in the memory of things past, in the hope of things to come, in letters, in study, and in the fact that Fortune is an inconstant game that comes and goes; for the spirit is always free, and its riches cannot be taken away.

Marcantonio Trevisan, Francesco Venier, Lorenzo Priuli, and Girolamo Priuli govern the Republic of Venice one after the other. <note>These were successive Doges of Venice serving between 1553 and 1567.</note>

War of the Protestants in Germany.

**PAUL IV**, Pope, previously the Theatine Cardinal. <note>Giovanni Pietro Carafa, who co-founded the Theatine Order before becoming Pope in 1555.</note>

Great floods in Nîmes, in Florence, and in Sicily.

At the beginning of his reign, several gentlemen and others assembled in arms near the town of Amboise, where he was in the company of the Cardinal of Lorraine, Monsieur de Guise, and other princes. They claimed to act for the "public good," seeking to drive out certain foreigners <note>This refers to the House of Guise, whom the conspirators viewed as foreign usurpers from Lorraine.</note> whom they alleged were usurpers of the kingdom's government and captors of the persons of the King, the Queen, and the King's brothers. # OF THE NAME OF THE HUGUE-
## *nots derived from Jan Hus.*

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap 'L' within a square border, featuring a classical figure (possibly a child or putto) leaning against an urn amidst foliage.</image-desc>

The name of Huguenous or Huguenots took its beginning during the reign of King Francis II, in the year 1560, in the city of Tours (according to the account of some) because of the "Gate of King Hugo" <note>Original: *porte du roy Huguon*. King Hugo was a legendary figure in Tours folklore, said to haunt the city at night.</note>, one of the gates of the said city, near which those of the so-called reformed religion withdrew to perform their sermons and prayers. For this reason they were called Huguenots, a word that was immediately adopted by those who followed the court, and afterwards published everywhere.

But there is another reason why they were so named. It is that a preacher in Paris said in his sermon that those of the said religion were "true monkeys of Jan Hus" <note>Original: *vrays guenons de Iean Hus*. Jan Hus was a Czech reformer burned at the stake in 1415; his followers were the Hussites.</note>, the heretic: for just as a guenon <term>guenon</term> <note>A term for a long-tailed monkey, often used in this period to mock someone as a "mindless imitator."</note> or ape tries to counterfeit and imitate everything it sees being done, so these people are imitators of Jan Hus, following his doctrine in everything. This was immediately imprinted on the brains of some great lords, who named these new religious followers "Huguenots"—that is to say, by reversing the words, "Hus’s monkeys" <note>Original: *guenõs d’Hus*. The author is proposing a folk etymology where "Huguenot" is a scrambled version of "Guenon d'Hus."</note>, a name composed just as the Hussites were named from Hus, meaning followers of Hus. For after Jan Hus was burned, some of his acquaintances joined his sect. Thus, in our time, the common people began to pass the name from hand to hand to name such so-called reformers as Huguenots and Huguenauds, according to the accent of various places in France. The Italians afterwards called them *Hugonotti*, a word of derision in which they take no pleasure, although the Italians think it is a title of honor that they them-

<page-num>514</page-num>
<header>PROSOPOGRAPHY</header>

<note>A "prosopography" is a study of a group of people based on their common characteristics, in this case, the military and political leaders of the French Wars of Religion.</note>

Lyon, Rouen, Orléans, Poitiers, Bourges, and several others are occupied by those of the so-called <note>Original: *prétendue*, a standard Catholic descriptor for the Reformed faith at the time.</note> religion called Huguenots, whose principal leaders are the Prince of Condé, the Prince of Porcien, the Admiral <note>Gaspard de Coligny, Admiral of France and a major leader of the Huguenots.</note>, the Lords d’Andelot, Montgomery, La Rochefoucauld, Genlis, d’Acier, Mouy, and several others aided and supported by the Germans <note>Referring to the German mercenary *reitres* and Landsknechts hired by the Protestant side.</note>: all of whom he <note>Likely referring to the King, Charles IX, or his brother the Duke of Anjou, as the figurehead of the royalist victories.</note> overcame in four battles fought in various places and at various times. This is what I touched upon in my *Homonyms*:

> -> They thought they had the upper hand over you; <-
> -> Four times, and just as many they found themselves deceived. <-
> -> Blind Fortune is the mistress of victories: <-
> -> Followed by chance, she never shows herself consistently. <-
> -> But your brave soldiers, not seized by a vain heart, <-
> -> Along with your rightful cause, have rendered you the victor. <-

The first battle was fought near Dreux <note>The Battle of Dreux, 1562.</note>, in which the Prince of Condé was taken prisoner, and Marshal Saint André was killed in cold blood. The second was near Saint-Denis in France <note>The Battle of Saint-Denis, 1567.</note>, and in it was killed Anne de Montmorency, Constable <term>Constable</term> <note>The *Connétable de France* was the highest military officer in the French kingdom, second only to the King.</note>, at the age of 80. The third was between Cognac and Châteauneuf <note>Known as the Battle of Jarnac, March 1569.</note>, where Henry, Duke of Anjou, of Bourbonnais and Auvergne, Count of Forez and Montfort, brother of the King and his Lieutenant General <note>The future King Henry III.</note>, put to flight all the cavalry of the Prince of Condé. The Prince, his horse having been killed and fallen upon him, was taken by the Lords of Saint Jean and Argences, French gentlemen; he was afterwards recognized by a man named Montesquiou, who killed him from behind with a pistol shot to the head, to the great regret and displeasure of the said two French gentlemen, who had promised to save his life. Two hundred men on the side of the said Prince of Condé were slain in this encounter. The fourth was at Moncontour in

Poitou: and there the said Lord Duke of Anjou <note>The future King Henri III, who served as Lieutenant-General of the kingdom and won significant victories at Jarnac and Moncontour in 1569.</note> cut to pieces the entire enemy infantry, numbering thirteen thousand and more, with their cavalry put to flight. And in all these four battles the field always remained to the King: in which can be seen a divine favor toward him, as in infinite other encounters in the lands of Poitou, Île-de-France, Guyenne, Languedoc, Provence, Auvergne, Forez, and elsewhere, as well as sieges of cities, assaults, defenses of fortresses, and other military actions carried out in this kingdom over the space of ten years, during which the French people have endured great calamities and afflictions, as I sang in my *Homonyms* <note>Original: *Omonimes*. This refers to a work by the author, likely Antoine Du Verdier, who wrote "Les Omonimes" in 1572.</note> to ensure our descendants are certain of it:

> A single beginning of the troubles in France
> Was suddenly (I know not how) sowing
> So many bitter cruelties that no one was safe near
> Those holding another party or wishing to approach:
> The husband against the wife, brothers against their kin
> Banded together, they dealt each other many assaults and dangers.
> Because of the sedition in this time, did you see a father
> Who did not receive insults from his rebellious sons?
> In short, since the year fifteen hundred and sixty-two <note>The year the First War of Religion began following the Massacre of Vassy.</note>
> There is no living man who does not feel their weight.
> I had made it my project to recite in ten verses
> The abuses, the misfortunes, the diverse affairs
> Which in these troubles are overturned beneath France,
> By which the people are reduced to extreme suffering:
> And there is none among the Estates <note>Refers to the "Three Estates" of French society: the Clergy, the Nobility, and the Commoners.</note> who does not go about saying
> That it is too much suffering to have suffered for ten years.

During these ten years a good number of valiant men, captains, and great lords died on both one side and the other: the King of Navarre <note>Antoine de Bourbon, father of the future Henri IV, who died from wounds sustained during the siege of Rouen while fighting for the Royalist/Catholic side.</note> at the siege of

Troubles and commotions in Flanders regarding the matter of religion. He has written (and still continues to do so) several books of no less labor than erudition and elegance, which are cherished and received as a holy oracle throughout all Europe. ->Great earthquake at Ferrara.<-

<margin>1572</margin>
**GREGORY XIII,** Pope, previously named Ugo, Cardinal *Buoncompagni*, a Bolognese gentleman, was first a lecturer in law at Bologna, then an auditor of the Rota <note>The Roman Rota is the highest appellate tribunal of the Catholic Church.</note>, and subsequently bishop and referendary <note>A high-ranking administrative official in the Papal court.</note> during the time of Pius IV, having been his intimate friend when the said Pius was called Cardinal Medici. Since then, Pius V gave him the [cardinal's] hat, saying at the time: "I am not making a cardinal, but a pope." This came to pass, as he was elected on the occasion that it is said he was one of the principal authors of the Holy League against the Turks, and that he had persuaded Pope Pius V of it and put it in his mind. In his nature and morals, he is severe, but otherwise straightforward and frank.

Jeanne d’Albret, Queen of Navarre, died in Paris in the month of June 1572, while the marriage of the Prince her son <note>The future King Henry IV of France.</note> to Madame Marguerite, sister of the King of France, was being negotiated.

# SONNET BY FRANÇOIS
## d’Amboise, Parisian, to Antoine du Verdier,
## a gentleman of Forez,
## learned poet.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'V' depicting a seated male figure under a tree in a landscape, possibly representing a poet or Apollo.</image-desc>
Such greenness, my learned du **VERDIER**, <note>The author plays on the name "Verdier," which sounds like "verdure" (greenness), symbolizing youth, vigor, and eternal life in poetry.</note>
Is found in your beautiful field, that the same greenery
Is not more green and gay, even though nature
Has prodigally displayed its springtime treasure.
Your green gaiety deserves that a laurel
Gird your learned brow with a triple binding:
**Phœbus** <note>The Greek god Apollo, the patron of poets.</note> already weaves the texture of your hat,
Which for your brave verses will be the green reward.
Meanwhile, my **VERDIER**, while for your reward
You await the payment that our France owes you,
Be content with the favors of the **Delphic prince**: <note>Another reference to Apollo, whose oracle was at Delphi.</note>
For he will always cause your green renown
To bloom in its greenness, without being consumed
By the cold, flower-stripping **Scythian** wind. <note>original: "vent Scitonien"; referring to the Scythians of the far north, often used to represent bitter, freezing winds.</note>

->Time for the Muses is timeless.<- <note>original Latin: "Muſis ſine tempore tempus."</note>

---

## SONNET.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring intricate foliate and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
If the blind writer <note>Homer, the legendary Greek epic poet, traditionally described as blind.</note>, whom **Salamis** <note>One of the cities that claimed to be Homer's birthplace.</note> claims,
For having sung aloud of furious **Achilles**'
Invincible prowess and generous heart,
Deserves to be highly praised forever:
If that historian who was born in **Padua** <note>Titus Livius, known as Livy, the famous Roman historian.</note>,
For having written well of the warlike Romans,
And the courageous acts of the Carthaginians,
Is endowed with great and famous praise for his labor:
One would do you great wrong, learned **French Livy**, <note>A title of high honor bestowed upon Du Verdier by the poet.</note>
If for this labor of yours you did not have as a reward,
Even after a thousand years, wandering praise.
For the first of the two sang learnedly only of the Greeks,
And the other sang learnedly of the Romans:
But you are the herald of the entire world.

->LOYS DU PUI OF FOREZ.<-

<vocab>François d’Amboise, Antoine du Verdier, Loys du Pui, sonnet, Phœbus, Achilles, Salamis, Padua, French-Livy, poetry, 16th century, French literature</vocab>

<summary>This page contains two commendatory sonnets praising Antoine du Verdier for his literary and historical contributions. The poets use classical metaphors, comparing Du Verdier to Homer and Livy, and suggesting his work provides him with eternal "greenery" or fame.</summary>
<keywords>Antoine du Verdier, François d’Amboise, Loys du Pui, sonnets, Homer, Livy, Phœbus Apollo, 16th-century French poetry, commendatory verses</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as an errata and a notice to the reader, appearing at the end of the volume (as indicated by the signature Y iiii). It follows the laudatory sonnets and provides corrections for typographical errors found throughout the work.</meta>

# NOTICE
## TO THE READER

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'L' featuring an ornate rectangular border with floral scrollwork. Inside the letter, a small figure, possibly a putto or a youth, is depicted standing amidst the foliage.</image-desc>

The **Author** having left the description of **Licinius Murena** <note>A Roman consul famous for his wealth and his elaborate salt-water fish ponds; his name "Murena" refers to the moray eel.</note> blank in his manuscript, the printer, being ready to print the sheet where the said figure was contained, inserted the following description without notifying the author: who had only left it incomplete for the purpose of seeking more carefully at leisure the life of the said L. Murena, and to discourse upon the diversity, nature, and quality of pond fish.

---

## Errors occurring in the printing.

On page 5 line 18 "than malice," read, "than **your** malice." p. 25 "Claudine," read, "**Claudia**." p. 39 "beginning of nobility," these words are misplaced in this location, and must be moved after the word **Nineveh**, in the heading, and in the same typeface: For this nobility began at **Ninus** <note>The mythical founder of Nineveh; the author is drawing a linguistic and historical link between the city and the rise of aristocratic power.</note>. Wherefore it must be known that in the first age everyone was equal without any difference: but since then malice has so grown in the world, that whoever could usurp more, took more dominance, and the strong subjugated the weak, and made their own what was common: thus the greatest were esteemed the most noble. And in this regard, **Innocent** <note>Likely referring to Pope Innocent III (c. 1160–1216), who wrote extensively on the human condition.</note> says: "Nature produced us free, but fortune made us slaves." <note>original Latin: "Natura nos liberos genuit: sed fortuna nos fecit servos."</note> **Nimrod** <note>A biblical figure described as a "mighty hunter," traditionally credited with building the Tower of Babel and being the first king after the Great Flood.</note> was the first who took the form of reigning, making people believe that if the flood returned once more, they could save themselves in his **Tower of Babel**: and he did not let it seem that he did it for any mastery over them. But **Belus** <note>In ancient historiography, Belus was often cited as the father of Ninus and an early king of Babylon.</note> did not act thus. And furthermore **Ninus**, son of Belus, did worse: for he began to reign with great rigor and violence, so that from him came the domination of lords by way of servitude and subjection. p. 51 line 21 "the nine," read, "the three." p. 105 "carmento" read "**Carmenta**" <note>An ancient Roman goddess of prophecy and the inventor of the Latin alphabet.</note>. p. 129 last line "40 years," read, "2 years." p. 106 "Centinian," read, "**Centiman**," which **Cicero** in the 3rd book of *Offices* calls **Centimalus** <note>Referring to Marcus Marius Gratidianus, whose name is sometimes corrupted to 'Centimalus' in early editions of Cicero's "De Officiis."</note>. p. 19 line 9 "**Ses**" [His], read, "**ces**" [these]. p. 201 "**Curfius**," read, "**Curius**" <note>Manius Curius Dentatus, a Roman <meta>This page serves as an "errata" and "advertisement" section, common in early modern printing, where the author corrects mistakes made during the production of the book. It specifically addresses a misunderstanding regarding the Roman figure Licinius Murena.</meta>

-># NOTICE TO THE READER.<-

<note>The text on this page is heavily affected by ink bleed-through from the reverse side, making parts of the errata list very difficult to transcribe with certainty.</note>

The AUTHOR had left the description of <term>Licinius Murena</term> <note>Lucius Licinius Murena was a Roman statesman famous for his wealth and his elaborate saltwater fish ponds, particularly for breeding moray eels (murenae)</note> blank in his manuscript; the printer, being ready to print the sheet containing the aforementioned figure, placed the description below it without informing the Author. The Author has only now filled it in for the purpose of researching the life of the said L. Murena more carefully, and to uncover the full diversity, nature, and quality of pond fish.

---
